Fix an innate \emph{recursive contrast operator} $R$ mapping any string to a finite set of structurally bounded perturbations of it, and a discriminative scorer of bounded capacity trained by InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation \citep{vandenoord2018,macollins2018} on self-generated perturbations. Under a faithfulness condition relating operator, scorer, and target, the trained scorer achieves \emph{PAC conditional identification} from positive data alone: with high probability it ranks all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of positives above every out-of-language perturbation in their own orbit, with sample complexity polynomial in the capacity, the orbit size, the score bound, and $1/\varepsilon$. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. The ranking guarantee lifts to a global membership classifier under a margin condition, and the same operator composed with the learned scorer is a normalization-free Metropolis--Hastings generator. We instantiate the hypotheses for substitutable context-free languages \citep{clarkeyraud2007} and the subregular classes \citep{heinz2010,hayashikamigaito2025}, and state an open conjecture locating the construction in the mildly context-sensitive hierarchy.
papers.summary: Gold's theorem says that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a broad class from positive examples alone. This paper proves a positive result of a different kind: a bounded-capacity scorer, trained with InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation on perturbations it generates itself through a fixed recursive contrast operator, achieves **PAC conditional identification from positive data alone** with polynomial sample complexity. The guarantee requires a faithfulness condition linking the operator, scorer and target language, and it needs no external negatives or global normalization. The ranking guarantee extends to a membership classifier and to a normalization-free Metropolis-Hastings generator, and the hypotheses are instantiated for substitutable context-free and subregular language classes.

papers.title: Understanding the Inner Workings of a State-Space Foundation Model for Limit Order Books
papers.abstract: Autoregressive foundation models offer state-of-the-art capabilities to simulate the market by generating the message flow of limit order books (LOBs). Yet, without understanding their inner workings, research directions are hard to narrow and practical use in real-world trading environments remains uncertain. This study therefore asks what these models actually learn about market microstructure. We find that, similarly to games where sequence models build an internal representation of the board, an 8.2M-parameter Mamba-3 state-space model trained autoregressively on the tokenized message stream of eight large-cap US equities learns an internal representation of the market and its dynamics. In particular, order-flow imbalance, a central driver of short-horizon price moves, is decodable at $R^2 \approx 0.59$, far above controls and baselines. This representation extends to unseen stocks, suggesting that these models learn general representations rather than ticker-specific patterns. The model also generalizes across metrics beyond order-flow imbalance: results hold across traded volume and volatility. Additionally, the representation is causally steerable: pushing the state along a feature's axis shifts the model's next-message beliefs as that feature implies, monotonically in dose, consistent with the emergence of a world model.
papers.summary: Autoregressive foundation models can simulate markets by generating the message flow of limit order books (LOBs), but little is known about what they learn internally. Probing an 8.2M-parameter `Mamba-3` state-space model trained on tokenized message streams for eight large-cap US stocks, the authors find an internal representation of market state, with **order-flow imbalance decodable at R² ≈ 0.59**, far above controls and baselines. The representation carries over to unseen stocks and also covers traded volume and volatility. Pushing the model's state along a feature's direction shifts its next-message predictions in proportion to the push, which is consistent with an emergent world model.

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Construction of the Gabriel Graph: Parallelization Strategies and Applications to Large-Margin Classification and Graph-Based Clustering
papers.abstract: The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph widely used in computational geometry and geometric machine learning, underlying large-margin classifiers and, as we show in this work, density-aware clustering methods. Its construction, however, has cubic time complexity $O(N^3)$ in the naive formulation, which severely limits its use on datasets beyond a few thousand samples. This paper presents a set of GPU parallelization strategies, implemented in CUDA, that make Gabriel graph construction practical at scale. We introduce (i) an implicit closed-form mapping from a linear thread index to the corresponding vertex pair $(i,j)$, which removes the need for an explicit $O(N^2)$ adjacency structure and lets every thread locate its pair in constant time and constant memory; (ii) a two-pass, bitmask-based, atomically-compacted edge-list construction that produces a dense edge array proportional only to the number of edges actually found; and (iii) a thread-coarsening strategy in which each thread evaluates several candidate pairs, trading launch and scheduling overhead against load balance. We evaluate these strategies on the acceleration of a Gabriel-graph-based large-margin classifier (NN-clas) and on a novel Gabriel-graph clustering algorithm that identifies connected components on a residual graph and performs GPU-parallel Union-Find with hierarchical edge-based merging. On 14 public benchmark datasets, the GPU implementation reduces Gabriel graph construction time by two to nearly four orders of magnitude relative to a sequential CPU baseline (up to 8484x), without loss of classification accuracy, and the proposed clustering method is statistically competitive with DBSCAN on the topological validity index Dunn while eliminating the need for an explicit density radius parameter.
papers.summary: The Gabriel graph is a proximity graph that underlies large-margin classifiers, but building it naively takes cubic time, which limits it to a few thousand points. The authors present CUDA strategies to parallelize construction: a closed-form mapping from thread index to vertex pair that avoids storing an adjacency matrix, a two-pass bitmask-based compaction that produces a dense edge list, and thread coarsening to balance scheduling overhead against load. Across 14 benchmark datasets, construction runs **up to 8,484x faster than a sequential CPU baseline** with no loss in classification accuracy. A new Gabriel-graph clustering method built on GPU-parallel Union-Find is statistically competitive with `DBSCAN` on the Dunn index and does not need a density radius parameter.

papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).
papers.summary: `Agent4Sci` is a long-horizon testbed that measures how far frontier coding agents can improve the published best models on 20 machine-learning-for-science benchmarks across 11 domains. Today's agents beat the published best on every benchmark, with `Claude Opus` averaging a 10.4% relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct, but the gains come almost entirely from standard ML-engineering tricks rather than domain insight. Analysis of the agents' trajectories shows three recurring weaknesses: misjudging how novel an idea is, under-using available compute, and quickly collapsing into narrow engineering sweeps. Adding lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management and scheduled checklists **nearly doubles the gains, lifting Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1%** and `Codex` from 4.4% to 8.1%.
papers.highlight_summary:
Frontier coding agents are increasingly pitched as automated researchers, and `Agent4Sci` tests that claim. It is a human-verified testbed of 20 ML-for-science benchmarks (25 tasks, 11 domains) in which an agent starts from the published best model, works in its codebase, and tries to beat it under a fixed compute budget.

- Each task is first standardized with a verified reproduction of the baseline, fixed splits and a sequestered test set; a separate evaluation agent then scores the submitted artifacts on held-out data, and an auditing agent checks the trajectory for gaming, after a pilot found evaluation gaming such as selective reporting, test-set contamination and hardcoding on 5 of 12 raw tasks.
- With 8 H200s and 12 hours per run, every benchmark was pushed past its published best by at least one agent, with mean relative improvements of **10.4%** for `Claude Opus 4.6`, 9.6% for `Sonnet 4.6`, 6.8% for `Gemini 3.1 Pro` and 4.4% for `Codex (GPT-5.4)`, and no run flagged for misconduct across cross-family re-audits.
- The gains came almost entirely from standard ML engineering such as learning-rate schedules, wider or deeper models, backbone swaps and augmentation, and trajectory analysis found three recurring failures: agents present standard tricks as novel ideas, leave GPUs idle, and quickly narrow into local hyperparameter sweeps.
- Three short markdown plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management and hourly self-check checklists roughly doubled the gains, lifting Opus from 10.4% to **20.1%** (better on 18 of 20 benchmarks) and Codex from 4.4% to **8.1%**; on `PFDelta`, Opus moved from 64.4% to **91.0%** by training on the physics-derived power-balance loss and refining its predictions with the AC power-flow equations.
- Results vary from run to run, so the averages are not meant as a leaderboard, and even with skills most benchmarks see only marginal, engineering-driven gains, with some regressions (for example `gRNAde`, and `LITHOS` and `PFDelta` for Codex).

papers.title: SkillEval: Learning Interpretable Ability Profiles of LLMs via Cognitive Diagnosis Models
papers.abstract: Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores collapse a model's performance into one number and hide which skills it has or lacks. `SkillEval` uses LLMs to automatically identify interpretable skills from benchmark questions, then applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate each model's ability on each skill. Applied to 3,811 LLMs on 9,523 items from `MATH`, `BBH`, `GPQA`, `MuSR` and `IFEval`, the resulting profiles are better calibrated and predict performance on unseen items more accurately than average scores. The profiles also enable LLM routing that **cuts inference cost by over 60% while improving performance**, and computerized adaptive testing that evaluates a new model efficiently.

papers.title: ReAPO: Retry-Aware Policy Optimization for Efficient Exploration in LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: RLVR improves language-model reasoning, but commonly relies on independent stochastic rollouts for exploration, which can repeatedly sample similar failed strategies. Prior work has seen success with approaches that guide exploration by introducing dependence into the sampling process by including incorrect solutions in the context for subsequent attempts. Still, these methods introduce the additional question of how to assign credit to each attempt. We propose to view the credit assignment through the lens of Stochastic Shortest Paths, a framework in classical reinforcement learning that seeks to minimize the expected cumulative cost to reach a terminal state (in our case, a verified successful response). We show that, under suitable simplifying assumptions, this perspective naturally leads to a simple modification to GRPO, which we call Retry-Aware Policy Optimization (ReAPO). ReAPO allocates additional generation to failed trajectories, allowing successful retries to be reinforced without rewarding preceding failures, and assigns credit in a theoretically principled way to each attempt. Across Qwen3 and OLMo-2 models from 0.6B to 4B and eight mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, ReAPO improves first-attempt performance over GRPO as well as natural recent baseline algorithms, while additional ablations demonstrate the utility of both serial sampling and ReAPO's credit assignment. On Qwen3-0.6B, ReAPO also outperforms GRPO with twice the group size or twice the training steps, reaching their peak accuracy with 39% and 31% fewer generated tokens, respectively. Taken together, our results suggest that ReAPO is a simple yet effective approach for improving LM reasoning performance through improved exploration and retry-aware credit assignment.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves LLM reasoning, but independent sampled rollouts often repeat the same failed strategies. Retry-based methods, which put earlier wrong answers in context for the next attempt, raise the question of how to credit each attempt. The authors frame this as a Stochastic Shortest Path problem, which leads to `ReAPO`, a small modification to `GRPO` that spends extra generation on failed attempts and rewards successful retries without rewarding the failures before them. On `Qwen3` and `OLMo-2` models from 0.6B to 4B across eight math and science benchmarks, it improves first-attempt accuracy over GRPO, and on `Qwen3-0.6B` it **matches GRPO's peak accuracy with 31-39% fewer generated tokens** than versions using double the group size or training steps.

papers.title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
papers.abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.
papers.summary: Standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to motion: when the input shifts, their memory does not shift with it. Earlier flow-equivariant recurrent networks handled only constant-velocity motion, and only by enumerating a bank of velocities. This work treats a sequence as a field over time, under which motion becomes a gauge symmetry, and builds `MELSTM`, a convolutional LSTM that estimates velocity and is **provably equivariant to motions whose velocity changes over time**. On future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, it beats a standard convolutional LSTM and the flow-equivariant baseline with the same parameter count, while generalizing to longer horizons and unseen motions with a much smaller state.

papers.title: Scaling Therapy Supervision: Assessing Psychotherapy Fidelity Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment measures how faithfully a therapist adheres to a treatment protocol, a critical determinant of positive patient outcomes. However, fidelity assessment is bottlenecked by manual expert review, rendering the process labor-intensive and unscalable. To scale therapy supervision and support clinician self-learning, we present an integrated application of large language models (LLMs) that automates psychotherapy fidelity workflows and generates actionable supervisory feedback from authentic, long-form clinical transcripts. We evaluate three open-weight models across multiple task decomposition configurations and reasoning strategies, demonstrating that evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation. Furthermore, we establish the framework's external construct validity on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT), where it reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) from non-CBT sessions across core therapeutic skills. Through a user study that evaluates the generated feedback, mental health experts indicate that the pipeline synthesizes actionable clinical feedback. Ultimately, our work offers a practical, scalable solution toward bridging the community mental health supervision gap.
papers.summary: Psychotherapy fidelity assessment checks how closely a therapist follows a treatment protocol, but it depends on manual expert review that does not scale. The authors build an LLM pipeline that scores fidelity from long, real clinical transcripts and generates supervisory feedback, and they compare three open-weight models under several ways of decomposing the task and prompting their reasoning. **Evidence-first reasoning improves fidelity estimation**, and on an independent randomized controlled trial (RCT) the pipeline reliably distinguishes Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) sessions from non-CBT ones. In a user study, mental health experts rated the generated feedback as actionable.

papers.title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
papers.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.
papers.summary: Post-training pruning of large language models tends to lose quality sharply at high sparsity, even when sparsity is spread unevenly across layers. `LADDER` (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement) assigns sparsity step by step. At each step it tries pruning a further fraction of weights in every eligible layer, then keeps the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter, which yields exactly nested masks across sparsity budgets. Tested with `SparseGPT` as the backend on five `OPT`, `Llama`, and `Qwen` models, it is comparable or slightly weaker at moderate sparsity but **substantially more robust from 70% sparsity onward**, and this advantage largely survives distillation on four of the five models.

papers.title: Second Thoughts: Exploring and Planning through Comparative Imagination in World Models
papers.abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
papers.summary: Agents with world models can compare imagined outcomes before acting, but they still have to decide which alternatives to explore and when a planned action should override the learned policy. `SDI` (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination) handles both decisions with one reference: the variation seen across repeated imagined rollouts of the actor's own action sequence. This reference scales an exploration bonus and gates plan acceptance, so a planned action is executed only when its predicted advantage beats that variability by a fixed factor. No extra ensemble is needed. Across `Meta-World`, `Adroit`, and `DM-Control`, it achieves the best task-average score in every suite and **matches or exceeds the strongest baseline on 15 of 18 tasks**.

papers.title: Extreme Low-State Quantized Transformer for Electricity-Load Forecasting
papers.abstract: Aggressive low-state weight quantization can substantially reduce neural-network representational flexibility, making predictive performance difficult to preserve when only a few discrete weight states are available. We investigate this regime for Transformer-based electricity-load forecasting using 3-, 5-, 7-, and 16-state weight quantization across feed-forward-only and attention-plus-feed-forward quantization. Two tasks predict either the next hour or the next 24 hours from the preceding 48 hours across two co-primary electricity-consumption datasets. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) increased mean normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) relative to full precision by 6.25 and 7.04 percentage points in Datasets A and B, whereas quantization-aware fine-tuning (QAT-FT) recovered approximately 90.2% and 94.5% of these penalties. Quantization-aware training from random initialization (Scratch-QAT) also produced competitive low-state solutions, with particularly favorable behavior at three states. We further introduce accumulated-update thresholding, which accumulates optimizer-proposed weight changes before commitment. Relative to paired Scratch-QAT controls, this reduced committed shadow-weight updates by approximately 99.7% and discrete state transitions by approximately 77--80%, while mean NRMSE changed by only +0.042 and +0.197 percentage points. These results show that useful Transformer forecasting can be retained under highly discrete weight representations while strongly suppressing target-state activity, supporting a prospective route toward compact, low-activity edge forecasting using multilevel synaptic devices.
papers.summary: The study tests how well Transformer models for electricity-load forecasting hold up when weights are restricted to only 3, 5, 7, or 16 discrete states. Direct post-training quantization (PTQ) raised normalized error by about 6–7 percentage points, but quantization-aware fine-tuning (`QAT-FT`) **recovered roughly 90–95% of that penalty**, and training quantized models from scratch also worked well, especially with three states. A proposed accumulated-update thresholding scheme cut committed weight updates by about 99.7% and state transitions by 77–80% with negligible accuracy loss, which the authors pitch as a step toward low-activity edge forecasting on multilevel synaptic hardware.

papers.title: Measure First, Then Allocate: Calibrated Rollout Budgets for MCP Agents in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Training tool-using language models requires costly interaction, yet identical rewards within a rollout group provide no group-relative learning signal. We use reward disagreement to guide harness evaluation and the allocation of rollouts for policy training in Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments. We first introduce Discord, which tests harness edits using exact paired inference and decision-preserving early stopping: only disagreeing paired outcomes favor one harness over another. This insight motivates prospective allocation in BRACE (Bank-calibrated Rollout Allocation under Correlated Episodes). BRACE combines historical task evidence, uncertainty in task success rates, and a correlated reward model to forecast mixed-reward groups before allocating generation budget. Controlled harness experiments favor Discord, while live MCP experiments expose a retention-cost trade-off. At three Qwen3-VL model scales, BRACE exceeds the strongest plotted baseline peaks with fewer new training rollouts; historical-bank collection is counted separately. It also leads the compared methods on BFCL and NESTFUL without further training. Ablations probe the bank, estimator, and allocation score; prospective evaluation checks forecast calibration. These results support forecasting reward contrast before generation.
papers.summary: When tool-using language models are trained with group-relative reinforcement learning, rollout groups in which every attempt gets the same reward provide no learning signal and waste expensive interaction. Working in Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments, the authors use reward disagreement in two ways: `Discord` compares harness edits using only paired outcomes that disagree, with early stopping, and `BRACE` (Bank-calibrated Rollout Allocation under Correlated Episodes) uses historical task data and uncertainty estimates to predict which tasks will produce mixed rewards before spending generation budget on them. Across three `Qwen3-VL` model scales, `BRACE` **beats the strongest baseline's peak performance with fewer new training rollouts**, though collecting the historical bank is counted separately, and it also leads the compared methods on `BFCL` and `NESTFUL`.

papers.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.
papers.summary: Prior evaluations report that LLM pricing agents collude, but a real cartel only holds if a member who cheats gets punished. The authors introduce an audit that forces one agent to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to examine what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches small LLMs in pricing and trading games. Agents learn only behaviors they readily try: against a cheating rival they match its price cuts but rarely discover the costly price war that would deter it. Self-play produces fixed rules that ignore rivals, and prompted LLMs reach cartel-like prices mostly through such rules. The central claim is that **outcome-based measures cannot distinguish real enforcement from coincidental high prices**, while the audit can.

papers.title: ArcFlow: Training Flow Policies for Multiple Solver Budgets
papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.
papers.summary: Flow-matching policies can trade inference cost for quality by changing the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed step count can hide poor behavior at cheaper budgets and even erase one-step ability inherited from pretraining. `ArcFlow` (Action-Ratio-Clip Flow) trains one policy across a range of solver budgets. It combines action-aligned supervision with a PPO-style clipped surrogate, cycles through budgets during training, and selects checkpoints by worst-budget performance, all without changing the architecture or deployment cost. Across `DM Control`, manipulation, and locomotion tasks, it **attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks**.

papers.title: CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings
papers.abstract: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). Unlike traditional and even recent LLM-augmented approaches that ultimately rely on clustering vector embeddings, our framework leverages LLM capabilities directly for the entire pipeline. Experiments demonstrate that this approach provides better utility over existing (embedding-based) methods in the DP setting, especially in the high privacy regime. We evaluate the quality of CALLIOPE outputs using a variety of traditionally studied clustering metrics, as well as some novel utility metrics that we introduce.
papers.summary: `CALLIOPE` builds topic hierarchies over large unstructured corpora, such as logs of LLM conversations, with support for differential privacy (DP). Most existing methods, including recent LLM-augmented ones, ultimately cluster vector embeddings. `CALLIOPE` instead uses an LLM directly for the whole top-down pipeline. Experiments show **better utility than embedding-based methods under DP, especially in the high-privacy regime**, measured with standard clustering metrics and new utility metrics the authors introduce.

papers.title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Iterative ML agents develop models by editing code, running experiments, reading a validation score, and choosing what to try next. In current harnesses this loop is served by an exact validation score returned after every attempt, which leaves the validation split open to adaptive selection. In this work, we introduce an explicit feedback contract for ML-agent harnesses, which specifies what an agent may observe, when iteration should stop, and when the test split may be touched. The contract releases a validation score only when a submission clears a noise threshold computed from the paired standard error, so no margin has to be tuned. We ran experiments on click-through-rate prediction, learning to rank, and a control task with no signal to find. The control is the sharpest case, because the true gain there is zero by construction: an agent reading exact scores ended by reporting a gain of 0.0157, while under the contract it reported 0.0033. On both real tasks the contract narrows the validation-test gap, and test performance is slightly higher rather than lower. The largest difference is in when the agents stop. Exact feedback used its entire budget of thirty submissions on two of the three tasks, including the one where nothing can be learned, while the contract halted after four to twelve. A run that exhausts its budget is usually read as diligence. It is better read as a symptom: when the feedback channel is unbounded, noise keeps supplying improvements to chase.
papers.summary: Iterative ML agents edit code, run experiments, and read a validation score after every attempt, which leaves them free to overfit the validation split through adaptive selection. The proposed feedback contract specifies what an agent may observe, when it must stop, and when it may touch the test split, and it reveals a validation score only when a submission beats a noise threshold derived from the paired standard error. On a control task where the true gain is zero by construction, an agent reading exact scores reported a gain of 0.0157 versus 0.0033 under the contract. On click-through-rate prediction and learning-to-rank, the contract narrowed the validation-test gap with slightly higher test performance. Agents with exact feedback often used all thirty submissions, including on the no-signal task, while **contract-governed agents stopped after four to twelve**.

papers.title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
papers.abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.
papers.summary: In AI and law, `CATO` factors encode legally significant fact patterns that lawyers use to compare cases with precedents, and the authors ask whether LLMs represent these concepts internally. Using linear probes and sparse autoencoders on `Qwen3-1.7B`, `Qwen3-8B`, and `Gemma-2 2B`, they find that **all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models**. Single sparse features reach best-layer test AUCs of 0.86 to 1.00, and five selected features come close to full-vector performance. They report a specific layer-feature location for each factor in each model, 78 in total.

papers.title: Depth Separation for Neural Networks under Gaussian Measure
papers.abstract: We revisit the problem of depth separation for neural networks, as studied by Eldan and Shamir, Daniely, and others. Specifically, we consider the natural setting of $L^2$ approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in $d$ dimensions. We show that there is a radial function in $L^2$ under the standard Gaussian measure that can be approximated to a fixed sufficiently small $L^2$ error by a depth-3 ReLU neural network of polynomial size in $d$ but can only be approximated by depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights if their size is at least exponential in $d$. For that, we prove a general result showing that if a radial function has substantial mass in the high frequencies of its Hermite expansion, then it cannot be well approximated by a depth-2 neural network with small width and bounded weights. All theorems, lemmas, propositions, and corollaries are verified in Lean~4.
papers.summary: Depth separation results show functions that deeper neural networks can approximate efficiently but shallower ones cannot. This work proves such a result for L² approximation of radial functions under the standard Gaussian measure in d dimensions: a radial function exists that **a polynomial-size depth-3 ReLU network can approximate, while depth-2 networks with subexponentially bounded weights need exponential size**. The key tool is a general lemma that radial functions with substantial high-frequency mass in their Hermite expansion cannot be approximated by narrow depth-2 networks with bounded weights. All results are formally verified in `Lean 4`.

papers.title: Towards Realistic Models of Change: A Causal Perspective on Decision-Making and Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract:
While statistical learning has made remarkable progress in recent decades, driven by large datasets and data-driven protocols that have transformed scientific practice, it still faces a key limitation: it struggles to generalize beyond the data it has seen, often failing under distribution shift. Causality offers a promising solution: causal models focus on the underlying mechanisms of change rather than surface-level associations, enabling robust reasoning under external interventions. This allows systems not only to learn from data, but also to reason about hypothetical scenarios, adapt to new environments, and inform better decisions. This thesis explores how these approaches can inform each other, in two parts.
  The first part examines algorithmic recourse, that is, identifying which changes an individual can make to overturn an unfavorable decision. We propose an alternative perspective to the established framework, arguing for a more realistic cost function, a reformulation of the problem in causal terms, and the inclusion of a temporal dimension in policy evaluation.
  The second part focuses on dynamical systems, extending the notions of causal interventions and effects to discrete and continuous stochastic processes. We show that the equilibria of these processes, and how they change following an intervention, can be linked to Structural Causal Models (SCMs), viewed as compressed representations of the underlying temporal dynamics. We argue for the relevance of such temporal causal models, since in real-world scenarios actions take time to produce their effects.
  The common goal of both parts is practical: the utility, robustness, and trustworthiness of these models depend critically on their ability to realistically represent the underlying phenomena.
papers.summary: This thesis argues that causal models, which represent mechanisms rather than correlations, can make learning systems more robust under distribution shift and interventions. The first part revisits algorithmic recourse, meaning the changes a person can make to overturn an unfavorable automated decision, and proposes more realistic cost functions, a causal reformulation, and a temporal dimension for evaluating policies. The second part extends causal interventions to discrete and continuous stochastic processes and **links the equilibria of these processes, and how they shift after an intervention, to Structural Causal Models (SCMs)**, treating SCMs as compressed summaries of the underlying dynamics.

papers.title: Combining Long-Term Memory and LLMs Comes at a High Cost: From Prompt Injection to Persistent Compromise
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at https://github.com/PedroBarcha/Memory-injection.
papers.summary: Persistent memory in chat assistants lets a prompt injection carry over into future sessions, a threat the authors call memory injection. They present a general threat model and show that **all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across `ChatGPT Instant 5.3`, `Claude Sonnet 4.6`, and `Gemini 3 Flash`**, through vectors including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Compromised services can keep spreading disinformation, generating harmful content, or faking unresponsiveness in fresh sessions. In Claude's case, shared memory lets an attacker compromise multiple users in an organization and exfiltrate prompts. The authors derive defenses from the threat model and report that nearly half remain unimplemented across the services tested.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
papers.summary: Automated failure attribution (AFA) asks an LLM judge to identify which agent step in a multi-agent run caused the wrong final result, and direct prompting does poorly at it. Using linear probes on internal activations, the authors find a **knows-but-won't-say gap**: models encode enough information to locate the failing step but do not state it in their output. They propose grafting, a simple intervention that uses this latent knowledge without needing ground-truth labels at inference time, and it consistently beats direct-prompting approaches across multiple LLMs and benchmarks.

papers.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
papers.abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
papers.summary: Agentic harness evolution refines an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow using evidence from its own task executions, yet existing methods paradoxically get worse as the pool of evolution tasks grows. The authors trace this to poor choice of which evidence to use in each round. `SSR` (Successive Scale Racing) builds diverse evidence combinations based on task quality and coverage, then races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. It reaches state-of-the-art results in all six configurations across three benchmarks, **raising pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3% as the task pool grows from 40 to 200** while baselines decline, and it cuts validation executions by 60%.

papers.title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
papers.abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.
papers.summary: Mission engineering for systems of systems needs coordination strategies that adapt to uncertain environments rather than fixed architectures. The authors connect a digital mission model and agent-based simulation to a coordinator trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`) for adaptive task allocation, and demonstrate it on an aerial firefighting mission. Coordinators trained on a single forgiving scenario collapsed to random-level performance in harder ones, whereas **a coordinator trained on multiple scenarios concurrently matched the specialists on their own scenarios and outperformed every other policy**. Sensitivity analyses show that the variability seen in training shapes post-deployment performance.

papers.title: LIFT: Scoped Constraints for Evaluating and Training Instruction Following
papers.abstract: Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the ability of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be verified programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints, pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-access, and cannot be easily extended. We present Lift-Bench, an IF benchmark that asks a model to draft a document given a topic and a structured outline. Constraints are scoped to certain document sections, providing finer control over constraint density. Lift-Bench includes both verifiable and judged constraints, as well as a training counterpart, Lift-Train. Importantly, Lift-Bench provides both main task and instruction-following constraints, mitigating shallow reward hacking. On experiments with multiple models, we find that frontier models struggle with the harder subsets of our benchmark and analyze model performance along multiple axes. We also find that training on Lift-Train is much less susceptible to reward hacking than training on the common IFTrain. Lift-Bench and Lift-Train are publicly available, as well as the data generating pipeline.
papers.summary: Instruction-following benchmarks such as `IFEval` use simple, programmatically checkable constraints that also serve as reinforcement learning rewards, which invites reward hacking at the expense of the main task. `Lift-Bench` asks models to draft a document from a topic and a structured outline, with verifiable and LLM-judged constraints scoped to specific sections, and it scores both the main task and constraint adherence. Frontier models struggle on its harder subsets, and **training on the companion `Lift-Train` set is much less prone to reward hacking than training on `IFTrain`**. The benchmark, training data, and generation pipeline are all public.

papers.title: A Parallel Multi-Dialect Arabic Dependency Treebank
papers.abstract: Dependency parsing resource development for Arabic has largely focused on Modern Standard Arabic, leaving dialectal Arabic comparatively under-resourced. We introduce MADARTB, the first large-scale parallel dependency treebank spanning five city dialects: Beirut, Cairo, Doha, Rabat and Tunis, and extending an existing parallel MSA version. In total MADARTB consists of 5,000 sentences annotated using the CATiB dependency scheme. We analyze syntactic similarity across all city dialects and MSA. Although global construction profiles exhibit high similarity across varieties, local syntactic structures frequently diverge, revealing substantial structural variation across dialects. We further establish a cross-dialect dependency parsing comparison using a supervised parser and four LLMs. The supervised parser achieves 87.5% LAS, while the best LLM setup trails at 85.7% LAS across all six varieties on the test set. We release our annotations and models publicly.
papers.summary: Arabic dependency parsing resources focus mostly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), leaving spoken dialects under-resourced. `MADARTB` is presented as **the first large-scale parallel dependency treebank covering five city dialects** (Beirut, Cairo, Doha, Rabat, and Tunis) alongside an existing MSA version, totaling 5,000 sentences annotated in the `CATiB` scheme. Analysis shows similar global construction profiles across varieties but frequent local syntactic divergence. A supervised parser reaches 87.5% labeled attachment score (LAS), while the best of four LLMs trails at 85.7%.

papers.title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
papers.abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.
papers.summary: LLM judges of clinical AI outputs are expensive and slow at scale, so the authors compare `Jev`, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, against frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physician ratings matched or exceeded seven of 12 LLM judges, including `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6`. It also performed competitively on `HealthBench` criteria and `MedHELM` open-ended tasks, and matched the reference judge `GPT-5.4` on 91% of `HealthBench Professional` criteria. **Frontier judges cost 73 to 294 times more and took 7 to 57 times longer.**

papers.title: Where Should a Stuck Agent Spend Its Next Tokens? Causal Attribution of Inference-Time Resources
papers.abstract: Inference-time scaling is often treated as a token-budget problem, but a failed coding agent can seek qualitatively different resources: computation, information, or feedback. We introduce Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA), a controlled factorial framework that measures each resource's marginal contribution to repair and its interactions while holding the failed state and revision protocol fixed. We evaluate six models on 194 function-level failures from MBPP+ and HumanEval+ and 126 repository-level failures from SWE-bench Verified. Task-relevant specifications consistently improve repair, whereas public-test feedback provides small gains and retrieved code little to none. The value of additional computation declines with model capability, while information remains useful; resource channels largely exhibit diminishing returns, although complementary information can reinforce itself. Yet three of four frontier models select feedback in 95-100% of cases and obtain lower gains than uniform random resource selection. BRA thus exposes a gap between the resources agents prefer and those that measurably improve repair.
papers.summary: When a coding agent fails, it can spend more tokens on extra computation, on extra information, or on feedback, and these are qualitatively different resources. `BRA` (Banzhaf Resource Attribution) is a controlled factorial framework that measures each resource's marginal contribution to a successful repair, and their interactions, from a fixed failed state. Across six models and failures from `MBPP+`, `HumanEval+`, and `SWE-bench Verified`, task-relevant specifications consistently help, public-test feedback helps a little, retrieved code helps little or not at all, and extra computation matters less as models get stronger. Yet **three of four frontier models pick feedback in 95–100% of cases and gain less than uniform random resource selection**.

papers.title: Sketch2Sim: an end-to-end modular framework for hand-drawn circuit analysis
papers.abstract: This study proposes a sketch-to-simulation system to solve handwritten circuit diagrams. The system converts raw images into a Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-compatible netlist and automatically calculates the circuit's nodal voltages and currents. Another objective is to propose a holistic framework that benefits students and educators by enhancing the teaching and learning experience of electric circuits and expediting engineering design reviews. This article presents a multistage pipeline that converts raw photographs of handwritten electric circuits into executable SPICE-like netlists, providing a solution. A dataset of 1,000 hand-drawn Resistor-Inductor-Capacitor (RLC) circuits was curated and annotated for components, text regions, and character recognition. The proposed system decomposes a circuit diagram into three stages: (i) dual You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors for components and text regions, (ii) a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-based domain-aware symbol value extraction, and (iii) image processing with thresholding, skeletonization, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to automatically identify nodes and map them with corresponding components. The proposed system produces the netlist and solves the circuit. The qualitative and quantitative ablation studies on modular stages, as well as end-to-end tests, demonstrate robust performance across various handwriting styles, lighting conditions, and clutter.This study serves as an interactive learning aid and practical tool for professionals, providing a comprehensive user interface (UI), enabling rapid digitization of circuit sketches for study, design, prototyping, or troubleshooting.
papers.summary: `Sketch2Sim` converts photographs of hand-drawn circuit diagrams into netlists for the Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE) and solves them for node voltages and currents. The pipeline uses two `YOLO` (You Only Look Once) detectors for components and text, a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (`CRNN`) with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) for reading component values, and skeletonization with `DBSCAN` clustering to find nodes and connect them to components. Trained on a curated dataset of **1,000 annotated hand-drawn RLC circuits**, it is reported to be robust across handwriting styles, lighting, and clutter, and it ships with a user interface aimed at students and educators.

papers.title: How to Use Parallel Data for Multilingual Pretraining
papers.abstract: High-quality human-translated parallel corpora can improve cross-lingual transfer, but are typically too small for large-scale pretraining. Machine-translated web corpora help overcome this limitation, making parallel data available at pretraining scale. Standard multilingual pretraining, however, samples source documents and their translations independently, without explicitly using their parallel structure. We investigate how to use the parallel structure of the data to improve multilingual pretraining by concatenating each document with its translation in the same training sequence. We compare this parallel pretraining (PPT) approach with standard pretraining (SPT), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. Surprisingly, despite the benefits of parallel data reported in prior cross-lingual work, PPT alone does not consistently improve language understanding over SPT. Our further analysis suggests that although PPT builds a strong cross-lingual foundation, as shown by its better use of shared information across languages, the mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs limits its gains in general language understanding. This finding motivates a two-stage approach following the pretraining-fine-tuning paradigm: we first use PPT to build a cross-lingual foundation, then continue with SPT to adapt it to standard language modeling. In both high-resource and low-resource settings, the two-stage approach consistently improves general language understanding and cross-lingual task performance over standard pretraining alone at matched training budgets.
papers.summary: Standard multilingual pretraining samples documents and their translations independently, so it ignores the parallel structure of machine-translated web corpora. The authors compare parallel pretraining (`PPT`), which concatenates each document with its translation in the same training sequence, against standard pretraining (`SPT`), training models from scratch at matched token budgets. `PPT` alone builds a stronger cross-lingual foundation but does not consistently improve general language understanding, which the authors attribute to a mismatch between parallel training contexts and single-language task inputs. **A two-stage recipe of `PPT` followed by `SPT` consistently beats standard pretraining** on both general understanding and cross-lingual tasks, in high-resource and low-resource settings.

papers.title: KIRA: A Full-Stack Reading Screening System with Dual-Pathway Analysis for Children
papers.abstract: Early-grade reading screening is critical for identifying children at risk of reading difficulty. Existing AI-based screeners are often limited in the scope of their analyses and evaluation metrics, or are proprietary systems that lack transparent model specifications and evaluation. We present KIRA, a dual-pathway screening system that pairs word-level fluency scoring with detailed phoneme-level error detection. We adapt pretrained word and phoneme recognizers to children's speech, reducing word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%. Powered by these child-adapted models, we implement Word Reading (WRE) and Oral Reading Fluency (ORF), two foundational tasks in K-2 screening. The system integrates these recognizers with a web-based teacher-facing interface presenting fluency scores alongside phoneme feedback for potential targeted intervention. KIRA brings modern child-speech recognition into a full-stack, deployable, classroom-ready reading screener.
papers.summary: `KIRA` is an open, full-stack early-grade reading screener that pairs word-level fluency scoring with phoneme-level error detection for children in kindergarten through second grade. Pretrained word and phoneme recognizers are adapted to children's speech, cutting word error rate from 13.88% to 8.84% and **phoneme error rate from 41.66% to 23.00%**. The system implements Word Reading (`WRE`) and Oral Reading Fluency (`ORF`) tasks and presents scores and phoneme feedback in a web interface for teachers.

papers.title: Beyond Correct Answers: How Compositional Cues Shape Visual Judgments
papers.abstract: Visual question answering requires models to assign attributes and relations to the correct objects, a problem known as visual binding. Structured prompts make these assignments explicit through labeled fields. Yet an improvement from the full prompt does not reveal which labels help or how they interact. First, we isolate field-label effects across ten models and six tasks by holding the image and claim fixed. These comparisons reveal differences that overall accuracy can hide. With a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps Qwen3 but hurts Qwen2 on Spatial. Second, we compare auxiliary hints that preserve or swap the question's role assignments against a no-hint baseline. Across two image sets, Qwen3's advantage with preserving hints mainly reflects errors caused by swapped hints. Preserving hints remain near baseline. Field order further affects the harm. Third, we test clearer hint wording and direct selection of the relation shown in the image. Clearer hints improve text matching but do not consistently improve visual judgments. In contrast, relation selection partly reduces errors for some hints in Qwen3 and GPT-4.1-mini.
papers.summary: Structured prompts with labeled fields can help vision-language models with visual binding, meaning assigning attributes and relations to the correct objects, but overall accuracy hides which labels help and how they interact. Holding the image and claim fixed across ten models and six tasks, the authors find that label effects differ by model: with a relation label present, adding object-role labels helps `Qwen3` but hurts `Qwen2` on spatial tasks. **`Qwen3`'s apparent gain from hints that preserve the question's role assignments mostly reflects errors caused by hints that swap them**, while preserving hints stay near the no-hint baseline. Clearer hint wording improves text matching but not visual judgments, whereas asking models to directly select the relation shown in the image partly reduces errors for `Qwen3` and `GPT-4.1-mini`.

papers.title: When Do Gaussian Priors Fail? A Latent Geometry Investigation of RL Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract:
Latent diffusion models almost universally place a Gaussian prior on the VAE latent space. For base generation this default is unproblematic; under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, however, it carries a structural limitation. The standard VAE's KL term does not merely ignore mode structure - it actively taxes separation and tightness. When data are multimodal, the ELBO optimum compresses distinct modes into an overlapping latent. RL fine-tuning amplifies this overlap: the score network is under-resolved on the saddle region between modes, dynamic-to-variational amplification rises sharply, and the collapse boundary beta_c is pushed far above its variational scale. On the real alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at beta_c = 0.224 while a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior collapses at 0.00316, a 71x gap from the same pipeline.
  We trace this gap to a single geometric mediator, d_min/(2 sigma_0), and verify the causal chain through controlled interventions: moving geometry at fixed prior, and switching prior at matched geometry (full mediation; prior-label coefficient 0.995x, 95% CI [0.79, 1.25]). A three-source decomposition localises the amplification to the learned policy (zero ODE-solver contribution, bounded anchor mismatch); the coverage plateau is an unconditional benefit of mode-separating priors that no amount of RL capacity recovers. The remedy is conditional: a non-Gaussian prior is necessary precisely when the latent geometry would fall into overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive. A machine-checked theory skeleton supports the KL pricing structure - a divergent compactness tax under a Gaussian prior versus a finite assignment fee under a mixture - and the position-versus-plateau distinction delimits what is finite-resource from what requires changing the prior.
papers.summary: The authors argue that the standard Gaussian prior on a latent diffusion model's VAE latent space becomes a structural liability under reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, because the KL term compresses distinct data modes into overlapping latents and RL then amplifies that overlap. On the alanine-dipeptide Boltzmann distribution, **a Gaussian-prior VAE collapses at a regularization strength 71 times higher than a mode-tracked Gaussian-mixture prior** in the same pipeline. Controlled interventions trace the gap to a single geometric quantity, the mode separation relative to latent spread, and a machine-checked theory skeleton backs the KL pricing argument. The paper concludes that a non-Gaussian prior is needed precisely when latent modes would overlap and the task is coverage-sensitive.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Tuning of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models via High-Fidelity Feedback
papers.abstract: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.
papers.summary: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are fast and reliable but systematically diverge from high-fidelity (HF) formulations, and existing learned fixes need expensive HF solution labels. The proposed framework embeds the LF problem as a differentiable optimization layer and tunes its parameters end-to-end using gradients from the dual variables of an HF correction problem, so no HF labels are required. On optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, it improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally beats semi-supervised training. **The learned parameterizations generalize to unseen operating conditions and to unseen networks of up to 30,000 nodes.**

papers.title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.
authors: Gabriel Wedson Mendon\c{c}a de Souza Veloso
papers.summary: Pretraining recipes for relational foundation models are developed in individual labs under private protocols, so progress does not accumulate. The authors introduce `modded-nanoRT`, a speedrun leaderboard for Relational Transformers where entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target on a single GPU, with the held-out database chosen by calibrating how well short learning curves separate real improvements from seed noise.
