The opening recipe combines typed trilinear attention, which conditions attention on the foreign key traversed, with the `Muon` optimizer and `SIGReg`, and **reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one H200, 8.11 times faster than the reference implementation**, winning 13 of 15 comparisons outside the development database.

papers.title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
papers.abstract: Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.
papers.summary: Aligning distilled few-step diffusion models with rewards is hard because methods built for multi-step models need differentiable rewards or stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. `DualHeads` adds two lightweight binary-classifier heads to a frozen diffusion backbone: one learns which samples for the same prompt score higher under an external reward, the other separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. With optimal heads this objective equals KL-regularized reward maximization, with the head-weight ratio setting the regularization strength. **A few-step `DualHeads` generator reaches task rewards close to 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality**, at no extra inference cost.

papers.title: Agent AI Zarz\k{a}dzaj\k{a}cy Sieci\k{a} Open RAN Zorientowana na U\.zytkownika
papers.abstract: Jednym z najwa\.zniejszych wyzwa\'n zwi\k{a}zanych z implementacj\k{a} sieci Open RAN o architekturze zorientowanej na u\.zytkownika jest odpowiednie formowanie tzw. klastr\'ow obs{\l}uguj\k{a}cych. Problem ten mo\.ze by\'c efektywnie rozwi\k{a}zany za pomoc\k{a} zaproponowanego Agenta AI bazuj\k{a}cego na modelu j\k{e}zykowym. Wyniki symulacji pokaza{\l}y, \.ze zaproponowane rozwi\k{a}zanie pozwala na ponad 2-krotne zwi\k{e}kszenie mediany rozk{\l}adu przep{\l}ywno\'sci u\.zytkownik\'ow wzgl\k{e}dem standardowej architektury zorientowanej na sie\'c.
papers.summary: A key challenge in user-centric Open RAN (open radio access network) architectures is forming the clusters of cells that jointly serve each user. The authors, writing in Polish, propose an AI agent built on a language model to form these serving clusters. In simulation, **the agent more than doubles the median user throughput** compared with a standard network-centric architecture.

papers.title: A General Topological Symmetry Index for Critical Orbits In Neural Network Loss Landscapes
papers.abstract: A systematic understanding of the global structure of neural-network loss landscapes remains challenging due to their high dimensionality. Symmetries arising from network architectures and learning objectives provide a way to investigate aspects of this structure. Although a growing number of studies have drawn attention to these symmetries, a systematic characterization of them, as well as of the critical orbits they give rise to, remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this work we establish a topological symmetry index, based on the methodologies from the family of equivariant degree theories, to decode these symmetries. The frameworks apply to arbitrary network architectures and include methods applicable to degenerate critical orbits. The index detects the isotropy of the critical points and quantifies the corresponding net topological contributions. Several examples, including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks, are presented to illustrate the computations.
papers.summary: Symmetries from network architectures and training objectives shape the structure of neural-network loss landscapes, but the critical orbits they produce lack a systematic characterization. The authors build a topological symmetry index using equivariant degree theory that applies to arbitrary architectures, including degenerate critical orbits. **The index detects the isotropy of critical points and quantifies their net topological contributions**, illustrated with worked examples on softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks.

papers.title: How Much Gradient Does Truncated Backprop Lose in Looped Transformers?
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops. We measure how much of the weight gradient this throws away, exactly and for every k from one backward pass, on nine looped language models, and report three findings. First, on a trained model this lost gradient is set near the output: once the loop count is well above k, it barely changes with the loop count (within about 0.03 from 32 to 64 loops on the three models we tested, as a pre-registered test predicted for Parcae). Where the backward signal shrinks, $\rho^k$, with $\rho$ the signal's fitted shrink per loop, approximates it at moderate loop counts but overstates it at long ones, because the fitted $\rho$ drifts up as the fit takes in more loops. On Ouro the signal grows, and keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient. Second, the lost gradient falls during fine-tuning, by 0.07-0.22 within 300 steps on three of four models, on held-out problems too. The fall is not just the read-out's share of the gradient; training only the layers outside the loop reproduced up to half of it, and it also falls under truncated training. So a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. Third, we could not show that it predicts the training cost of truncation better than rules that need no measurement: on two new models it tied Parcae's cost at the same k, in a test too small to separate them.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers many times and are often trained by backpropagating through only the last k loops; the authors measure exactly how much weight gradient this discards, for every k, across nine looped language models. On trained models the lost fraction is set near the output and barely changes with loop count, and a simple geometric-decay estimate overstates it at long loop counts; on `Ouro`, where the backward signal grows, **keeping two of four loops still loses 81% of the final output's gradient**. The lost fraction drops by 0.07 to 0.22 within 300 fine-tuning steps on three of four models, so a trained model's value overstates what truncation removes later. The authors report that they could not show the measurement predicts the training cost of truncation better than measurement-free rules.

papers.title: LEAN: Loss-Engineered Modulation of the Model Weight-Sensitivity Distribution for Efficient, Error-Tolerant Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The weights of a trained network do not have uniform sensitivity to model accuracy: the 1% most sensitive weights carry about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. This distribution decides the bit-flip tolerance of a model, the fraction of weights a code must cover and the bits each weight needs; existing schemes work with the distribution training leaves. We show that we can systematically modulate or alter the weight sensitivity distribution of a trained model, thereby shifting weights from one sensitivity bin to another. The sensitivity of a stored weight is the product of its gradient and the step a flip takes in the storage format, and LEAN adds a composite regularizer on both factors, a range term that bounds the flip step and a tail term that lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, with one coefficient {\lambda} setting how far the distribution moves. Ten epochs with the term, as a fine-tune or as the last epochs of training, shrink the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times on nine vision models (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) within 0.5 points of accuracy; real flips confirm that the reshaped weights do less damage, a plain gradient-norm penalty does not reproduce the effect, and a preliminary extension to three small language models shows the same tail shaping. With a BCH code over 1% of the weights the model then survives 300 progressive bit-search flips in every training seed and 500 in two of three, where three of four published defenses with the same code fail by 300 and WCAT falls to 75% at 500. The reshaped distribution also cuts the parity for a fixed guarantee 3.7 times and makes a sensitivity-ordered 8/6/4/3-bit format affordable, which stores ImageNet ResNet-50 at a 3.29-bit weight payload, 2.4 times smaller than INT8, above the accuracy of LSQ at 3 bits.
papers.summary: A trained network's weights differ widely in sensitivity: the 1% most sensitive weights account for about a fifth of the damage a bit flip can do. `LEAN` adds a regularizer during the final training or fine-tuning epochs that bounds the step a bit flip can take and lowers the gradient of the most sensitive weights, reshaping the sensitivity distribution. Across nine vision models (`ResNet-18`, `ResNet-50`, `VGG-16` on `CIFAR-10`, `CIFAR-100`, and `ImageNet`) it **shrinks the sensitive tail 5 to 13 times within 0.5 points of accuracy**, and with an error-correcting `BCH` code over 1% of weights the models survive 300 adversarial bit flips where most published defenses fail. The reshaped distribution also enables a mixed 8/6/4/3-bit format that stores `ImageNet` `ResNet-50` at 3.29 bits per weight, 2.4 times smaller than INT8 and more accurate than `LSQ` at 3 bits.

papers.title: To Manipulate or Not: Opinion Dynamics in LLM Interactions
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly take part in extended conversations where they can both shape and be shaped by another party's views, yet most persuasion research measures only one side of that exchange. We introduce a controlled LLM-LLM debate framework in which two language-model roles repeatedly discuss a contested topic (climate-change attribution): one is given an assigned stance and, in some conditions, an explicit instruction to persuade, while the other receives no assigned position. Across four ordered model combinations involving GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, we track both each role's explicitly reported position and a separate measure of its turn-by-turn behavior inside the conversation. Opinion dynamics differ substantially across model combinations: same-model interactions narrow the opinion gap on average, clearly for only one of the two models, while cross-model interactions widen it. Explicit reports and in-dialogue behavior capture distinct aspects of opinion dynamics, and a blanket instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence. These findings suggest that conversational influence depends not only on assigned roles and initial positions but also on the participating models, with implications for how opinion change is measured in extended LLM interactions.
papers.summary: Most persuasion research measures only one side of a conversation, even though LLMs in extended exchanges can both shape and be shaped by the other party. The authors run controlled LLM-LLM debates on climate-change attribution, where one role is assigned a stance and sometimes told to persuade while the other has no assigned position, across four pairings of `GPT-6 Luna` and `Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite`, tracking both stated positions and turn-by-turn behavior. Same-model pairings narrow the opinion gap on average (clearly for only one of the two models) while **cross-model pairings widen it**. Stated positions and in-dialogue behavior capture different aspects of opinion change, and an explicit instruction to persuade does not reliably increase influence.

papers.title: Actually, All Learnable Distribution Classes Are Privately Learnable
papers.abstract: We show that every class of distributions that is learnable up to arbitrarily small target error in total variation distance with finitely many samples is also learnable under ($\varepsilon, \delta$)-differential privacy up to arbitrarily small target error with finitely many samples. This proves a conjecture of Ashtiani. Previous work by Bun, Kamath, Mouzakis, and Singhal [arXiv:2402.00267] gave a weak refutation of this conjecture, showing that this implication is not true when learnability is defined with respect to a fixed target error. In contrast, we show that, under the standard definition of learnability, the conjecture is true.
papers.summary: The paper settles a conjecture by Ashtiani about whether learnability of distribution classes implies private learnability. **The authors prove that every class of distributions learnable to arbitrarily small total variation error with finitely many samples is also learnable under (ε, δ)-differential privacy**. This complements earlier work showing that the implication fails when learnability is defined at a fixed target error; under the standard definition, the conjecture holds.

papers.title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
papers.summary: Long-horizon robot operation needs memory that scales with essential information rather than with execution time. `inr2action` stores each episode as the weight delta of a neural implicit representation fitted to the episode's video from a shared, meta-learned initialization, so **each memory stays a fixed size whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames**. A learned projector maps these deltas into tokens that condition a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint-command regression, without retrieving frames at query time. On `RoboMME` the language model beats chance on all question types and the decoder reaches a mean R² of 0.51, while ablations show the meta-learned initialization is essential.

papers.title: RL-IF: Tracking Non-local Training Data Influence for Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks, but modern online RL remains highly sensitive to the quality of training experience. Understanding the contribution of individual training instances is therefore central to data-centric RL, with applications ranging from experience selection to policy interpretation. Existing data attribution methods for online RL primarily focus on local influence within a single training round, overlooking the non-local data influence across multiple training rounds. In this work, we formalize data attribution in online RL through a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, RL-LOO, which measures how one training sample influences a downstream target after subsequent online updates have taken place. We then derive RL-IF, a first-order estimator that propagates data influence through both optimization effects and policy-induced sampling effects, and provide theoretical guarantees on its approximation accuracy under smoothness assumptions. Our analysis further disentangles these two effects and shows both theoretically and empirically that the full RL-IF estimator can often be well approximated using the optimization effect alone. Building on this observation, we develop RINSE, a practical data filtering method for online RL. Experiments on standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation setting show that RINSE improves training efficiency and final performance over standard PPO and local attribution baselines. These results suggest that RL-IF provides a practical and principled framework for understanding and improving online RL.
papers.summary: Data attribution methods for online reinforcement learning (RL) mostly measure a sample's influence within a single training round and miss its effects across later rounds. The authors define a trajectory-level leave-one-out quantity, `RL-LOO`, and derive `RL-IF`, a first-order estimator that propagates influence through both optimization updates and changes in which data the policy samples, with approximation guarantees under smoothness assumptions. They show **the full estimator is often well approximated by the optimization effect alone**, and build on this to create `RINSE`, a data-filtering method. On standard control benchmarks and an RLHF-style toxicity-mitigation task, `RINSE` improves training efficiency and final performance over standard `PPO` and local attribution baselines.

papers.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
papers.abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).
papers.summary: LLM judges are now used for benchmarking, model selection, and training, but existing reliability tests rely on human-written perturbation recipes with assumed scorer types. `SANE` is an agent-based metamorphic testing framework that, given a scorer's specification, implementation, and sample inputs, identifies the capabilities that scorer should have, derives perturbation recipes and expected score changes, and validates the generated tests against scorer intent. Across five domains it produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (`JRH`) and finds scorer deficiencies in every domain, including two where `JRH` finds none. **On faithfulness, its test scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled `FaithBench` performance (Spearman ρ = 0.852), versus 0.100 for `JRH`.**

papers.title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.
papers.summary: The authors study how to organize teams of autonomous AI researchers to avoid local minima when experiments are costly. Their team consists of persistent agents, each grounded in a different scientific discipline, that keep private research histories, share experimental results, and receive experiment slots through adaptive allocation that balances exploration and exploitation. Deployed to search for linear attention architectures, **the team discovers a design that outperforms `GDN2` at 1.3B scale** on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and retrieval tasks. Ablations show that removing disciplinary backgrounds, private histories, or adaptive allocation each yields markedly weaker discoveries.
papers.highlight_summary:
Autonomous research agents often get stuck exploring a narrow part of the design space, especially when experiments are expensive and only a few ideas can be tested. The proposed fix is a team of 16 persistent AI researchers, each given a different scientific background, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and are picked for each new experiment by an adaptive bandit scheduler; the team is used to search for linear attention architectures starting from `GDN2`.

- In each of 80 iterations, a discounted UCB rule picks one researcher (all running `GPT-6 Astra`) whose proposal must pass a technical review and a novelty review. A separate agent implements it, and it must train no slower than **1.2× `GDN2`** per step. It is then trained FLOP-matched on `FineWeb-Edu`, and the reward is its gain over the best model so far on a normalized average of language modeling, common-sense reasoning and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval.
- The best discovery, `CFDN` (Context-First DeltaNet), adds a recurrent vector alongside `GDN2`'s matrix memory: the vector absorbs the prediction error first, and the matrix then fits what remains. At 150M parameters it reaches a search utility of **1.04 vs. 0.00** for `GDN2`, with NIAH accuracy of **29.76 vs. 25.79** and WikiText perplexity of 33.84 vs. 34.93, though its common-sense reasoning accuracy is slightly lower (43.29 vs. 43.60).
- Scaled to 1.3B parameters, `CFDN` beats `GDN`, `KDA` and `GDN2` in every category, including common-sense reasoning at **54.53 vs. 52.65** and real-world retrieval at 33.41 vs. 32.52, but some margins are small (NIAH 67.29 vs. 66.86, LAMBADA perplexity 11.04 vs. 11.22).
- Removing any one organizational component weakens the best result found: utility drops to **0.54 without backgrounds** (which stops improving after iteration 22), 0.56 without private memory, and 0.76 when researchers are taken in a fixed rotation. A search that optimizes language modeling alone gets better LAMBADA perplexity (46.40) but does worse on common-sense reasoning and retrieval.
- Each condition is a single search run with no reported variance, and the 80-iteration budget yielded only 63 trained candidates. During search, retrieval was scored with a teacher-forced proxy rather than actual generation, which leaves open how much of the ablation gap is noise.

papers.title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
papers.abstract: Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet-ai/fig.
papers.summary: Social evaluations of multiagent systems usually wait for behaviors to emerge rather than deliberately eliciting them. `Fig` (Finding Interactions in Games) is an agentic system that takes a natural-language behavior description, breaks it into sub-behaviors, generates or selects social games, and intervenes in the game engine, opponents, instructions, or context to elicit the target behavior, scoring results with mechanical checks and rubric-based judgments. For six behaviors including deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage, models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes in valid generated scenarios, and **`Fig`'s interventions raise attempt rates by 10.9% on average over matched control games**.

papers.title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
papers.abstract: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing mitigation methods largely treat forgetting as a consequence of excessive model drift. They therefore constrain updates by preserving old outputs, replaying old data, or regularizing changes to parameters and representations so that the updated model remains close to its previous state. We take a different view: Rather than pulling the updated model back toward its old state, we translate the new domain into the model's pre-existing knowledge space, making unfamiliar knowledge learnable through familiar procedures. Therefore, we propose Skill Schema Transport (SST), a post-training framework that transports new knowledge into the model's existing skill space. SST abstracts each example type into a skill schema, preserving its essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while removing domain-specific surface forms. By recasting new examples as instances of reusable procedures, SST turns knowledge update from trajectory memorization into procedural reuse. In continual domain adaptation settings, SST consistently reduces forgetting while improving generalization to related tasks. Across two 3B instruction-tuned backbones, SST improves average final performance on streamed domains by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training. It also lowers max-drop forgetting in all evaluated settings, with the largest reduction from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the Qwen-3B MATH stream, while substantially recovering the OOD degradation induced by sequential updates.
papers.summary: Most methods against catastrophic forgetting during domain adaptation constrain how far a language model drifts from its previous state. Skill Schema Transport (`SST`) instead recasts new-domain training examples as instances of abstract skill schemas that keep essential operations, dependencies, and verification steps while dropping domain-specific surface forms, so the model learns new knowledge through procedures it already knows. On two 3B instruction-tuned backbones in continual domain adaptation, `SST` improves average final performance by 2.53 to 5.75 points over sequential post-training and lowers forgetting in every setting, **cutting the maximum drop from 42.41 to 7.10 points on the `Qwen`-3B `MATH` stream**.

papers.title: CSD: Common-Support Distillation for Cross-Tokenizer Knowledge Transfer
papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer logits distillation enables knowledge transfer across model families, allowing students to learn from stronger or more specialized teachers. However, differences in vocabulary and segmentation make teacher and student next-token distributions difficult to align. Existing logits-based methods are easy to integrate into standard distillation pipelines, but often rely on restrictive heuristics or tokenizer-pair-specific choices. They may restrict supervision to shared vocabulary subsets, require manually selecting different objectives for different tokenizer pairs, or match only the observed chunk and its complement rather than individual alternative continuations. We introduce Common-Support Distillation (CSD), a unified logits-based framework that constructs a shared support between the teacher and student at each aligned input chunk and matches the induced distributions with a single objective. For one-to-one alignments, CSD uses explicit common-token pairs as the shared support. For other alignments, it constructs a virtual support whose probabilities are computed using the autoregressive chain rule. A residual event captures probability mass outside the explicit support, ensuring that both induced distributions remain normalized. Across four teacher-student settings comprising Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B-PT students with Qwen and Phi teachers, CSD consistently achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated cross-tokenizer methods, outperforming the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and surpassing both continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For Llama-3.1-8B, CSD improves average accuracy over the strongest evaluated baseline by up to 4.2 points for the base student and 1.6 points for the instruction-tuned student.
papers.summary: Distilling knowledge between models with different tokenizers is hard because their next-token distributions are defined over different vocabularies and segmentations, and existing methods rely on shared-vocabulary subsets or pair-specific heuristics. Common-Support Distillation (`CSD`) builds a shared support at each aligned input chunk, using common-token pairs for one-to-one alignments and a virtual support computed with the autoregressive chain rule otherwise, plus a residual event that keeps both distributions normalized, and matches them with a single objective. Across `Llama-3.2-1B` and `Gemma3-1B-PT` students with `Qwen` and `Phi` teachers, **`CSD` achieves the best average performance among cross-tokenizer methods**, beating the strongest alternative by up to 1.8 points and also surpassing continued pretraining and same-tokenizer distillation. For `Llama-3.1-8B` it improves over the strongest baseline by up to 4.2 points.

papers.title: Is Refusal Direction Universal across Low-Resourced Languages?
papers.abstract: Refusal directions have been shown to transfer cross-lingually with near-perfect effectiveness across safety-aligned languages (Wang et al., 2025), reportedly regardless of resource level. However, the only truly low-resourced language evaluated is Yoruba, which is strongly misaligned and shows limited transfer, leaving open how refusal directions behave for other low-resourced languages. We extend PolyRefuse to three additional low-resourced languages (Belarusian, Bashkir, and Tajik) and replicate the pipeline of (Wang et al., 2025) on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. We find that universality is graded rather than binary: directions from safety-aligned and partially-aligned languages transfer broadly, while those from strongly misaligned languages fail to reliably modulate refusal behavior on any target tested, including other misaligned languages, once ceiling effects are accounted for. Geometric alignment and behavioral transfer are further shown to be partially dissociated. These findings complicate the universality claim and suggest that users of the least-resourced, most strongly misaligned languages may face weaker safety guarantees.
papers.summary: Earlier work reported that refusal directions, the internal activation directions that control whether a model refuses a harmful request, transfer almost perfectly across languages regardless of how much training data a language has. That conclusion rested on only one truly low-resourced language, Yoruba. The authors extend the `PolyRefuse` dataset to Belarusian, Bashkir, and Tajik and replicate the original pipeline on `Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct`. They find that **universality is graded rather than binary**: directions taken from safety-aligned or partially aligned languages transfer broadly, while directions from strongly misaligned languages fail to reliably change refusal behavior in any target language. Geometric similarity between directions also turns out to be only partly linked to whether they actually transfer behaviorally.

papers.title: Minimax-Optimal Predictive Flow Matching under Distribution Drift
papers.abstract: Flow matching learns a generative velocity field by regression, but under distribution drift a field must be deployed before the current data arrive. We study this predictive problem for a fixed, possibly nonconvex, neural class, with dynamic regret against the best represented field of each round. We propose DyProd-FM, which refits flow matching on dyadic historical prefixes and selects among the fits with a sleeping Prod master. Without knowing any drift budget, it attains regret $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\omega+1,1+\sqrt{T\Omega}\})$ in the relative velocity risk variation $\Omega$ and $\widetilde{O}(\min\{N_\mu+1,1+T^{1/3}V_\mu^{2/3}\})$ in the target-law variation $V_\mu=\sum_t W_2(\mu_{t+1},\mu_t)$, up to approximation and fitting costs. Matching lower bounds for fixed classes show that both rates are optimal in $T$ and in the budgets up to logarithmic factors. Prior optimal dynamic-regret guarantees rely on a convex decision set with strongly convex or exp-concave losses, whereas our class may be nonconvex and no curvature in its parameters is assumed. The target-law rate rests on a second-order link between the two variations, which the base noise of flow matching provides.
papers.summary: Flow matching trains a generative model by regressing a velocity field. When the data distribution drifts over time, the field has to be deployed before the current data arrive, which makes training a prediction problem. The proposed `DyProd-FM` refits flow matching on historical data windows of doubling length and picks among those fits with a sleeping-experts `Prod` aggregator, without needing to know how much the distribution drifts. It achieves dynamic-regret bounds that come with **matching lower bounds, so they are optimal up to logarithmic factors**, and unlike earlier optimal guarantees it allows a nonconvex neural model class with no curvature assumptions on the parameters.

papers.title: Tropical Cyclone Attributes in Sparse Autoencoder Features of an AI Weather Model
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models now forecast weather events skillfully, but how they represent these events internally remains unknown. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide sparse features for probing hidden states, but how information about multiple physical attributes of an event is organized across them remains unclear. Using tropical cyclones in GraphCast as a test case, we analyze 2,115 six-hourly timesteps from 205 cyclones, relating SAE activations to position, intensity, and pressure structure across five Layer-8 decompositions and 16 processor layers. Each attribute relates to multiple features; position and pressure-structure relations overlap in a smaller subset. This organization recurs across independent SAEs and layers without feature alignment. In deeper layers, the leading position feature aligns better with position and pressure structure six hours ahead than at present. These results suggest that the organization of physical-attribute relations provides a reproducible level of description for interpreting cyclone-related information in GraphCast.
papers.summary: The study asks how the AI weather model `GraphCast` represents tropical cyclones internally. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose its hidden states into sparse features, and the authors relate those features to cyclone position, intensity, and pressure structure across 2,115 timesteps from 205 storms, 16 processor layers, and several independently trained decompositions. Each physical attribute is spread across multiple features, with position and pressure structure overlapping in a smaller subset, and **this organization recurs across independent SAEs and layers**. In deeper layers, the leading position feature matches the cyclone's state six hours ahead better than its current state.

papers.title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems built on diffusion language models usually communicate only through decoded text and throw away the continuous intermediate denoising states. In the proposed `Hidden Messages` setup, a sender compresses its denoising state into four dense vectors that a receiver agent consumes alongside its own context. The authors test causally whether the receiver actually uses the content of the message, either by removing it or by swapping in a message from a different example. On `QASC`, with the two supporting facts split between agents, matched messages reach 80.8% accuracy against 46.8% for a mismatched message, and **a single late transfer (87.8%) outperforms four repeated exchanges by 7 points**, suggesting that when information is passed matters more than how often.

papers.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) can fill simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers, but it has seen little use in macroeconomics, partly because training is very slow. `JaxMARL-BC` is a JAX-accelerated reimplementation of the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (`MARL-BC`) model, in which deep RL households live in a real business cycle economy. It trains **75x to 724x faster than the reference implementation** and scales to 200,000 independently learning households. The authors check its correctness against known dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) limits and run a calibration in two hours that would previously have taken over a month. The simulator is released as open source.

papers.title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.
papers.summary: Deep research agents repeatedly plan, retrieve, synthesize, and revise, so end-to-end latency limits interactive use. `DiffResearch` is an open multi-agent deep research framework built on a diffusion language model (dLLM). To isolate the effect of the backbone, the authors keep the scaffold, retrieval, and prompts fixed and swap only between a diffusion model and a comparable autoregressive model. On 100 `Deep Research Bench` tasks, the diffusion backbone is **roughly 6x faster end-to-end**, mostly due to much faster planning and writing. A mode called `dFast` reads intermediate denoising states to extract subqueries before generation finishes, which roughly halves decomposition time with no loss in report quality.

papers.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
papers.abstract: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.
papers.summary: Natural direct and indirect effects in causal mediation analysis are usually defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. The authors propose an alternative based on backtracking counterfactuals: instead of intervening on the treatment or the mediator, they use a backtracking conditional distribution to build an alternative exogenous state that satisfies a desired treatment-mediator constraint. This yields **backtracking versions of the direct, indirect, and total effects**, and the same idea is used to adapt population intervention effects.

papers.title: Simply Logical -- The First Three Decades
papers.abstract: This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical -- Intelligent Reasoning by Example from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions, to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate -- from both the writer's and the reader's perspectives -- the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book's philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.
papers.summary: The authors trace the Prolog textbook `Simply Logical` from its 1994 print edition, which shipped runnable programs on a diskette, to today's fully interactive online version. The original author describes the book's philosophy and experience teaching from it, a second author shows how modern web programming makes the content interactive, and a third describes the authoring toolkit behind the online edition. Together they reflect on **how web technology can reshape interactive Prolog teaching materials**.

papers.title: D-Skill: Distilling Teacher Knowledge through Agent Skills
papers.abstract: Frontier language-model agents excel at complex tasks, but high inference costs make transferring their capabilities to smaller models essential. Traditional knowledge distillation achieves this through parameter updates, requiring access to the student's weights and additional training compute while encoding the transferred knowledge implicitly in the parameters. We introduce D-Skill, a framework that treats the teacher as a black box and distills its behavioral advantage into an interpretable natural-language skill by analyzing paired rollouts and identifying behavioral divergences and agreements. The resulting lessons are consolidated offline, with any compatible skill-update backend, into a skill document that is provided to the student at inference time. D-Skill constructs the skill entirely offline from fixed trajectories, without labels, further environment interaction, or weight updates after rollout collection. Across SpreadsheetBench-Verified, ALFWorld, and chess puzzles spanning multiple teacher-student pairs, D-Skill closes 75%-95% of the teacher-student gap without touching model weights. After a single offline pass over the paired traces, D-Skill outperforms one-epoch SFT baselines and remains competitive with multi-epoch SFT. Under the same model family, the resulting student also incurs 5.7x-8.3x lower inference cost per task than the teacher. Our results demonstrate that natural-language skill distillation offers a performant, interpretable, and efficient alternative to weight-based capability transfer.
papers.summary: Transferring a frontier agent's abilities to a smaller model normally means distillation through weight updates, which requires access to the student's weights and extra compute. `D-Skill` treats the teacher as a black box: it compares paired teacher and student rollouts, finds where their behavior diverges or agrees, and condenses the lessons into a natural-language skill document that the student reads at inference time. The process runs entirely offline on fixed trajectories, with no labels and no weight updates. Across `SpreadsheetBench-Verified`, `ALFWorld`, and chess puzzles, it **closes 75% to 95% of the teacher-student gap**, beats one-epoch supervised fine-tuning (SFT), stays competitive with multi-epoch SFT, and the student costs 5.7x to 8.3x less per task than the teacher.

papers.title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.
papers.summary: This work studies continuous-time reinforcement learning in which the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation, but only a fixed batch of off-policy, discrete-time transitions is available. Standard Q-learning breaks down at small sampling intervals because differences between action values vanish. Building on the `PhiBE-Q` formulation, the authors propose `PhiBE-PI`, a model-free policy iteration method that uses a single state-action critic, reuses the same batch throughout, and never estimates the drift or diffusion explicitly. Under linear function approximation they prove an end-to-end suboptimality guarantee and identify a bias-variance trade-off: **finer time discretization does not necessarily give a better policy** at a fixed sample size.

papers.title: Query Feedback and Teaching for Stable and Certifiable Language Generation
papers.abstract: Language generation in the limit studies whether a learner observing an enumeration of an unknown target language can eventually generate only valid, previously unseen elements. We study stability, introduced by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025), which requires the generator's infinite output set to eventually remain unchanged, and introduce the stronger notion of certifiability, which requires the generator to determine from its observations that its current output is valid. Drawing on teaching sets in learning theory, we introduce a hierarchy of teaching dimensions for generation under three increasingly strict success criteria: correctness, stability, and certifiability. These dimensions measure the minimum number of selected examples whose appearance guarantees the corresponding success condition. We also study stability and certifiability in the membership-query model of Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025). We characterize stable and certifiable generation, both with and without query feedback, and establish their relationships with uniform generation and identification in the limit. In particular, we give a finite-witness characterization of stable generation, analogous to Angluin's tell-tale characterization of identification, resolving a gap left open by Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Velegkas (2025). We further compare these generation notions with identification in the limit and contrast their teaching requirements on well-studied language families, including regular and erasing pattern languages.
papers.summary: Language generation in the limit asks whether a learner that sees an enumeration of an unknown language can eventually produce only valid, previously unseen strings. The authors study stability, where the generator's output set eventually stops changing, and introduce a stronger notion, certifiability, where the generator can tell from its observations that its current output is valid. They define a hierarchy of teaching dimensions for these success criteria, analyze them with and without membership queries, and relate them to uniform generation and identification in the limit. A key result is **a finite-witness characterization of stable generation**, analogous to Angluin's tell-tale condition, which resolves a previously open gap.

papers.title: One Policy, Many Styles: Where to Aggregate Preferences for Steerable Humanoid Control?
papers.abstract: Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics. We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.
papers.summary: Steerable robot control asks a single policy to change its behavioral style at runtime as user preferences change. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning makes this possible, but it does not guarantee that a requested change is strong, stays confined to the targeted behavior, and preserves task performance. Using a new Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) metric together with coverage and utility measures, the authors compare aggregating preferences at the reward, advantage, and loss levels, and via `PCGrad`, across two humanoid-control frameworks. **No aggregation level wins everywhere**: aggregating early gives a wider range of behaviors but more unintended side effects, while aggregating later gives more precise control at some cost to responsiveness.

papers.title: The Data Differentiator Framework (DDF): Quantifying Marginal Data Value with Information-Theoretic and Game-Theoretic Measures in an Agentic Evaluation Pipeline (SDSAE)
papers.abstract: In data-rich enterprises the hard question is not whether a candidate dataset is good in isolation, but whether it adds information beyond what the organization already holds, and whether that increment is worth its price. We present the Data Differentiator Framework (DDF), a composite scoring method for candidate data assets that combines (i) a mutual-information-based redundancy penalty against the existing portfolio, (ii) a cost-normalized, significance-gated marginal utility score derived from an ablation study, and (iii) explicit governance inputs (trust, identity resolution quality, strategic weights) set by the business. The framework is executed by a staged pipeline, the Strategic Data Sourcing Agent Ecosystem (SDSAE), that short-circuits expensive model-retraining steps for assets failing governance or redundancy gates. Conceptually, the DDF extends the relevance-minus-redundancy principle of mRMR feature selection from the feature level to the asset level, and adds cost normalization, a statistical significance gate, and governance terms that per-sample valuation methods such as Data Shapley do not model. We validate the framework on the public credit-card fraud benchmark (284,807 transactions) with five constructed candidate assets spanning the redundancy spectrum. Only the genuinely differentiated asset passes the significance gate ($\Delta$AUC = +0.0029, DeLong $p = 1.4\times 10^{-9}$, Holm-corrected $p = 7.2\times 10^{-9}$) and receives an acquire recommendation (DDS = +0.663); the fully redundant asset scores lowest (DDS = -0.135). The recommendation is stable across 19 of 22 admissible strategic-weight configurations and across all decision thresholds in [0.15, 0.66]. We state clearly which quantities in the case study are computed from data and which are simulated governance inputs, and we discuss the design limits of a single-dataset evaluation.
papers.summary: Enterprises considering a new dataset need to know whether it adds information beyond the data they already hold and whether that gain justifies the price. The Data Differentiator Framework (DDF) scores candidate datasets by combining a mutual-information redundancy penalty, a cost-normalized marginal utility score that must pass a statistical significance test in an ablation study, and governance weights set by the business. An agent pipeline (`SDSAE`) runs these steps and skips expensive retraining for datasets that fail early checks. On a credit-card fraud benchmark with five constructed candidate datasets, **only the genuinely differentiated one passes the significance gate** and earns an acquire recommendation, and the result holds across most weight settings.

papers.title: Back Up Before You Regret: Measuring Backup Awareness and Automating Backup in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents now complete tasks autonomously, modifying real-world state such as artifacts, software environments, and configurations along the way. Yet they show limited backup awareness: recognizing that an action will modify state that may later be needed, and preserving it beforehand. To evaluate backup awareness, we introduce RegretBench, a benchmark of 205 executable tasks grounded in regret moments reported on platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users explicitly regretted not preserving state they later needed. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before these moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Because it is hard to predict which changes will be regretted, we propose BackUpper, a harness plug-in backup layer that checks every tool call and preserves affected state before modification. It combines rule-based strategies for common operations with a lightweight subagent for complex cases, and its rule table can expand with subagent decisions over time. On RegretBench, BackUpper covers every regret moment action and restores states with 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 per task, with 7x fewer tokens than the main-agent self-backup baseline. When users have preferences on what to back up, BackUpper can also narrow its scope accordingly, matching human annotations on whether an action is worth preserving with an 84.5% F1 score. These results suggest that agents can keep actions reversible at low cost while respecting users' preferences.
papers.summary: Coding agents change real files, environments, and configurations, but rarely save state they may later need before modifying it. `RegretBench` provides 205 executable tasks drawn from real user-reported regret moments on X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks but **back up the affected state beforehand in only 15.2%**. The proposed `BackUpper` harness plug-in checks every tool call and preserves affected state using rules plus a lightweight subagent. It covers every regret moment, restores state with 92.2% average similarity, costs about $0.014 per task, and can follow user preferences about what is worth backing up.

papers.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is usually evaluated with the same inference settings at calibration and deployment, yet real deployments often change quantization or sampling temperature to meet memory or throughput limits. The authors formalize this as inference-time model shift and show theoretically that it breaks the exchangeability assumption that split-conformal guarantees rely on, even when the task and trained model are unchanged. Across 8 models, 4 benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations, **matched evaluation can substantially overstate the coverage actually achieved at deployment**, and the effect varies widely by model and dataset. They recommend reporting inference configuration as a standard axis in CP evaluations.

papers.title: StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion
papers.abstract: Voice style conversion (VSC) aims to transform a source utterance to match the timbre, accent, and emotion of a target voice while preserving linguistic content. StyleStream 1.0 introduced the first streamable zero-shot VSC system with state-of-the-art conversion quality, but remained limited in two ways: approximately 1s end-to-end latency on consumer hardware, and the lack of a text-based interface for designing or editing target voices. We present StyleStream 2.0, a fast and controllable streaming VSC framework that addresses these limitations. To reduce latency, we train a few-step pixel MeanFlow model and further fine-tune it with autoregressive feedback inspired by Self Forcing, improving robustness under streaming inference. This reduces end-to-end latency to 520~ms on a consumer GPU, a 2x speedup over StyleStream 1.0, while maintaining conversion quality. To enable controllable style manipulation, we remove the mel-spectrogram context and instead route target style information through a compact style embedding. In this embedding space, we train a unified text-conditioned flow matching model that supports both text-based voice design, which maps natural language prompts to voice styles, and instruction-based voice editing, which modifies a specific attribute of a source utterance while preserving the rest. Experiments show that StyleStream 2.0 achieves the strongest target style fidelity on VSC, voice design, and voice editing, while remaining competitive on intelligibility and non-edited attribute preservation.
papers.summary: Voice style conversion (VSC) changes the timbre, accent, and emotion of an utterance to match a target voice while keeping its words. `StyleStream 2.0` cuts streaming latency by training a few-step `MeanFlow` model and fine-tuning it with autoregressive feedback in the style of `Self Forcing`, reaching **520 ms end-to-end on a consumer GPU, about 2x faster than version 1.0**. It also routes target style through a compact embedding, which lets one text-conditioned flow matching model design voices from natural-language prompts and edit specific attributes of an existing voice. The authors report the strongest target style fidelity across conversion, voice design, and editing.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
papers.abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.
papers.summary: Protein engineering often needs to improve several properties at once with only a few rounds of lab measurements. `MODS` frames multi-objective optimization as inference-time steering of a diffusion model: for each proposal, it samples Chebyshev scalarization weights and one member of a fitness-surrogate ensemble to define a single steering reward, which varies the targeted trade-off and diversifies guidance. After each batch, only the surrogates are updated, not the generative model. Across six tasks with oracles trained on experimental assay data, two diffusion models, and two steering procedures, **MODS achieves competitive hypervolume on all tasks** and clearly beats the best baseline on several.

papers.title: Guilt by Association: Semantic Leakage Drives Associative Gender Bias
papers.abstract: Semantic leakage occurs when a concept in the prompt steers model generation about an entity, even though the concept is irrelevant to it (e.g., a person who likes yellow is said to work as a school bus driver). It has mostly been studied in settings where the concept is directly attributed to the entity the model is asked about. This leaves open whether leakage is a flawed heuristic, where the model builds a profile of that entity, or a much broader associative tendency, e.g., working across seemingly unrelated entities. We argue for the latter: even after removing the attribution of the concept to the specific entity, leakage persists. Next, we extend this idea to gender bias. While work on gender bias in LMs typically looks at cases where the stereotyped concept is attributed to an entity, our findings suggest that a concept may steer outputs with its mere presence in the scene. We show this using gendered concepts under two conditions: when the subject engages with the concept, and when the concept just sits in the scene. We find that both shift model generation toward the stereotype to a similar extent. Together, our results suggest that semantic leakage drives a form of bias that is overlooked by current evaluations.
papers.summary: Semantic leakage occurs when an irrelevant concept in a prompt steers what a language model generates about an entity, for example a person who likes yellow being described as a school bus driver. The authors show that leakage persists even when the concept is not attributed to the entity at all, which points to a broad associative tendency rather than the model building a profile of that entity. Extending this to gender, they find that a gendered concept merely present in the scene **shifts generations toward the stereotype about as much as when the subject engages with it directly**. Current bias evaluations, which focus on concepts attributed to the subject, would miss this form of bias.

papers.title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: The authors propose a test-time framework that helps LLM agents both anticipate outcomes and learn from experience during deployment, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control. At each step, the agent proposes several candidate actions, imagines their outcomes with a world model, scores each predicted outcome for task progress and risk, and combines the results with MPPI-style weights to choose an action. A two-branch experience memory improves both candidate generation and the world model's next-observation predictions over time. On `ALFWorld` and `ScienceWorld` with three backbone models, the method shows **strong overall performance** and confirms the value of experience-guided predictive control.

papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: NVIDIA tensor cores have supported 2:4 semi-structured sparsity since Ampere, and the pattern composes with quantization. When the two are combined, the practical question is which step to take next: from a given precision, add 2:4 sparsity or drop to the next lower precision? We compare the two at equal bits, with sparsity metadata counted, and at equal nominal tensor-core tiers, over all six GEMM operands of a transformer layer, with kernels measured on three GPU generations and online pruning and quantization included. Our results show that as long as a lower precision is available, adding 2:4 is the worse step, both less accurate and slower, because the energy that 2:4 discards from each group of four along the hardware-forced axis does not shrink with bits, while quantization error does. Once quantization reaches the lowest precision the hardware supports, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3--1.7\x{}, and on an H100 a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 by vLLM reaches 27\% higher prefill throughput than the dense FP8 model, with GSM8K accuracy on par. Its quality has to be won back by retraining, however, which restores perplexity long before reasoning; on Blackwell, whose sparse FP4 uses a pairwise 4:8 pattern, the loss is larger and our retraining budget did not recover it.
papers.summary: NVIDIA tensor cores support 2:4 semi-structured sparsity, which can be combined with quantization, so practitioners must choose between adding sparsity and dropping to a lower precision. Comparing both at equal bits (counting sparsity metadata) across all six matrix multiplications in a transformer layer on three GPU generations, the authors find that **while a lower precision is still available, adding 2:4 sparsity is both less accurate and slower**. Once the lowest supported precision is reached, 2:4 still speeds up linear layers by 1.3x to 1.7x, and a retrained 2:4 model served in FP8 with `vLLM` on an H100 gets 27% higher prefill throughput with `GSM8K` accuracy on par. Recovering quality requires retraining, and on Blackwell's sparse FP4 the accuracy loss was not recovered within the authors' retraining budget.

papers.title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing
papers.abstract: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.
papers.summary: Conventional wafer defect classifiers are trained offline on a fixed set of classes, so they miss new defect signatures that appear during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. `WaferHDC` uses hyperdimensional computing (HDC) to work online. It first models normal spatial distributions, then groups recurring failures into compact hypervector memories without labels or a preset number of classes. Memory grows as new defect modes appear, with no retraining and no need to store raw wafer history. On `WM-811K` it beats the strongest online baseline by **13.3 percentage points in adjusted Rand index** and 10.5 points in normalized mutual information.

papers.title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
papers.abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators.
