HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
papers.summary: `HyperDrone` is a batch quadrotor simulator that runs both multirotor dynamics and rendering entirely on the GPU, and the authors report it as **more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators**. Its new ray-tracing engine, `HyperLux`, supports OptiX, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends. It renders RGB, depth, segmentation, surface normals and optical flow, with optional reflections, motion blur and Physically Based Rendering (PBR), at millions of frames per second on consumer GPUs. To test transfer to real hardware, the authors train a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and deploy it fully onboard a real `Crazyflie` quadrotor with a camera.

papers.title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
papers.abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
papers.summary: `SLoSa` is a framework for building small, low-power robotic task planners that respect safety constraints, combining the flexibility of large language models (LLMs) with the guarantees of classical symbolic planners. It builds a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, a teacher LLM and formal verifiers. A compact model is then trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, guided by a verification-based reward machine. Across four Planning Domain Definition Language (`PDDL`) domains, this raises the success rate of 4B-14B planners to **70.5-76.0%**, and INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin draws about 18-26 W. Household simulators and a desktop robotic arm are also used to show the framework applies across settings.

papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.abstract: Scanning every passage in a long document seems thorough, but does it preserve more useful evidence or produce better answers? We compare 11 retrieval configurations spanning lexical and dense search, hybrid reranking, and full-document scanning with Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and Cloudflare Clef. Our evaluation uses 396 QASPER questions and 80 questions from eight complete textbooks, with common passages, a five-passage limit, and a fixed answer generator. On books, Hybrid + Jev achieves the highest observed evidence coverage (94.1%), compared with 88.7% for Jev full scan and 81.3\% for OpenAI dense retrieval. Full scans examine every passage initially, yet later reduction steps can discard relevant evidence. Higher evidence coverage also does not consistently produce better answers: Hybrid + Decisions achieves the highest observed book Answer Accuracy among retrieval methods (0.892), despite recovering less reference evidence. Full scanning incurs substantially higher latency on books under the tested deployments, while reusable dense retrieval has lower projected API cost than paid decision-based methods as queries accumulate. Most QASPER articles already fit within the hybrid candidate pool, limiting the benefit of scanning. These results highlight evidence retention, answer quality, and reuse cost as complementary criteria for choosing a long-document retrieval strategy.
papers.summary: The study asks whether scanning every passage of a long document actually beats index-based retrieval in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It compares 11 configurations covering lexical, dense, hybrid-reranked and full-scan approaches on 396 `QASPER` questions and 80 questions drawn from eight full textbooks, with a fixed answer generator. On books, `Hybrid + Jev` recovers the most evidence (94.1%, versus 88.7% for a full scan), since later reduction steps in full scans can discard relevant passages. **Higher evidence coverage does not reliably produce better answers**: `Hybrid + Decisions` gets the best answer accuracy (0.892) despite recovering less evidence, while full scanning adds substantial latency and reusable dense retrieval is cheaper as queries accumulate.

papers.title: Transformers as Generic Deep Neural Networks: Exact Compilation, the Cost of Removing Activation-Activation Products, and Multi-Agent Attention Clustering
papers.abstract: Transformers are deployed as a special model class. Neural processing units (NPU) add dedicated operators for attention and normalization, and quantization relies on Transformer-specific algorithms. We show the computation does not force this. Every Transformer block, with attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network built from fixed affine maps, routing and the square, sigmoid and inverse square root, plus GELU or its sigmoid approximation. Without activation-activation products, every transform-wise compilation adds at least $N^2$ scalar nonlinear evaluations per head for dense scores. Keeping that one operation type removes this cost; its elementwise form, present on every surveyed NPU, suffices with the sigmoid and inverse square root. For top-$k$ attention with exchangeable tail scores, we prove that exact or conditional-mean tail mass gives an unbiased, minimum-mean-square-error estimate of the attention distribution, while tail drop is conditionally biased. When queries or agents cluster, centroids choose the keys first, reducing the number of computed scores from $N^2$ to $Nk$ per head. On DeiT-Tiny, MambaIRv2-Light and Pythia-70M the compiled models match their references with all keys, standard post-training quantization applies, and the exact tail-mass estimate beats tail dropping with half as many keys on DeiT-Tiny and, for $k\le8$, on Pythia-70M.
papers.summary: The authors show that every Transformer block, including attention, LayerNorm and a GELU MLP, **compiles exactly into a generic deep neural network** built from fixed affine maps, routing, and a few elementwise nonlinearities. This suggests neural processing units (NPUs) do not need dedicated attention operators. They prove that without activation-activation products such a compilation needs at least N² extra nonlinear evaluations per head, and that the elementwise product found on every surveyed NPU removes this cost. For top-k attention, they show that estimating the dropped tail mass is unbiased while simply dropping the tail is biased, and that clustering queries around centroids reduces score computation from N² to Nk. Compiled versions of `DeiT-Tiny`, `MambaIRv2-Light` and `Pythia-70M` match their references and work with standard post-training quantization.

papers.title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
papers.abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
papers.summary: The authors test whether classically simulated quantum layers help vision-language models (VLMs). They insert 4- and 8-qubit circuits into, or substitute them for, components of `LLaVA-OneVision` at several locations. On the `Visual Spatial Reasoning` dataset, adding a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches **80.7% accuracy, 2.28 points above classical full fine-tuning**. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer keeps 79.22% accuracy with 13 million fewer trainable parameters. The gains depend heavily on placement: earlier replacements hurt accuracy, fewer parameters do not reliably cut compute, and robustness was also assessed under six attack settings.

papers.title: Black-Box Red-Teaming of Multi-Agent Systems via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user. Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.
papers.summary: Black-box red-teaming attacks built for single large language model (LLM) agents work far less well against multi-agent systems (MAS), where many sub-agents never interact with the user directly. `ReMAS` uses reinforcement learning to fine-tune attacker LLMs that generate prompts for extracting system prompts. A rewrite stage first sharpens base attack prompts, then a template-generation stage builds prompts that are more likely to invoke specific sub-agents and expose their system prompts. The method **substantially improves attack success rates over existing black-box attacks** and transfers across backend LLMs and MAS structures.

papers.title: Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
papers.abstract: Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.
papers.summary: Differential privacy (DP) adds noise that grows with the number of trainable parameters, which hurts small health cohorts. The authors therefore test whether parameter-efficient quantum machine learning (QML) keeps more utility than classical models at the same privacy budget. Across three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron and logistic regression models are compared over five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on the clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC but trails on the wearable data, and **no difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests**, so the authors report a trend rather than a quantum advantage. Inference runs on IBM's 156-qubit `ibm_fez` processor stay close to simulation, with mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 to 0.063.

papers.title: From Weather to Enhanced Weathering: Weather Foundation Models for Carbon Dioxide Removal at Operational Scale
papers.abstract: Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO$_2$ per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$$10^5$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. Few-shot prediction, blending the model with a few samples per field, is supported today: TerraNova-ERW recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields with two samples per field, roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field's mean removal, and can cut sampling on our densest fields by 28-98%.
papers.summary: Measuring how much CO₂ Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) removes currently requires dense soil sampling and lab analysis. The authors evaluate five weather foundation models as frozen encoders with lightweight decoders, on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields in Brazil and the US. The best model, `TerraNova-ERW`, built on `Aurora 1.5`, correctly orders measurements within unseen fields, but zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, which the authors attribute to limited data. With just two samples per field, the model **recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields** and roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field's mean.

papers.title: How Does Orthogonalization Adapt to the Neural Network Hessian Structure? A Gradient Self Outer-Product Analysis at Initialization
papers.abstract: Muon orthogonalizes a weight matrix's momentum before each step, and on neural networks this simple preconditioner beats AdamW in a wide range of tasks. Existing analyses explain Muon within general optimization frameworks or on a few specific models, and many of them view orthogonalization as a preconditioner. Since the Hessian is the optimal preconditioner under a quadratic approximation of the loss, these works leave a basic question open: what makes orthogonalization suited to the Hessian of a neural network? Prior work shows that the layer-wise Hessian of a neural network is row-block diagonally dominant, and Muon's implicit preconditioner, the Kronecker product $(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top)^{1/2}\otimes\mathbf{I}$ with $\mathbf{V}$ the momentum, has the same row-block structure exactly when $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ is diagonally dominant. Diagonal dominance of $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ has been observed in language models, but why a neural network produces it has not been explained. This work provides a quantitative asymptotic theory for neural networks at initialization, and points out the intuition that the overparameterization of the weight matrices drives the diagonal dominance. We analyze $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^\top]$, which equals $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top]$ at initialization, in four canonical models: symmetric matrix factorization, deep linear networks, two-layer ReLU networks, and single-layer linear attention. In each case the diagonal entries outgrow the off-diagonal ones at explicit rates as the hidden dimensions grow; for the query, key and value weights of attention the off-diagonal vanishes altogether. Simulations of the four models and experiments on language models at initialization confirm the predicted scaling.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer orthogonalizes momentum before each step, and its implicit preconditioner matches the row-block structure of neural network Hessians when the momentum's self outer-product VVᵀ is diagonally dominant. Why networks produce that dominance has been unexplained. The authors develop an asymptotic theory at initialization for symmetric matrix factorization, deep linear networks, two-layer ReLU networks and single-layer linear attention. In each model, **diagonal entries of the expected gradient outer-product outgrow off-diagonal ones at explicit rates as hidden dimensions grow**, which points to overparameterization as the cause. For attention's query, key and value weights, the off-diagonal terms vanish entirely, and simulations plus language-model experiments confirm the predicted scaling.

papers.title: SSMCGM-Stream: A Streaming State-Space Model for Personalized Diabetes Management
papers.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring supports diabetes management but requires forecasting models that are accurate, interpretable, and efficient enough for real-time deployment. We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space model that maintains a personalized hidden state updated with each incoming glucose reading to provide constant-time forecasting, physiologically structured counterfactual reasoning, and interpretable forecasts through hidden-state attribution. Built on this foundation, SSMCGM-Agent delivers risk-aware, natural-language decision support by translating forecasts, explanations, and counterfactuals into grounded recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. Evaluated on the T1DEXI cohort, SSMCGM-Stream achieves forecasting performance comparable to strong neural baselines while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling continuous on-device diabetes decision support.
papers.summary: `SSMCGM-Stream` is a streaming state-space model for continuous glucose monitoring that keeps a personalized hidden state, updated with each new reading. This gives constant-time forecasts, physiologically structured counterfactuals, and interpretability through hidden-state attribution. A companion system, `SSMCGM-Agent`, turns the forecasts and explanations into risk-aware natural-language recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. On the `T1DEXI` cohort it **matches strong neural baselines at substantially lower computational cost**, enough for on-device decision support.

papers.title: Is In-Context Reinforcement Learning A Posterior Sampler? An Empirical Study
papers.abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.
papers.summary: In theory, the `Decision-Pretrained Transformer` (`DPT`) approach to in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) performs Bayesian posterior sampling, but only under idealized assumptions such as infinite pretraining data. The authors derive two necessary conditions for a posterior sampler, sufficient-statistic invariance and the martingale property, and build statistical hypothesis tests for each. In Gaussian, Bernoulli and linear bandit settings, **both conditions are consistently violated** by practically trained `DPT` models and proposed variants. This suggests ICRL does not behave as a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice, and the tests serve as a reusable toolkit for checking Bayesian behavior.

papers.title: From Common Information to Canonical Correlation Analysis and Beyond: Bridging Information Theory, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to G\'acs and K\"orner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.
papers.summary: Many problems involve several jointly observed views of one process, each mixing a shared component with a view-specific one, and the shared component must be recovered without supervision. This tutorial brings together how statistics, information theory and signal processing have each tackled this problem. It covers the Gács-Körner and Wyner notions of common information, canonical correlation analysis (`CCA`) and its multi-view extensions, and subspace methods for blind multiuser receivers. It then covers kernel, deep and probabilistic nonlinear `CCA`, when the common factor is identifiable, and links to self-supervised learning, **distinguishing exact equivalences from mere analogies** in a self-contained exposition.

papers.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.
papers.summary: The authors test whether large language models (LLMs) that refuse harmful requests in text also refuse when acting as tool-calling agents. They use a 2,304-prompt benchmark of matched text-only, tool-enabled and adversarially framed tool-enabled variants, scored against 20 forbidden actions. Across five models, **10-52% of harmful requests refused in chat still produced unsafe tool calls** under standard tool prompting. A refusal direction in the residual stream weakens in tool contexts and predicts unsafe calls (AUC 0.76-0.86). Restoring or steering along it mostly suppresses tool use rather than producing safer calls, so the authors conclude that agent safety evaluations must examine actions directly.

papers.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
papers.summary: `PerMIT` is a memory architecture for large language model (LLM) agents that defends persistent memory against injection and poisoning. It routes all untrusted, environment-derived values through a finite interface and a confirmation gate. Two integrity theorems, machine-checked in `Lean 4`, guarantee that untrusted memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate, which reduces every attack in the threat model to one auditable decision. It records **zero observed attack success on `Trojan Hippo`**, and logged confirmations let communities of up to 90 agents on `τ²-bench` build shared knowledge bases that improve new agents without promoting injected memory.

papers.title: Attention-based Classification for Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, in which adversarial instructions are embedded in external data processed by a language model, pose a significant threat to the integrity of deployed LLM agents. Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) is a recently proposed white-box detection method that identifies prompt injection attacks by monitoring how a model's attention is distributed between user task tokens and data tokens, claiming dataset-agnostic detection via a scalar focus score threshold. In this paper, we provide the first evaluation of Attention Tracker in a realistic agentic IPI setting using the AgentDojo benchmark, finding that the dataset agnosticism claim does not hold. We find that in agentic environments, long structured tool outputs subvert the fundamental assumptions Attention Tracker makes about attention that the method depends on and produces near-chance detection on AgentDojo across most model families. We propose AttnDA, an extension replacing the scalar threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over the per-head focus score vector, and evaluate both methods in a cross-dataset setting spanning four benchmarks. AttnDA improves detection performance across agentic and tool-integrated benchmarks, though transfer to AgentDojo remains challenging regardless of classifier choice. A covariance ablation further shows that removing inter-head correlation structure substantially contributes to performance, with complex covariance assumptions causing significant degradation on cross-domain data. These results indicate that the attentional distraction signal underlying focus-score-based detection does not transfer reliably to agentic environments, and that learned linear classifiers over head-level attention features offer improved detection performance, provided training data from the target deployment domain is available.
papers.summary: `Attention Tracker` detects indirect prompt injection (IPI) by thresholding a scalar focus score derived from attention, and claims to work regardless of dataset. Evaluated on the agentic `AgentDojo` benchmark, it gives **near-chance detection across most model families** because long structured tool outputs break its assumptions about attention. The proposed `AttnDA` replaces the threshold with a Fisher Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier over per-head focus scores and improves detection across four benchmarks. Transfer to `AgentDojo` remains hard, so learned detectors need training data from the target deployment domain.

papers.title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
papers.abstract: Customized agent deployments define policies over tools, resources, and execution conditions. Providing these policies in the task agent's prompt does not reliably prevent violations. Training a guard requires examples of tool calls that comply with or violate those policies. We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy guards. With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset across ten policy families using 698 scenarios for training data generation and 254 separate held-out scenarios for human-reviewed test sets. Tool calls are executed and their outcomes recorded to help determine whether they comply with the policy. Every violating case uses a permitted tool, requiring checks of arguments, resources, and context rather than tool identity alone. The case construction process supports iterative guard training: an attacker generates requests using retrieved strategies, and the guard is fine-tuned on balanced, environment-verified examples. Training improves policy enforcement even with a fixed archive. Updating the archive further reduces in-domain attack success compared with keeping it fixed. We compare policy-aware task agent self-regulation with a trained policy guard. On PolicyGym, the final guard-based configuration achieves a 40-44% relative reduction in attack success rate and fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.
papers.summary: Placing deployment policies over tools and resources in an agent's prompt does not reliably prevent violations, and training a separate guard model requires verified examples of compliant and violating tool calls. `AgentPolicyForge` executes tool calls in real environments to label them and builds `PolicyGym`, a dataset spanning ten policy families. Every violating case in `PolicyGym` uses a permitted tool, so a guard must check arguments, resources and context rather than which tool is called. An attacker-guard loop iteratively fine-tunes the guard, and the final configuration achieves a **40-44% relative reduction in attack success rate** with fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.

papers.title: Doob-Based Generative Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob's $h$-transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies.
papers.summary: Diffusion and flow policies are expressive, but their action likelihoods are intractable, which blocks standard policy optimization methods such as `PPO` and `GRPO`. `DoobPO` uses Doob's h-transform to separate the two jobs. It first learns a lightweight ratio model representing the desired policy update, then distills the resulting tilted target into the generative policy through conditional drift matching. The authors prove that this practical objective is **gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective** and that it yields the minimum-energy modification needed for the desired update. On `MuJoCo` continuous-control benchmarks, it performs strongly against diffusion- and flow-policy baselines.

papers.title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.
papers.summary: Drawing on clinical aphasia, the language impairment caused by localized brain damage, the authors ask whether large language models (LLMs) have a functional language structure analogous to the human one. They induce aphasia-like breakdowns using classifier-guided lesioning of circuits and continuous activation steering. Language functions can be isolated to discrete circuits and steering vectors, but they **remain densely entangled, with significant overlap across distinct aphasic profiles**. Steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, while structural lesioning is more constrained.

papers.title: The Optimal Sampler for Diverse TSP Solutions: Characterization, Limits, and Learning
papers.abstract: We address the Diverse Traveling Salesman Problem (D-TSP) that seeks a set of $k$ distinct TSP tours. Each selected tour must not exceed a prescribed multiple of the optimal tour length, while the maximum pairwise Jaccard similarity within the selected set is minimized. This formulation is important for applications requiring both solution quality and fault tolerance, such as logistics planning, robotics, and strategic patrolling. We propose a novel hybrid framework that decomposes D-TSP into a sampling stage and a selection stage. The selection stage is a max-min dispersion problem, for which any approximation better than a factor of two is NP-hard; we therefore focus on the sampling stage. Our contributions are both theoretical and empirical. Theoretically, we give two end-to-end guarantees for the optimal sampling distribution, from two perspectives: including an optimal set in the sampled pool, or having at least $k$ mutually distant tours in the pool. The second reduces the number of samples from exponential to linear in $k$, at the cost of weakening the benchmark from the best $k$ tours to the best $\beta k$ for some $\beta > 1$. For practical use, we prove that a pipeline that samples spanning trees and then converts to tours does not hurt the quality of the pool in principle. Empirically, both objectives are learnable, and our experiments not only validate the analysis but also outperform the baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, by a single trained model with no fine-tuning.
papers.summary: The Diverse Traveling Salesman Problem (D-TSP) asks for k distinct tours, each within a set multiple of the optimal length, while minimizing their maximum pairwise Jaccard similarity. The authors split it into a sampling stage and a selection stage. Because the selection stage is hard to approximate better than a factor of two, they focus on sampling and give two end-to-end guarantees for the optimal sampling distribution. One guarantee **cuts the required samples from exponential to linear in k** at the cost of a weaker benchmark, and they prove that sampling spanning trees and converting them to tours does not degrade the pool. A single trained model beats the baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances without fine-tuning.

papers.title: Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective
papers.abstract: Tokenization that partitions time series into subsequences has become a foundational paradigm in modern time series modeling. However, we find that current tokenization strategies inherently introduce spectral distortions, forcing the learned representations to diverge from the true underlying patterns such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, thereby impairing model performance. Through theoretical analysis from a frequency perspective, we derive the boundary conditions under which such distortions occur. To overcome this distortion, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data. TimeFT obtains tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting, and Nyquist sampling. The method is parameter-free, incurs negligible computational complexity, and can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizers. Our extensive experiments on diverse tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that TimeFT consistently and significantly improves performance.
papers.summary: Splitting time series into subsequences (patches) is now the standard way to tokenize them, but the authors argue it introduces spectral distortions that push learned representations away from the true trends, periodicity and seasonality. A frequency-domain analysis gives the boundary conditions under which these distortions occur. The proposed tokenizer, `TimeFT`, builds tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting and Nyquist sampling. It is parameter-free, adds negligible compute, can replace existing tokenizers directly, and **consistently improves forecasting, classification and anomaly detection**.

papers.title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL) requires both efficient rollout generation and training on long sequences. However, the memory requirements and model-specific operators of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next make this difficult with existing open-source implementations. To resolve these limitations, we introduce FlashNext-RL, a model-specific RL training optimization framework based on prime-rl, with vLLM for software engineering (SWE) rollout generation. Our main focus is BF16 training of the full 48-layer model on a single 8xB200 node, with the first two layers, the n-gram table, the sparse-attention indexer and the multi-token prediction head frozen. We optimize host offload, gradient accumulation and the kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. In the full-model development study, non-padding training throughput increases from approximately 395 tokens/s/GPU in the initial 32K-token configuration to 4,438 tokens/s/GPU in the optimized 131K-token configuration, with hardware matmul throughput (aka without considering the cost of attention components) increasing from approximately 20 to 213 TFLOPs/GPU. A controlled cumulative study on an 8-layer model further quantifies the contributions of individual optimizations. Together with three inference nodes, the system supports a live SWE RL run with a target batch of 1,024 trainable rollouts and a 131,072-token context limit. Over steps 5-15, an iteration takes 22.4 minutes on average, with bounded entropy and trainer-sampler mismatch KL. These results highlight the importance of tailoring RL training to the model's architecture, memory layout and kernel requirements, rather than relying only on general-purpose RL infrastructure.
papers.summary: Existing open-source RL stacks struggle with the memory demands and custom operators of `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` when running long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning (RL). `FlashNext-RL` is a model-specific training framework built on `prime-rl`, with `vLLM` generating software engineering (SWE) rollouts. It trains the full 48-layer model in BF16 on a single 8xB200 node by optimizing host offload, gradient accumulation, and kernels for mixture-of-experts, sparse attention and the gated residual stream. Training throughput rises from about 395 to **4,438 tokens/s/GPU** at a 131K-token context, and with three inference nodes the system sustains a live SWE RL run of 1,024 rollouts per batch at about 22 minutes per iteration.

papers.title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract:
A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce \textsc{VeriEvolve}, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent. From task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them. During each round of workflow evolution, the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds, VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases.
  Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. Cross-environment studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, and GitHub further expose complementary limits from observability, state representation, and search/execution capacity. These results show that executable evaluators can be synthesized and used to guide search when task success is observable and an external verifier is available for calibration.
papers.summary: Self-improving agents need a reliable fitness signal, and realistic stateful tasks rarely provide one. `VeriEvolve` builds the evaluation layer first: from the task instruction alone it synthesizes challenge states plus an executable evaluator, freezes that evaluator as the fitness signal while the agent workflow evolves, and between rounds refines it using counterfactual test cases taken from strong and weak runs. On all 30 `MCPMark` Filesystem tasks, the evaluators agree with 113 of 122 held-out states. Evaluator-guided evolution raises externally verified success **from 6/30 to 18/30 for `GLM-5.2`** and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude. Follow-up studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion and GitHub show the approach is limited by how observable the environment is, how its state is represented, and how much search and execution capacity is available.

papers.title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
papers.abstract: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.
papers.summary: The authors analyze a Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) under energy kernels, adding a jump term that moves mass toward smaller values of the first variation. They prove global well-posedness under density and moment assumptions. They also show that zero jump dissipation forces the measure to equal the target, which yields **convergence to the target from any finite-second-moment initial data**. A collision-free particle system with nonincreasing energy, along with mean-field and propagation-of-chaos results, completes the analysis.

papers.title: Enhancing Cross-Grade Generalization in Banana Variety Classification via Hybrid CNN-Transformers and Knowledge Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: In recent years, automated fruit classification systems have become a more critical component in precision agriculture for efficient yield estimation, quality control, and supply chain optimization. However, they still face significant challenges under varying quality, fruit maturity, illumination, texture degradation, morphological attributes, domain shift, and post-harvest handling conditions. In this study, we address the challenging issue of cross-grade banana variety classification. This is a real-world setting where models that have been trained on specific quality grades must generalize to unseen grades to handle significant domain shift. Under a rigorous Leave-One-Grade-Out evaluation protocol, we present a thorough comparative analysis of CNNs, ViTs, and dual-stream hybrid architectures using a large-scale dataset of 31,678 banana images with three varieties and three quality grades. Specifically, to address the drawbacks of single-paradigm frameworks, we present a dual-stream Swin ResNet hybrid framework enhanced with KL-divergence-based self-distillation to align probabilistic feature representations across the CNN and Transformer streams. Comprehensive experimental analyzes show that the presented hybrid framework with KL-divergence based self-distillation achieves better overall performance, i.e., it attains a mean accuracy of 81.25% and significantly surpasses CNN and Transformer baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the hybrid framework in this study improves discriminative feature transferability, improves attention localization, and stabilizes optimization.
papers.summary: Banana variety classifiers need to work on quality grades they never saw during training, a domain-shift problem evaluated here with a Leave-One-Grade-Out protocol on 31,678 images covering three varieties and three grades. The authors compare CNNs, vision transformers (ViTs) and hybrid models, and propose a dual-stream `Swin`-`ResNet` hybrid in which KL-divergence self-distillation aligns the predictions of the CNN and Transformer streams. The hybrid reaches a **mean accuracy of 81.25%**, beating the single-paradigm baselines.

papers.title: Local and Sparse Kernel Operator Learning for Incompressible Flows: An Operator Lagrange Formulation
papers.abstract: We present a local and sparse kernel method for learning the solution operators of incompressible flows. It builds on our earlier property-preserving kernel method, whose global output reconstruction and dense operator regression scale poorly. Our method replaces the global output reconstruction by local divergence-free interpolants with divergence-free polynomials of any degree, solved in parallel on the GPU. These interpolants are divergence free, periodic on periodic domains, and, with a multiscale kernel, approach Kolmogorov statistics under refinement. A compactly supported kernel, positive semidefinite in any input dimension, makes the operator regression sparse. Its support radius, and hence the sparsity, is fitted to data, and optional affine polynomials in the input capture global trends. Operator Lagrange weights join the two. They cost one sparse solve per new input and act on the training fields before the output reconstruction, so their local coefficients are never formed. We show that, unlike direct evaluation, Lagrange evaluation does not amplify solve errors by the cancellation among spatial coefficients. On ten fluid benchmarks, validation selects sparse matrices nearly everywhere, with densities that mostly decrease as the training set grows, and affine augmentation lowers the error by more than an order of magnitude for forced isotropic turbulence. These sparse models are at least as accurate as our earlier dense method and more accurate than neural operators. Lagrange evaluation is as accurate as direct evaluation with local output reconstructions, and up to nearly three orders of magnitude more accurate with global ones. We also present GPU timings and storage.
papers.summary: An earlier property-preserving kernel method for learning solution operators of incompressible flows scaled poorly because it reconstructed outputs globally and used dense regression. The new version replaces global reconstruction with local divergence-free interpolants solved in parallel on the GPU, uses a compactly supported kernel whose support radius (and therefore sparsity) is fitted to data, and connects the two parts through 'operator Lagrange weights' that avoid amplifying solve errors. Across ten fluid benchmarks, the sparse models are at least as accurate as the dense method and more accurate than neural operators. Adding affine terms **cuts error by more than an order of magnitude** on forced isotropic turbulence.

papers.title: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Compound AI System for Head and Neck Proton Radiotherapy Planning
papers.abstract: Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.
papers.summary: Proton pencil-beam scanning (PBS) radiotherapy planning has to balance competing clinical objectives against each physician's preferences. In the proposed compound system, a policy trained with proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) first generates candidate plans automatically. An LLM multi-agent layer then refines difficult cases through conversation: a planning agent proposes evidence-backed adjustments, an evaluation agent checks metrics and constraint violations, and a chatbot provides the interface. The planning agent is built on `Qwen3-14B` and post-trained with supervised fine-tuning and `GRPO`. On 21 head-and-neck cancer patients, the post-trained model **improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing ones** better than the base LLM.

papers.title: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel. New draft-training objectives are usually credited with the acceptance they add over cross-entropy on externally written responses, yet many pipelines let the target rewrite them. We ask how much of that gain survives. With a vision-language target and a block drafter, we train three objectives on four versions of one corpus: cross-entropy on corpus tokens, token-level distillation from the target, and distillation gated to positions that would survive verification. Distillation and the gate add large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration, distillation adds a smaller gain and the gate little or none. The shrinkage persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures and, for distillation, initializations and learning rates. Most of it remains at matched supervised length and at each objective's best measured training length. A second vision corpus shows the shrinkage, as does a text-only replication, for distillation also with an autoregressive drafter. Objective gains should therefore be measured against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRegeneration.
papers.summary: New draft-training objectives for speculative decoding are usually measured against cross-entropy training on externally written responses, but many pipelines have the target model regenerate that data first. Using a vision-language target and a block drafter, the authors compare cross-entropy, token-level distillation, and a verification-gated distillation variant on four versions of the same corpus. Both distillation methods show large gains on external responses, but **after target regeneration, distillation's gain shrinks and the gated variant's nearly disappears**. The effect holds across data orders, verifiers, temperatures, a second vision corpus, and a text-only replication, so the authors recommend measuring objectives against a target-regenerated baseline and across training lengths.

papers.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
papers.abstract: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.
papers.summary: Writing extended reality (XR) applications depends on continuous user motion, spatial input and environmental sensing, which existing coding-agent benchmarks do not test. `GenXR-Bench` provides 112 expert-written tasks covering feature implementation, bug repair and full application generation. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual checks, and they match blinded expert judgments 96.5% of the time on consumer XR hardware. Across 10 models, **the best configuration reaches only 50.9% Pass@1**, with recurring failures around asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding and embodied interaction semantics.

papers.title: Inheritance as an Admission Test for LLM Prompt Merge Operators
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often improved by iterating until a fixed verifier is done. Once that verifier saturates, the loop has nothing left to climb. We instead score agents against the current population, and a frozen panel records whether anyone got better. The panel mean can rise inside the seeds by elimination alone. We therefore count a run as training only when its final mean beats the best generation-zero member. A merge is admitted only when the child moves toward the donor, past the child the same operator produces at zero dose, and the lower confidence bound on that movement reaches half the requested dose. That is the admission test. A detectable shortfall rejects the operator, and the test is otherwise undetermined. We keep realised fitness \phi as the selector and reference performance \theta as the unused ruler. Every measurement uses gemini-3.1-flash-lite on one negotiation task, and no fixed-oracle arm was run. In the open loop, tactic append grafts short donor rules and is admitted. Free rewrite moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected. Template append pastes raw donor replies into the child. Its movement clears the bound on the first probe but not on the re-probe, and it is left undetermined. A held-out re-probe on the five situations the merge never saw confirms that both appends move, and it does not rescue free rewrite. Neither append rises with the dose. Constrained rewrite is admitted in the open loop and was not run in the closed loop, which changes only the operator. The population, the scores and the task stay fixed. No free-rewrite run beats the best generation-zero member. Every tactic-append run and every template-append run does. Sampled loop children keep that split. Free rewrite moves no further toward the donor, and both appends still clear the bound, by less than in the open loop.
papers.summary: Once a fixed verifier saturates, an LLM agent improvement loop has nothing left to climb. The authors instead score agents against the current population and propose a statistical 'admission test' for prompt merge operators: a merge is accepted only if the child measurably moves toward the donor's behavior by at least half the requested dose. All experiments use `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` on a single negotiation task. Appending short donor tactics is admitted, while free-form rewriting moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected. **No free-rewrite run beat the best initial population member, while every append run did.**

papers.title: Dissimilarity-Based Markov Decision Processes for Stabilizing State Distributions
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for stochastic systems typically optimizes expected cumulative rewards, while reliable and repeatable behavior also depends on how the state distribution evolves over time. Optimizing expected return alone does not guarantee that this distribution converges to a desired target or remains stable. This paper develops a theoretical framework for learning policies that stabilize state distributions. We formulate the problem as a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its dissimilarity to a target distribution. We establish sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable. To support policy learning, we introduce a finite-dimensional representation of distributions and show how stability guarantees for its parameter dynamics extend to the underlying state distributions. We further develop certificates for the learned policies, including their deployment using estimated distribution parameters. These results quantify how learning and estimation errors affect the guarantees and identify conditions under which learned policies retain asymptotic stability. For practical implementation, we combine distribution estimates and target-dependent rewards with PPO and SAC. A computable example on a linear system illustrates the proposed theoretical certificates. Furthermore, experiments on a HalfCheetah task demonstrate the benefits of distribution feedback and explicit target matching for regulating the velocity distribution.
papers.summary: Maximizing expected return does not guarantee that a stochastic system's state distribution converges to, or stays at, a desired target. The authors formulate a Dissimilarity-based Markov Decision Process (DMDP), in which the policy acts on the current state distribution and the objective measures its distance from a target. They give **sufficient conditions under which the optimal policy makes the target distribution asymptotically stable**, plus certificates that account for learning and estimation errors. A practical version that combines distribution estimates with `PPO` and `SAC` is demonstrated on a linear system and on regulating the velocity distribution in `HalfCheetah`.

papers.title: Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits
papers.abstract: Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.
papers.summary: The authors study a common loop in which a component verifier is audited against the full success label on fresh policy outputs and refreshed whenever its score falls. For a conjunctive success condition, as the policy masters one component, failures of that component become rare in the audit data. The audit then increasingly rewards information about the other component, which the authors call **on-policy audit collapse**, and it can end up preferring a worse verifier. They derive exact thresholds and demonstrate the effect on an oracle, a multi-label text task and an ECG study where acting on the audit increased downstream constraint violations. The fix is to audit each component on its own failures and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.

papers.title: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits
papers.abstract: Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work. As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention. Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication. Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.
papers.summary: Tendon-driven dexterous robot hands are expensive, hard to maintain and short-lived, and linkage-driven alternatives struggle to fit three degrees of actuation (DOA) into each finger. `PHD-Hand` uses a novel flexure hinge and spring-steel elastic drive rods to simplify the linkage drivetrain, avoiding most miniature moving parts. As a result, the **hand can be fabricated on a budget 3D printer** and sized close to a human hand. A prototype is evaluated on grasping and object manipulation, alongside new results on the hand's kinematics and control.

papers.title: Gate Initialisation versus Recurrent Dropout and Zoneout in Learning Long Dependencies: A Controlled Study of LSTM and GRU Networks on Synthetic Tasks
papers.abstract: Dropout and zoneout are routinely added to long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, but, to our knowledge, their placements have not been crossed with gate initialisation in a factorial design, and it is not known whether early gradient propagation tells which runs will learn long dependencies. We trained one-layer LSTMs and GRUs on the adding problem and on delayed recall in a factorial grid of 720 runs, crossing conventional and chrono gate initialisation with up to six recurrent regulariser placements at one rate each, with pre-specified follow-ups, and recorded how sensitive the final hidden state was to the input at every lag. Because both tasks supply fresh or exhaustive training data, the study measures the regularisers' effects on optimisation and does not assess generalisation from a finite training set. At lengths chosen to make conventional initialisation difficult, all 360 chrono-initialised runs reached the validation criterion within 5000 updates, as did 119 of 120 unregularised runs with a horizon about four times too short or too long, whereas conventionally initialised networks learned slowly or did not reach the criterion within the budget at the longer lengths. Under conventional initialisation, dropout generally delayed learning and zoneout helped only in some conditions. The early input sensitivity added little to predicting which conditions learn once the early validation loss was modelled per task, architecture and initialisation. Within conditions, a flatter early decay went with the seeds that learned, but in a pre-specified test the association was modest (concordance 0.61), condition-dependent and not robust to resampling seeds. The results support chrono initialisation, even with a rough horizon, on such tasks.
papers.summary: A factorial study of 720 runs crosses gate initialization (conventional or 'chrono') with up to six placements of recurrent dropout and zoneout in one-layer long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, trained on the adding problem and delayed recall. Because training data is fresh or exhaustive, the study measures effects on optimization rather than generalization. **All 360 chrono-initialized runs learned the long dependencies within 5,000 updates**, even when the assumed time horizon was about four times off, while conventionally initialized networks learned slowly or not at all, and dropout generally slowed them further. Early measurements of gradient sensitivity added little to predicting which runs would succeed.

papers.title: GRAIL: From Saliency to Semantics in Time-Series Explanation
papers.abstract:
Explaining a time-series model requires both locating the evidence and extracting meaningful knowledge from it. Yet a single timestep is not a semantic unit: the meaningful patterns live across many samples, not in any one of them. Per-timestep saliency is therefore noisy, high-dimensional, and unstable. Existing methods address this by introducing fixed-size windows and treating them as independent players in a cooperative game. Evaluating a coalition of such players requires defining a ``baseline'' region, which prior work tackles with fixed counterfactuals (e.g., a flat line, noise, or a spectral surrogate). This choice frequently dominates the resulting explanation, obscuring the model's true decisions.
  To address these issues, we propose GRAIL, a region-based time-series explanation framework that uses domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and the QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players. We describe each region with human-readable features and generate counterfactual baselines with an on-manifold conditional generator. Such a choice of players also admits non-temporal features: static covariates enter as singleton players attributed with the temporal regions on one scale, so a patient's tabular evidence (e.g., age, sex) is weighed directly against the signal. We attribute the predictions to the features via Owen values with common-random-number variance reduction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that the proposed framework produces faithful and robust explanations, evaluated under matched on- and off-manifold operators, offering meaningful knowledge to domain experts.
papers.summary: Per-timestep saliency explanations for time-series models tend to be noisy and unstable, and window-based methods depend heavily on arbitrary baselines such as flat lines or noise. `GRAIL` instead treats domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players in a cooperative game. It describes each interval with human-readable features and generates on-manifold counterfactual baselines with a conditional generator. Static covariates such as age and sex enter the same game, and attributions are computed as Owen values with variance reduction.
