Experiments on synthetic and real data show **faithful and robust explanations** under matched on- and off-manifold evaluations.

papers.title: HumanCentric-Scenes-AI: A Human-Curated Multimodal Dataset of AI-Generated Human-Centric Scenes Across Surveillance, Occupational Portraits, AI-Edited Images, and Short-Form Video
papers.abstract: We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56 AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and per-stimulus metadata. We report depicted-gender distributions from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset and subject-category coverage for the Video subset. HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research, and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of generative models.
papers.summary: `HumanCentric-Scenes-AI` is a manually curated set of 296 photorealistic AI-generated stimuli depicting people, intended mainly for human-perception research. It has four subsets: CCTV-style surveillance images, gender-paired portraits for 64 occupations, real photos with AI-edited regions, and short videos. Each item comes with its file, the generation prompt where recorded, and metadata. The authors compare depicted gender in unprompted occupational generations with U.S. labor statistics and report that **edit-region size is associated with zero-shot detection difficulty**, positioning the dataset for calibrating AI-image detectors and auditing generator bias.

papers.title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
papers.summary: LLM-based specification synthesis for C code has focused on functional contracts and loop invariants, largely ignoring frame conditions, which state which memory locations a function may or may not modify. The proposed approach extracts frame-relevant information from code property graphs (CPGs) and uses it to guide an LLM toward accurate ANSI/ISO C Specification Language (`ACSL`) frame specifications that capture region separation and data dependencies. On 84 real-world functions, it produces **error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of them, a 179% relative improvement** over prior techniques. Plugged into existing ACSL synthesis frameworks, it improves frame-specification generation by up to 61.9%.

papers.title: ART-MPG: Autoregressive R/T Manifold Path Guiding
papers.abstract: Specular chains concentrate important transport in small regions of path space and the structure depends on chain topology. We introduce ART-MPG, a compact neural model that samples chain length, an autoregressive reflection/transmission (R/T) string, and a direction from a topology-conditioned four-component von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture. We extend the repeated trial weighting in Manifold Path Guiding (MPG) by conditioning retry sampling on both chain length and the sampled R/T string, accounting for its known mass outside the stochastic re-hit trials. For a fixed proposal and target chain, this preserves the ideal expectation while reducing the expected retry count and reciprocal-estimator variance compared with retries conditioned on chain length alone. We distinguish the formal unbiasedness result from the capped and clamped renderer used in experiments. We evaluate fourteen scenes across a range of samples per pixel (SPP) against existing online and offline rendering algorithms. Our method consistently produces lower mean squared error at equal SPP than the online and offline baselines, with lower standard deviation across runs.
papers.summary: In physically based rendering, light paths that bounce through chains of mirror-like (specular) surfaces carry important energy concentrated in tiny regions of path space, which makes them hard to sample. `ART-MPG` is a compact neural model that samples the chain length, an autoregressive string of reflection and transmission events, and a direction from a topology-conditioned von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture. It extends the retry weighting of `Manifold Path Guiding` to condition on the sampled event string, which keeps the estimator unbiased while reducing retries and variance. Across fourteen scenes, it **consistently achieves lower mean squared error at equal samples per pixel** than online and offline baselines.

papers.title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
papers.abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.
papers.summary: A 'typed decision' returns a probability for each option in a fixed set from a single forward pass, read from a language model's logits or a small head, rather than by generating and parsing text. In the first part of the paper, a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 `LoRA` adapter replaces a frontier LLM judge for triaging about 148K agentic coding sessions. It judges 1,000 sessions in about three GPU-minutes at **roughly 1% of the frontier judge's cost**, and the frontier judge's stored labels turned out to match a fresh consensus on only 26.9% of sessions. In the second part, the public `Eikos` recipe applied to 1B to 35B backbones yields a 35B model scoring 79.3% on the hard tier of `JevBench`, statistically on par with the commercial reference, though retraining on a later data release shifted one small model's score by 11.7 points.

papers.title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
papers.abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.
papers.summary: A model's current predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. The authors formalize this through two operations: Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT), which covers protected repair of existing behavior, and Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT), which covers forming and renewing trainable structure, and they characterize how the two constrain each other. A finite construction shows that combining them can produce learning responses neither achieves alone. Implemented as protected head repair plus fixed-capacity `LoRA` renewal in `Qwen2.5-32B`, **the coordinated policy beat either operation alone in all four comparisons** on teacher-forced exact match.

papers.title: Does Every Instance Count Equally? Order Effects in LLM Multi-Instance Processing
papers.abstract: Users increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to analyse collections of independent inputs, such as product reviews or social media posts, and return a single aggregated answer. This setting requires multi-instance processing (MIP), where a model combines information from multiple instances into one prediction. We study a task in which the model must infer a binary label for each instance, and identify the most frequent label among the full instance set. The correct answer should be invariant to instance order. By evaluating fifteen LLMs across five datasets and seven instance order patterns, with each instance set held fixed across patterns, we find substantial order sensitivity. Accuracy can differ by about 90 percentage points between the best and worst order patterns, with models generally more accurate when majority-label instances appear at the start than when they appear in the middle or at the end. For subsets of models, available reasoning traces and gradient-based attribution reveal uneven emphasis across positions. Traces disproportionately mention early instances, while attribution scores are generally higher near the beginning and end than in the middle. These results show that instance order can systematically bias aggregated predictions, highlighting the need to evaluate MIP across different input arrangements.
papers.summary: When large language models (LLMs) aggregate many independent inputs into one answer, such as labeling a set of reviews and reporting the most frequent label, the result should not depend on the order of those inputs. The authors test this multi-instance processing (MIP) setting on fifteen LLMs, five datasets and seven ordering patterns, keeping each instance set fixed while only the order changes. Accuracy can swing by **about 90 percentage points between the best and worst orderings**, and models do best when majority-label instances come first. Reasoning traces mention early instances disproportionately, and gradient-based attribution scores are higher at the start and end of the input than in the middle.

papers.title: OccJEPA: Occlusion as Masking for Amodal Video Segmentation
papers.abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
papers.summary: Amodal video segmentation predicts an object's full mask in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The current best methods use fine-tuned video diffusion models, which are slow, need a separate depth network, and give a different answer on each sample. `OccJEPA` treats occlusion as masking: it drops the tokens outside the object's visible mask, lets the pre-trained `V-JEPA 2.1` predictor fill them in, and decodes the features with a light head. The resulting model is deterministic and **33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art** while being more accurate on `SAIL-VOS`, `TAO-Amodal` and `Kubric`, and controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than its size.

papers.title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.
papers.summary: Different unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors catch different kinds of anomalies, but running them all as an ensemble means paying the inference and maintenance cost of every detector. `AnoMix` distills several frozen teacher detectors into one lightweight student without any anomaly labels. It normalizes each teacher's scores separately and trains the student with `CoRank`, a ranking objective that turns teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision wherever the teachers agree. Across seven benchmarks the student, **with under 80k parameters**, beats both the individual detectors and static score ensembles, and a zero-shot variant can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models on unseen datasets.

papers.title: The Price of Choice in Selective Prediction
papers.abstract: A selective classifier may be claimed to satisfy a risk-coverage contract if some rule from a predeclared menu (a threshold or a union of $K$ score intervals) attains coverage at least $\kappa$ and error at most $\alpha$. Refuting this existential claim requires ruling out every permitted rule. The intersection-union test (IUT) achieves validity without a multiplicity correction, but its sample cost can increase with menu richness. We characterize this cost and compare it with the optimal audit. For a fixed interior risk target $\alpha$ and gap $\gamma$, the minimax sample size for K-interval menus at coverage floor $\kappa$ is $K(1-\kappa)/(\kappa\gamma^2)$, up to logarithmic factors, in the stated small-gap, large-menu regime; exact IUT attains this rate. The lower bound holds even with a known score distribution, while the upper bound extends to menus of VC dimension $d$. Procedures that refuse to reject whenever any rule appears feasible on the audit sample can pay a linear $K$ cost even when a square-root rate is possible. Reference-free testing reaches a smaller scale under constant-risk alternatives, whereas unknown heterogeneous risks can make the linear cost unavoidable. In simulations with $K=4$, the raw menu cost varies 7.7-fold between $\kappa=.5$ and $\kappa=.95$; after theorem-motivated normalization the endpoint values differ by approximately 5%. Held-out experiments with three VLM judges show positive exact-hiding windows in all 60 split-specific confidence-gate families, with 28/30 contracts chosen on audit-A remaining hidden on untouched audit-B. On a cleaner multi-annotator target, hiding is weaker and transfers in 3/10 resplits. Frozen image and multimodal classifiers show boundary behavior consistent with the IUT guarantee and strong power relative to practical certificates.
papers.summary: A selective classifier abstains on some inputs, and it may be claimed to meet a risk-coverage contract if any rule from a predeclared menu (a threshold or a union of K score intervals) achieves enough coverage at a low enough error. Refuting that claim means ruling out every rule on the menu, and the authors characterize how many audit samples this takes using the intersection-union test (IUT), which needs no multiplicity correction. They show that the minimax sample size grows as **K(1-κ)/(κγ²) up to logarithmic factors**, where κ is the coverage floor and γ the gap, and that exact IUT attains this rate. Experiments with vision-language model (VLM) judges and frozen image classifiers show that richer menus can hide contract violations in practice, and that IUT behaves as its guarantee predicts.

papers.title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.
papers.summary: Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (`RE-ZS-CoT`) is a prompting framework that tells a large language model (LLM) to adopt a domain-expert role before reasoning step by step, without any task examples. Roles are either picked from eight predefined experts (static selection) or chosen by the model itself for each benchmark (dynamic selection). Across 20 LLMs from 2B to 14B parameters and seven arithmetic, commonsense and reading-comprehension benchmarks, the method often beats zero-shot and zero-shot chain-of-thought baselines, with **gains of up to 44 percentage points**. Static and dynamic selection tend to help on the same benchmarks, static roles reach the highest peaks, and roles that do not fit the task hurt performance.

papers.title: Value-Rectified Distillation for Flow-based Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging, a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q, which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R, which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets.
papers.summary: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), distilling a Flow Matching (FM) behavior policy trained on multi-modal data tends to average across distinct behaviors, producing invalid out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Value-Rectified Distillation (`VRD`) recasts distillation as a value-guided alignment of generative trajectories, separating behavioral modes and keeping the high-value actions. It comes in two versions: `VRD-Q`, which uses value quantiles to filter out low-value behaviors, and `VRD-R`, which reorganizes the latent space to isolate high-value trajectories. On `D4RL`, `OGBench` and `Minari`, VRD improves existing generative baselines on continuous control and planning tasks, **especially on multi-modal, non-expert datasets**.

papers.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.
papers.summary: Reward guidance samples a reward-tilted version of a distribution from a diffusion model trained only on the base distribution, usually by adding external terms to the drift or the transition probabilities. The authors propose internal guidance, which leaves the denoiser's output unchanged and instead changes where the denoiser is evaluated. For discrete data embedded in the hypercube {-1,1}^d, **the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input**. Because those inputs would be out-of-distribution for a normally trained network, training adds random diagonal rescalings of the data, which lets a single denoiser sample binary reward tilts, class-conditional outputs and infillings with no fine-tuning.

papers.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
papers.abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R2 over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task-seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p = 0.002). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R2 of 0.755 - 0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
papers.summary: World models that predict how embodied systems respond to actions often break when physical conditions move outside the training range. The authors study two levers: which inputs a predictor is allowed to use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. On a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from interventions cuts mean out-of-distribution (OOD) error from 1.769 to 0.697, close to an oracle mask. For robot link-mass extrapolation in `CausalWorld`, models in which mass enters the dynamics through explicit physical coefficients and a known PD controller **turn out-of-range masses into a predictive gain (median joint R² from 0.609 to 0.727)**, whereas the same inputs sharply degrade MLP and recurrent predictors.

papers.title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
papers.abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images.
papers.summary: Deep learning models for abdominal organ segmentation need large amounts of real medical images, which raises privacy concerns and limits how well they generalize to new scanners and modalities. `ReSeg` trains entirely on synthetic data in two stages. A Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (`GSRNet`) is first pretrained on diverse organ-agnostic synthetic images, and its weights then initialize an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (`OESNet`), which is trained on synthetic images that preserve realistic abdominal layout. On seven datasets spanning CT, MRI and PET, ReSeg **outperforms state-of-the-art methods without using any real training images**.

papers.title: Context-Augmented, Session-Calibrated Blood Pressure Tracking from Photoplethysmography
papers.abstract: Objective.To distinguish the contributions of acquisition context and photoplethysmography (PPG) to session-calibrated blood pressure (BP) tracking.Approach. The original comparison used three repeats of five-fold participant-level cross-validation in 653 AuroraBP participants, excluding calibration-labelled prediction targets. Matched analyses separated context and PPG and removed elapsed-time terms. Later exploratory follow-ups retained PPG, accelerometer signals and three initial cuff readings. Separate studies evaluated pulse-rate fusion and an intraoperative VitalDB model. Main results.The original wearable-state model achieved participant-level mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.697/6.139 mmHg for systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP). Added context reduced MAE by 0.436/0.126 mmHg (97.5% intervals 0.305-0.573/0.053-0.200). In the matched factorial without the external PPG prior, PPG improved on calibration, time and protocol-provided posture/activity by 0.214/0.135 mmHg; removing time left the DBP interval including zero. Standard PPG descriptors contributed, but additional nonlinear/attractor benefit was not established. In a separate follow-up series, a sensor-history ensemble achieved 7.299/5.445 mmHg versus its static-rich reference's 7.363/5.470, small gains of 0.064/0.025 mmHg. Larger DBP errors did not improve uniformly. Quality-weighted fusion reduced pulse-rate MAE from 3.985 to 3.690 beats per minute. VitalDB MAEs remained 15.375/8.833 mmHg despite small PPG gains. Significance. The contribution is a calibrated evaluation framework with explicit controls, reproducible feature-cache-to-results analyses and retained negative findings. The sensor-history gain is exploratory after repeated dataset reuse. Independently estimated wearable states, complete raw-signal reproduction of the supplied richer features, external transfer and clinical adequacy remain unestablished.
papers.summary: The study separates how much acquisition context and the photoplethysmography (PPG) signal each contribute to tracking blood pressure (BP) after a per-session cuff calibration, using 653 participants from `AuroraBP` with participant-level cross-validation. The base wearable model reaches mean absolute errors of 7.697/6.139 mmHg for systolic/diastolic BP. Adding context lowers error by 0.436/0.126 mmHg, and PPG adds only **small gains of about 0.2/0.1 mmHg** beyond calibration, time and posture. An intraoperative `VitalDB` model stays at 15.375/8.833 mmHg, and the authors frame the work as a reproducible evaluation framework that keeps its negative findings rather than as a clinically validated method.

papers.title: Same Answer, Different Reasons: Trace-Level Divergence in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where visible reasoning traces support verification, education, and safety auditing, yet standard evaluations typically measure only final-answer agreement or holistic response similarity. As a result, they establish outcome consistency without determining whether users across languages receive comparable supporting evidence. We introduce a trace-level divergence framework that compares visible reasoning traces as structured sequences, decomposing agreement into structural similarity, order consistency, and holistic similarity, with pair-specific calibration to enable comparison across languages. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs, the natural baseline---embedding each whole response and comparing the two by cosine---systematically overstates agreement: $52.1\%$--$67.3\%$ of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity. This dissociation is stable across sentence encoders and step segmentations, and blind bilingual annotation studies in two English-anchored language pairs show that human judgments align with structural similarity rather than with the holistic baseline. A same-language control shows that the level of divergence is language-specific: two English traces for paraphrases of the same question agree more closely than an English trace and its counterparts in other languages. Our results show that answer-level and holistic evaluations can substantially overestimate the consistency of multilingual explanatory artifacts, motivating trace-level evaluation for reliable multilingual deployment.
papers.summary: Multilingual large language models are usually checked for whether they give the same final answer across languages, not whether their visible reasoning is comparable. The authors compare reasoning traces as structured step sequences, scoring structural similarity, order consistency and holistic similarity, with calibration for each language pair. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages and six frontier models, the common shortcut of embedding each whole response and taking cosine similarity overstates agreement: **52.1%–67.3% of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity**. Blind bilingual annotators agree with the structural measure, and two English traces for paraphrased questions agree more closely than an English trace and its translated counterparts.

papers.title: Agentic Music Post-Production
papers.abstract: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.
papers.summary: `MixAgent` is a multi-agent pipeline that mixes music the way audio engineers do, producing an interpretable and editable mixing plan guided by a reference song. A grouping agent routes related tracks into subgroups, a planning agent uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, and a detector and critic then propose numerical parameter fixes. Because simply prompting multimodal models to listen and revise often made mixes worse, the authors built `MixCritic`, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques, and trained the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization. On `MedleyDB`, learned refinement **reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix**, and listeners rated MixAgent's output above mixes from `Qwen3-Omni`, `Gemini 3.8 Flash` and `GPT-4o-audio`.

papers.title: Multi-level Encoder with Global Topic for Task-oriented Dialogue Summarization
papers.abstract: Task-oriented dialogue summarization aims to automatically extract key information to generate domain summaries to improve service efficiency and quality. Task-oriented dialogue is inherently logical and surrounds specific topic. How to effectively capture the dialogue topic and the most salient information becomes one of the major challenges of this task. In this paper, we propose a task-oriented dialogue summarization model utilizing a multi-level encoder with global topic (MLEGT). This model discovers temporal and spatial dependencies through a multi-level encoder, while simultaneously obtaining a simple yet effective global topic in the process of graph construction. It not only captures the crucial details but also breaks the long-range limit and discover the intrinsic structure across the dialogue. Then, a global topic guided pointer mechanism is added into the summrizer to capture ignored but important information, which is helpful to improve the accuracy of the summary. A comprehensive study of two public datasets, including a real-world large-scale Chinese police interrogation dataset and a medical reporting service dataset proves the superiority of our method on several strong baselines.
papers.summary: Summarizing task-oriented dialogues means capturing the conversation's topic and its most important details, which can be spread across a long exchange. The proposed multi-level encoder with global topic (`MLEGT`) models temporal and spatial dependencies across the dialogue and extracts a global topic while building a graph over it. A topic-guided pointer mechanism in the summarizer then pulls in important information that would otherwise be missed. On a large real-world Chinese police interrogation dataset and a medical reporting service dataset, the model **outperforms several strong baselines**.

papers.title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
papers.abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.
papers.summary: One-shot landmark localization finds anatomical landmarks in 3D scans from a single labeled example, but existing self-supervised methods generalize poorly across imaging modalities and fields of view (FOVs). `UNIVERS` learns universal voxel-wise embeddings from pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, randomizing layout, appearance, FOV and pose, and trains them end to end with cross-domain voxel-wise contrastive learning. This pushes the network to ignore domain-specific cues such as contrast and resolution. On three adrenal gland datasets, it **outperforms state-of-the-art one-shot methods, with the largest margins in cross-modality settings**.

papers.title: Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoding of Sperm Whale Coda
papers.abstract: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.
papers.summary: Sperm whales communicate with short click sequences called codas, which carry both a rhythm, set by inter-click intervals (ICI), and the spectral content of the clicks. The Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (`DCCE`) encodes rhythm and spectrum separately before fusing them, and is evaluated with linear probes on social-unit, coda-type and individual identification across 1,383 codas. It reaches **mean macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597** for unit/type/identity on random splits, though raw ICI features remain best for coda type and simple ICI-plus-spectral statistics are a stronger identity baseline. Date-grouped and year-holdout evaluations expose generalization limits, and the authors make no claim of general architectural superiority.

papers.title: DriftNeRF: Cross-Ray Density Drifting for Sparse-View Neural Radiance Fields
papers.abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We attribute a specific, measurable defect to the objective itself: the rendering loss is a sum over independent rays and contains no term comparing densities that different rays assign to the same region of space, so nearby 3D points can settle on contradictory densities while every training pixel is reproduced correctly. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. We then close the gap with DriftNeRF, a drop-in regularizer that instantiates the drifting-field template on density samples: a masked exponential kernel aggregates densities from nearby points on other rays into a stop-gradient consensus target, and the resulting drifting field penalizes unsupported disagreement while leaving agreed-upon boundaries intact. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. On NeRF-Synthetic it reduces residual disagreement by an order of magnitude, and across NeRF-Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF it improves 3-view PSNR over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline by 0.42-0.65 dB and remains competitive with sparse-view Gaussian pipelines under a matched protocol without their depth, flow, or covisibility preprocessing.
papers.summary: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) degrade sharply with only a few input views, and the authors trace part of this to the training loss itself: each ray is scored independently, so different rays can assign contradictory densities to the same region while still reproducing every training pixel. They measure this cross-ray density disagreement during training and find it tracks held-out quality in the sparse-view regime. `DriftNeRF` is a drop-in regularizer that pulls each density sample toward a consensus of nearby samples on other rays, needing no pretrained model, external geometry or extra images. It cuts disagreement by an order of magnitude on `NeRF-Synthetic` and **improves 3-view PSNR by 0.42–0.65 dB** over the strongest MLP-NeRF baseline across `NeRF-Synthetic`, `DTU` and `LLFF`.

papers.title: GRAM: Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging via Subspace Alignment
papers.abstract: Merging different models into a single model is highly desirable for multi-task deployment, particularly in regulated domains like healthcare. In such settings, models are often locally fine-tuned due to strict data privacy policies, necessitating that aggregation operates exclusively on the fine-tuned weights. Existing methods apply a uniform merge across all tasks, ignoring the geometric relationships among their learned subspaces. When task updates occupy misaligned subspaces, projecting them onto a shared low-rank basis discards task-relevant directions, a failure mode named \emph{subspace interference}. Through this study, we show that the per-task projection error of a merged model is governed by the principal-angle alignment between each task and the shared subspace, so that grouping geometrically compatible tasks provably reduces this error within each group. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging (GRAM)}, which uses the principal-angle geometry of task vectors to decide which tasks should be merged together and then performs a standard SVD-based merge within each coalition; the pipeline requires only the fine-tuned weights at merge time. With only one additional model ($\nK{=}2$), GRAM significantly mitigates subspace interference and consistently outperforms prior merging methods across language understanding (GLUE with Flan-T5), 8-task CLIP vision, and medical instruction tuning (Qwen2-7B-Instruct with four English/Chinese medical LoRAs).
papers.summary: Model merging combines several fine-tuned models into one, which is useful when privacy rules mean only the fine-tuned weights are available, but merging everything uniformly loses task-relevant directions when task updates live in misaligned subspaces. The authors show that each task's projection error after merging depends on the principal angles between that task's subspace and the shared one, so grouping compatible tasks provably lowers the error. Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging (`GRAM`) uses this geometry to cluster tasks and then runs a standard SVD-based merge within each group. **With just one additional model (K=2)**, it consistently beats prior merging methods on `GLUE` with `Flan-T5`, an 8-task `CLIP` vision suite, and medical LoRAs on `Qwen2-7B-Instruct`.

papers.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
papers.abstract: Predicting molecular magnetism often requires electronic-structure calculations with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which are costly to repeat across many molecules. The underlying electronic states can transform as spinors, yet equivariant surrogates typically use only integer-rank features. Inspired by the spinor nature of these electronic states, we develop eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features. We initialize spinor features from eigenvectors of an approximate SOC Hamiltonian and use gauge-covariant message passing with a gauge-invariant readout to make predictions independent of the arbitrary eigenbasis choice. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves zero-field-splitting predictions relative to NequIP, including for unseen ligands. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, eSpinor improves real electron-spin correlations over a Hamiltonian-informed baseline despite similar static crystal-field errors and fewer parameters, while accurately predicting low-field nuclear relaxation in water and after transfer to methanol without retraining. Overall, these results demonstrate that SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing is a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism. We also find that similar static tensor errors can yield different dynamical errors, motivating model selection based on accuracy for the intended physical observables.
papers.summary: Predicting molecular magnetism usually requires expensive electronic-structure calculations with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and equivariant neural surrogates typically ignore that the underlying electronic states transform as spinors. `eSpinor` is an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features, initialized from an approximate SOC Hamiltonian and processed with gauge-covariant message passing and a gauge-invariant readout. It improves zero-field-splitting predictions over `NequIP` on cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, including unseen ligands, and better predicts electron-spin correlations and nuclear relaxation for a dysprosium MRI probe. The authors also find that **similar static tensor errors can produce different dynamical errors**, so models should be selected on the physical quantities that actually matter.

papers.title: MHeatmap: Two-Walk Laplacian Reordering and Mosaic Layout for Rectangular Matrix Visualization
papers.abstract: Weighted rectangular matrices record relations between two types of objects, such as occupations and industries, documents and terms, origins and destinations, or annotated classes and computed clusters. Their heatmaps become difficult to read when arbitrary row and column orders scatter related objects, while equal size cells hide large differences in row and column totals. We present MHeatmap (Mosaic Heatmap), which addresses these problems in two stages. Two-Walk spectral seriation first represents the matrix as a weighted bipartite graph. Ordinary bipartite ordering uses only observed row to column links. Two-Walk also uses length-two walks, so rows that share columns and columns that share rows receive explicit similarity links. Sorting a Fiedler vector of the resulting graph Laplacian gives coordinated row and column orders. The Mosaic layout then partitions a unit square so that row height is proportional to the row total and column width is proportional to the column total, while color represents the observed entry. We prove how the Two-Walk energy combines direct alignment with shared-neighbor smoothness, derive an exact matrix vector product that permits sparse computation, and formalize the tiling and area semantics of Mosaic. Across 300 synthetic matrices and seven real data sets, Two-Walk obtains the lowest normalized 2-SUM in all 15 synthetic regimes and the highest Band@10% in 14. The largest gains occur when shared neighborhoods express the latent relational structure.
papers.summary: Heatmaps of weighted rectangular matrices, such as documents by terms or origins by destinations, are hard to read when rows and columns are in arbitrary order and every cell has the same size regardless of totals. `MHeatmap` first orders rows and columns with Two-Walk spectral seriation, which adds length-two walks to the bipartite graph so that rows sharing columns, and columns sharing rows, are explicitly linked. It then sorts by the Fiedler vector of the resulting graph Laplacian. A Mosaic layout sizes each row and column in proportion to its total. On 300 synthetic matrices and seven real datasets, Two-Walk **achieves the lowest normalized 2-SUM in all 15 synthetic regimes**, with the biggest gains when shared neighborhoods carry the hidden structure.

papers.title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven by Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence from Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul
papers.abstract: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on tens of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries with per-leg reliability annotations through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi, the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts were measured for Baku and estimated for the other four cities, and the comparison involves a single baseline, so the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.
papers.summary: Tourism trip planners usually treat travel times and ratings as exact numbers, even though travel times vary with departure hour and a rating may rest on only a handful of reviews. This planner represents both as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy estimate of a value with a fuzzy measure of how reliable it is, built from routing-service data at six departure hours and from review counts. It then searches for single-day itineraries with an adaptive large neighborhood search under a hybrid loss covering score, carbon, travel time and reliability. Across 150 paired runs in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent and Istanbul, it **lowers trip carbon by 19.3% and travel time by 11.5%** compared with a crisp-mean baseline, though the effects vary by city and the authors frame the results as evidence of feasibility rather than a general advantage.

papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement on a Budget: Scoring Code Edits Before They Run
papers.abstract: A coding agent that rewrites its own scaffold has to choose which proposed edit to expand before that edit has been evaluated, and the search then has to return one agent. Each run fits one linear readout on the parent's steering-split solve rate and eight coordinates of the proposed diff, from 96 scaffold edits labeled by four evaluations of a 16-instance fit split, and then freezes the coefficients. HumanEval+ reserves 48 instances as the steering split and Polyglot reserves 64. That split scores parents and keeps an archive of four nodes. Huxley-G\"odel Machine selection draws a parent by Thompson sampling on the steering counts of nodes that have already been evaluated, and it expands the child that parent proposes. Every method then returns the earliest evaluated node whose steering-split solve count is maximal. The tables report the held-out score of that node on the other 100 HumanEval+ instances and the other 145 Polyglot instances, next to the root scaffold and the calibration edit with the highest fit-split label. Twelve runs of GPT-4o return a node at 87.0% on held-out HumanEval+, against 84.2% for the parent-rate ablation. On that split Huxley-G\"odel Machine selection returns 85.1%, the root is at 81.2%, and the calibration-best edit is at 82.8%. On the same split Claude Sonnet 4.5 returns 86.6%, beside 86.5% for Huxley-G\"odel Machine selection, 85.3% for the parent-rate ablation, and 85.1% for the calibration-best edit.
papers.summary: A coding agent that rewrites its own scaffold has to decide which proposed edit to expand before that edit has been evaluated. The method fits a frozen linear readout that scores each candidate from the parent's solve rate on a steering split plus eight features of the proposed diff, calibrated on 96 labeled scaffold edits. Search returns the earliest node with the best steering-split score. Across twelve `GPT-4o` runs, the returned node reaches **87.0% on held-out `HumanEval+`**, compared with 85.1% for `Huxley-Gödel Machine` selection, 84.2% for a parent-rate-only ablation, and 81.2% for the root scaffold, while with `Claude Sonnet 4.5` the gains are marginal (86.6% vs. 86.5%).

papers.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
papers.abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.
papers.summary: Individual patient data are rarely released, so analysts often reconstruct them from published Kaplan-Meier survival curves, but existing tools return a single dataset and define fidelity inconsistently. `StochIKM` defines fidelity explicitly: a reconstruction must match the risk table exactly, follow the digitized curve within image resolution, and respect the printed median, interval and event count. It digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and then stochastically samples a whole set of admissible patient datasets under those constraints, with a solution guaranteed to exist whenever the figure is read correctly. In simulation and on 79 arms from published oncology trials, it **reproduces risk tables and medians more closely than an LLM-improved `IPDfromKM`**.

papers.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Realistic Scenarios Through Representation Engineering
papers.abstract: Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.
papers.summary: The authors study how to detect and reduce reward hacking in realistic settings that involve tool calls and long contexts. They derive steering directions in three ways: difference-in-means over labeled rollouts, gradient optimization, and activations recorded while models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. They apply these through a dynamic intervention that perturbs representations less than uniform residual-stream steering. The intervention **cheaply and significantly reduces reward hacking without major losses in coherence or capability**, and vectors extracted from coding environments generalize to other domains.

papers.title: NormTune: Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Reasoning-Intensive Tasks
papers.abstract: Full fine-tuning has achieved remarkable success on reasoning-intensive tasks, but it often requires substantial GPU resource consumption. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides a promising alternative for reducing this cost, yet we observe a substantial performance gap on reasoning-intensive tasks. In this paper, we present three key observations showing that this gap is closely associated with norm-related under-adaptation, where PEFT produces markedly smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we propose Norm-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (NormTune), a simple yet effective strategy that adaptively strengthens insufficiently updated layers according to their weight-update norms. Extensive experiments show that NormTune consistently enhances multiple PEFT methods across challenging reasoning benchmarks. Specifically, when trained on S1K-1.1, integrating NormTune into rank-8 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA yields substantial average accuracy improvements of 24.24\%, 11.33\%, and 16.21\% , respectively, across AIME 2024, MATH 500, GPQA, and AIME 2025. Moreover, NormTune-enhanced rank-256 LoRA, Bone, and MoRA achieve performance comparable to S1 full fine-tuning, with respective average gains of 2.17\%, 0.93\%, and 3.00\% over this baseline.
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) lags well behind full fine-tuning on reasoning-heavy tasks. The authors trace much of this gap to under-adaptation: PEFT produces much smaller weight-update norms than full fine-tuning. `NormTune` adaptively amplifies the updates of layers whose update norms are too small, and it works with several PEFT methods. Trained on `S1K-1.1`, it improves rank-8 `LoRA` by **24.24% average accuracy** across `AIME 2024`, `MATH 500`, `GPQA` and `AIME 2025`, with gains of 11.33% for `Bone` and 16.21% for `MoRA`, and rank-256 variants match or slightly exceed `S1` full fine-tuning.

papers.title: LaVGuard: Selective Decoding for Contextual Value Drift
papers.abstract: A content-safe response can still promote priorities that conflict with its task: an assistant may demand compliance when asked to preserve autonomy. We study contextual value drift as a task-relative decoding problem with an explicit allowance for change. LaVGuard separates an authorized ten-dimensional profile from a frozen estimate of the values expressed in the visible prefix. A profile-relative density gate selects when to evaluate candidate continuations; their signed progress determines a logit tilt constrained by both changed-position and cumulative-KL budgets. We establish local surrogate improvement, pathwise budget feasibility, and a bound on response-distribution change. Profile conditioning raises boundary TPR at 5% FPR from .58 to .72. At the same .12 mean intervention ratio, the selection study reports risk-safety scores of .88 for LaVGuard and .72 for position-matched edits. The resulting interface makes task priorities actionable while keeping the extent of intervention explicit and bounded.
papers.summary: A response can be content-safe yet still promote values that conflict with the task, for example pressing for compliance when the user asked for autonomy to be preserved. `LaVGuard` treats this contextual value drift as a decoding problem: it compares an authorized ten-dimensional value profile against values estimated from the text generated so far. A density gate decides when to evaluate candidate continuations, and a logit tilt steers generation under explicit budgets on changed positions and cumulative KL divergence, with formal bounds on how much the response distribution can change. Profile conditioning raises detection TPR at 5% FPR from .58 to .72, and at equal intervention rates `LaVGuard` scores **.88 on risk-safety versus .72 for position-matched edits**.

papers.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. Models such as ELF now report autoregressive-level quality at a fraction of the sampling steps of discrete-token diffusion models, and this design principle -- no step-wise discretization -- is what their own ablations credit for the gain. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. Across three ELF scales and on LangFlow, an independent continuous dLLM, GRAFT restores the rare-word share of generated text from 0.42-0.77x the human rate to 0.82-1.10x, a relative gain of 34-109%, and moves the entire word-frequency profile closer to human on every model tested, by 2.7x on ELF-B and 12x on LangFlow.
papers.summary: Continuous diffusion language models such as `ELF` never sample discrete words at intermediate steps. The authors show that this design collapses the lexical long tail: ELF's rarest words appear at only **0.30x the human rate**, a gap that persists from 105M to 652M parameters and that no exposed sampler setting closes. They attribute this to each step averaging over candidate tokens, which pulls rare words toward common competitors. `GRAFT` is a training-free fix that commits rare words while the model is still undecided and then regenerates the sequence with those commitments fixed, raising the rare-word share from 0.42-0.77x to 0.82-1.10x the human rate across `ELF` scales and `LangFlow`.

papers.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
papers.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
papers.summary: Frontier black-box LLM agents lack knowledge of how a specific environment behaves, and existing world models that predict the next observation at every step are costly and often uninformative. A pilot study finds that world-model guidance helps most when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step horizon. The Pitfall Anticipation World Model (`PAWM`) therefore intervenes only when a likely failure looms and warns the agent away from it. It is trained with supervised fine-tuning on synthetic pitfall-labeled data, then with `GRPO` co-training alongside the black-box agent, and it improves `Claude Sonnet 4.5` by **24.3% on `ScienceWorld`** and 7.7% on `WebArena-Lite`.

papers.title: From AI-Free Gates to AI-First Work: How Engineering Students in India Navigate University Education and Campus Placements Without AI Guidelines
papers.abstract: Engineering graduates in India enter a technology sector that is being reshaped by generative AI, yet the route into that sector runs through examinations and campus placement screens that largely exclude AI. Institutions in India have an approved intake of nearly 2.9 million seats in engineering and technology for 2026-2027, but HCI research on how students prepare for AI-mediated work has drawn mostly on Western and East Asian settings. We interviewed 23 students and recent graduates of Indian engineering and computing programmes about how they used generative AI across coursework, examinations and placements, and how they judged their own readiness for work. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we report five themes, covering AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, how participants prepared for placement, how they used AI in coursework, the role of faculty authority and enforcement, and participants' concerns about their readiness for work. Drawing on signaling theory, we discuss what grades and screen scores certify once AI can help produce them, and we offer recommendations for employers, institutions and AI tool designers.
papers.summary: Engineering graduates in India enter an industry increasingly built around generative AI, yet the exams and campus placement screens that lead there largely exclude AI. Through interviews with 23 Indian engineering and computing students and recent graduates, analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis, the authors identify five themes. These cover the gap between AI-first workplaces and AI-free placement screens, placement preparation, AI use in coursework, faculty authority and enforcement, and **students' concerns about their readiness for work**. Drawing on signaling theory, the authors ask what grades and screening scores still certify when AI can help produce them, and they make recommendations for employers, institutions and tool designers.

papers.title: VeeReview: Measuring Build-Verify Pairs in Agent-Authored Pull Requests from a V-Model Perspective
papers.abstract: Context: Reviewing a pull request requires verification evidence that addresses the proposed change. Coding agent benchmarks and studies of pull request outcomes do not directly assess this relationship. Objective: We test whether the V-Model's build and verify pairs can measure verification evidence in pull requests and support comparisons between agent-authored and human-authored changes. Method: VeeReview classifies four build and verify pairs using repository signals and a language-model judge. Three pairs use model judgements constrained by deterministic signals, and a rule over the diff and repository tree decides Module Design-Unit Test. We evaluated VeeReview against a 25-pull request reference set labelled by two raters and applied it to 1,454 matched pairs of agent and human pull requests from 741 repositories. Results: VeeReview assigned lower build-only rates to agent-authored pull requests on all four pairs, contrary to the preregistered hypothesis (mixed-effects odds ratios 0.52 to 0.86). Architecture-Integration was not significant. Standardization for linked issues, shipped tests and size reduced matched-rate differences by 34% to 60%, and the rule-decided pair's standardized interval included zero. The instrument did not meet its preregistered calibration criterion: agreement with adjudicated labels was 4% to 60% against a required 80%, and inter-rater agreement was weak (kappa = 0.154). Conclusions: The rule-decided pair shows that a process measure judged by a language model partly reflects how a pull request is presented rather than the verification work behind it. We report the cohort differences as observations made with this instrument, and we argue that such measures need a mechanically decided component and a validated human reference before they can support comparisons of verification practice.
