papers.summary: `VeeReview` tests whether the build-and-verify pairs of the V-Model can measure verification evidence in pull requests, and whether they can be used to compare agent-authored with human-authored changes. It classifies four pairs using repository signals and a language-model judge, with one pair decided purely by a rule over the diff and repository tree, and is applied to 1,454 matched agent/human pull-request pairs from 741 repositories. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis, agent-authored pull requests had lower build-only rates, but **the instrument failed its preregistered calibration criterion**: agreement with adjudicated labels ranged from 4% to 60%, and inter-rater kappa was 0.154. The authors conclude that LLM-judged process measures partly reflect how a pull request is presented, and that such measures need a mechanically decided component and a validated human reference.

papers.title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.
papers.summary: When LLMs turn natural-language problems into optimization models, checking that the math, the solver code and the reported results agree requires semantic comparison, because equivalent models can look different and inconsistent ones can produce the same objective. `ORSMT` uses exact satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) queries to align decision variables, project away auxiliary variables, prove or refute that feasible regions and objectives match, localize mismatches, and then reconstruct one artifact from another. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, protected selection raises the **model-code match rate from 43.2% to 88.2%**, and certified voting beats `ReLoop` and `Opt-Verifier` on refuted outputs.

papers.title: SAFTER: Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability for Robust Reinforcement Learning under Distribution Shift
papers.abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.
papers.summary: Safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) usually enforce only instantaneous safety, so a robot with limited actuation can still drift into states it cannot recover from. `SAFTER` embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter inside `Soft Actor-Critic` training. One certificate covers current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability and input limits, and it yields an exact minimum-intervention projection. In quadruped navigation it learns with about 30% fewer transitions than baselines, improves success in unseen environments by up to 61.4 points over `SEA-Nav`, and reaches 73-77% success on two real-world maps. Ablations show that **differentiating accurately through the filter is critical**: replacing its Jacobian with the identity drops high-shift success from 61.4% to 6.2%.

papers.title: Where Does Timbre Hide? Localizing Speaker Information in Speech Signals
papers.abstract: Timbre similarity is a key evaluation target for generative speech systems, including voice conversion, speaker-cloning text-to-speech, and zero-shot speech models. When the generated voice does not match the target speaker, the problem often reflects imperfect separation of speaker-related timbre from content, making it important to identify where timbre information resides and which representations still carry it. Using speaker identity as a measurable proxy, we probe frequency bands, phase/magnitude structure, WORLD source/filter decomposition, voiced/unvoiced regions, self-supervised learning (SSL) layers, EnCodec/HuBERT tokens, and a 45-listener test across Mandarin, English, and Japanese speech/singing data. Speaker information is distributed: 1--8 kHz magnitude and vocal-tract spectral-envelope structure dominate perception, above-8 kHz bands remain machine-discriminative, shallow SSL layers expose compact speaker information, and token leakage depends on tokenizer/layer choice. These findings indicate where generation systems should condition on or transform speaker information, and where content, codec, and token pipelines should audit residual speaker leakage.
papers.summary: Voice conversion and speaker-cloning systems often fail to match a target voice because timbre is imperfectly separated from content, so the authors map where speaker information actually resides. Using speaker identity as a proxy, they probe frequency bands, phase and magnitude, `WORLD` source/filter components, voiced and unvoiced regions, self-supervised model layers, `EnCodec` and `HuBERT` tokens, and a 45-listener test across Mandarin, English and Japanese speech and singing. Speaker information turns out to be distributed: **1-8 kHz magnitude and spectral-envelope structure dominate human perception**, bands above 8 kHz remain machine-discriminative, shallow self-supervised layers carry compact speaker cues, and token leakage depends on the choice of tokenizer and layer.

papers.title: From Augmentation to Synthetic Evidence: Evaluating Generated Chest Radiographs at Dataset Intake
papers.abstract: A generated chest radiograph can be useful as declared augmentation, but the same image becomes unsupported evidence when submitted as the record of a real examination. We study this problem by separating three questions: whether an image passes an automated quality check, whether an origin classifier flags it as generated, and whether a trusted record supports the claimed acquisition. In our experiments, Qwen selects up to 20 images from pools of 1,000 existing Cheff-identified or SynthCheX candidates. A receiver evaluates quality with MedGemma and predicted origin with a classifier on frozen DINOv3 features. Quality-based selection raises quality passes from 12 to 19 of 20 for Cheff-identified images and from 8 to 17 for SynthCheX. We find no evidence that selection improves passage through both checks: no selected Cheff-identified image passes both, while uniform, quality, and quality-constrained surrogate selection produce 2, 1, and 2 SynthCheX passes. On unprocessed test images, the origin classifier flags 4,677 of 5,000 SynthCheX images, but it also misclassify 110 of 2,297 NIH (real) images and 568 of 957 genuine images from another collection as fake. Our results further show that JPEG compression reduces SynthCheX-versus-NIH AUROC from 0.987 to 0.841. Even without processing, 152 SynthCheX images pass both pixel checks. These checks can filter submissions, but they cannot verify an acquisition claim. We strongly advocate that source and intended use must be recorded and checked separately for admission of chest radiographs in medical datasets.
papers.summary: A synthetic chest X-ray is legitimate as declared augmentation but becomes false evidence when it is submitted as a real examination. The authors separate three questions: whether an image passes quality checks, whether an origin classifier flags it as generated, and whether a trusted record supports its acquisition. Using `Qwen` to select images from `Cheff` and `SynthCheX` pools, judged by `MedGemma` and a `DINOv3`-based origin classifier, they find that quality-based selection raises quality passes but does not help images evade both checks. The origin detector itself misflags many real images, and JPEG compression cuts its AUROC from 0.987 to 0.841, which leads the authors to argue that **pixel checks cannot verify an acquisition claim** and that source and intended use must be recorded separately.

papers.title: AI-Based End-to-End Automotive Design and Software Development for SDVs
papers.abstract: This paper explores the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enable end-to-end automotive design and software development for Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs). Based on our contributions within the Central Car Server (CeCaS) and follow-up EU-funded projects, we present an AI-driven toolchain integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) to automate the transformation of natural-language requirements into system architectures, executable software, and validation artifacts. The approach emphasizes traceability, consistency, and compliance with safety-critical automotive development requirements. Validation is performed on a centralized vehicle computing platform supporting adaptive cruise control and emergency braking, tested in Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) environments. We discuss current capabilities, practical limitations, and future directions toward increasingly automated, reliable, and quality-assured automotive software development with minimal human intervention.
papers.summary: Building on the Central Car Server (`CeCaS`) and follow-up EU projects, the authors present a toolchain for Software-Defined Vehicles (SDVs) that combines LLMs with Model-Driven Engineering (MDE). The toolchain turns natural-language requirements into system architectures, executable software and validation artifacts while preserving traceability and safety-critical compliance. It is **validated on a centralized vehicle computer running adaptive cruise control and emergency braking** in Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) setups. The paper also discusses current limitations and the path toward more automated automotive software development.

papers.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
papers.abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.
papers.summary: The authors measure psycholinguistic features known to make text harder for humans to process, such as object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies and low-frequency n-grams, in a new cross-domain corpus of AI-generated text. **All nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more rare n-grams than human writers**, and most also use longer dependencies and more stacked nouns, with substantial variation across model families. The authors hypothesize that training for math, code and reasoning creates pressure toward information density at the expense of communication. As a proof of concept, they show that fine-tuning a model under a length penalty pushes its language away from human-like patterns.

papers.title: Carving Radiology Reports at Their Evidential Joints: Anatomical Region Sets as Generation Units
papers.abstract: Organizing radiology reports into independently generated units offers a way to generate fine-grained clinical content and bind it to visual evidence. However, existing methods typically adopt generation-unit structures not directly specified in natural reports or their annotations, introducing additional modeling compromises. We propose RadCarve, which instead defines generation units directly from the anatomical region sets in existing statement-region correspondences, unifying unit formation with visual evidence selection. RadCarve's planner uses composition-specialized query banks to jointly predict unit existence and region composition from the image, iteratively refining both with regional evidence aggregated according to current membership predictions. The generator independently produces each unit's text conditioned on the joint visual evidence of its predicted region set. Compared with strong baselines, RadCarve improves CXRFEScore by 9.4% in unit generation given region sets and achieves 2.4 times the end-to-end binding F1. It also achieves leading report-generation results on Chest ImaGenome and PadChest-GR, using fewer than one-sixth as many parameters as large-scale baselines.
papers.summary: Generating radiology reports as independent units tied to image evidence can yield fine-grained, well-grounded text, but existing methods define those units in ways not found in real reports. `RadCarve` defines each unit directly as an anatomical region set taken from existing statement-region annotations. A planner with composition-specialized query banks predicts which units exist and which regions they cover, and a generator then writes each unit from the joint visual evidence of its regions. It improves `CXRFEScore` by 9.4% and achieves **2.4x the end-to-end binding F1** of strong baselines, with leading results on `Chest ImaGenome` and `PadChest-GR` using under one-sixth the parameters of large-scale models.

papers.title: TeachBack: Learning to Teach via Bidirectional Preference Optimization for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. We find that access to sufficient privileged information allows the Teacher to generate highly accurate trajectories; however, accuracy alone does not guarantee that these trajectories are suitable for Student learning. Direct access to a complete solution may encourage shortened, reference-conditioned derivations that omit the exploration, verification, and self-correction required to solve problems without privileged information. We introduce TeachBack, a bidirectional preference-learning framework for on-policy self-distillation that learns not only from the Teacher but also how the Teacher should teach. TeachBack shapes the Teacher's generation behavior by controlling the length of the reference-reasoning suffix injected into the prompt and by varying the prompt style. While maintaining comparable Teacher accuracy, it encourages the Teacher to explore and re-solve problems, thereby reducing its reliance on the reference solution. At each rollout refresh, the shared policy generates both a privileged Teacher trajectory and a problem-only Student trajectory. A pairwise preference objective uses privileged Teacher trajectories to improve Student learning, while the reversed preference uses the Student's behavior to shape future Teacher supervision under the privileged condition. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show that TeachBack consistently improves Student performance over existing OPSD methods and related baselines.
authors: Linfei Ji (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Haozhao Wang (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Siyu Jiang (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Longtao Xiao (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
Ruixuan Li (Huazhong University of Science and Technology)
papers.summary: In on-policy self-distillation, a model learns from a copy of itself that has privileged information such as the reference solution. That copy produces accurate trajectories, but they tend to be shortcut derivations that skip the exploration and self-correction a student needs. `TeachBack` also trains how the teacher teaches, varying how much of the reference reasoning is injected into the prompt and the prompt style so that the teacher re-solves problems rather than copying. A bidirectional preference objective uses teacher trajectories to improve the student and student behavior to shape future teacher outputs, and it **consistently outperforms existing self-distillation methods** on math and logical reasoning tasks.

papers.title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones. We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it. Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy. We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold. Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models. In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy. Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
papers.summary: World action models (WAMs), which build robot policies on top of generative image or video backbones, generalize very differently depending on which backbone they use. The authors explain this through representational geometry, introducing nuisance orthogonality: the degree to which a backbone's features for out-of-distribution visual variations are orthogonal to the in-distribution manifold. Across image and video backbones, **higher nuisance orthogonality before policy training predicts stronger robustness to visual variation afterward**. Robust WAMs also suppress the feature displacement caused by such nuisances, giving a way to anticipate policy generalization from the choice of backbone.

papers.title: TrainBridge: Agentic NPU Training Optimization Guided by GPU Compilation Evidence
papers.abstract: We study how to improve training efficiency on Ascend NPUs. In the NPU training programs we study, framework-level compilation optimizations such as operator fusion are only partially applied, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable execution overheads. Profiling-guided tuning can address these inefficiencies, but it often requires costly trial and error. To make training on NPUs more efficient, we propose TrainBridge, an agentic approach for transferring GPU optimization guidance to NPU training. TrainBridge uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a task-specific reference for NPU tuning. It extracts optimization intents from the GPU training execution to guide NPU program rewrites and further refines the rewritten program through iterative profiling. Our GPU-to-NPU migration experiments show that TrainBridge achieves an average 1.7x speedup across four workloads covering LLM pretraining, image classification, and vision-language training, and an average speedup of nearly 2.0x across 27 Modded-NanoGPT speedrun records with highly optimized GPU implementations.
papers.summary: Training programs on Huawei's Ascend NPUs often miss compiler optimizations such as operator fusion, leaving fragmented computation and avoidable overhead that is costly to fix through profiling-guided trial and error. `TrainBridge` is an agentic system that uses the highly optimized execution produced by mature GPU compilation stacks as a reference: it extracts optimization intents from the GPU run, rewrites the NPU program accordingly, and refines the result through iterative profiling. It achieves an **average 1.7x speedup** across LLM pretraining, image classification and vision-language workloads, and nearly 2.0x across 27 `Modded-NanoGPT` speedrun records.

papers.title: Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
papers.abstract:
Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide?
  We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting epistemic uncertainty in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent aleatoric variance in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.
papers.summary: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly used in place of deterministic predictors, including for regression. The authors show that **CFM samples often have larger variance than the true conditional distribution**, even for nearly deterministic targets, because the model's uncertainty about an unresolved input dependence shows up as apparent noise in its samples. Synthetic and real-data experiments, along with comparisons to explicit smoothing estimators, show that this excess variance tracks underfitting and shrinks with more training or data. A simplified theoretical analysis explains the effect, and the authors use it to build high-coverage prediction sets for regression targets.

papers.title: ROCOCO: Robust Outline Completion of Occluded Curvilinear Objects
papers.abstract: We propose a learning-based generative model for completing curvilinear features under occlusion by environmental obstacles. To this end, we adopt a flow matching-based approach that supports the inpainting of occluded regions with the appropriate curvilinear features. To eliminate the reliance on privileged information about the occlusion a priori, we also train a UNet-based mask prediction model, which can identify regions for inpainting given only the occluded observation. The components of our approach are validated via experiments using procedurally-generated test cases, and the complete pipeline is validated using large public datasets for curvilinear objects. Against off-the-shelf inpainting baselines, ROCOCO is the strongest method by a wide margin when no occlusion mask is given, and is competitive with mask-supervised inpainting when one is, achieving best on full-image error and second only to LaMa on the occluded region, while using a completer of $7.7$M parameters against LaMa's $51$M and Stable Diffusion's $860$M.
papers.summary: Thin, line-like (curvilinear) structures such as roads or vessels are often partly hidden by obstacles, and standard inpainting methods usually need to be told which pixels are hidden. `ROCOCO` pairs a flow matching generative model that fills in the hidden curvilinear features with a `UNet`-based model that predicts the occlusion mask from the occluded image alone. When no mask is provided, it is **the strongest method by a wide margin** against off-the-shelf inpainting baselines. With a mask, it stays competitive with `LaMa` and `Stable Diffusion` while using a 7.7M-parameter completer, compared with 51M and 860M parameters for those models.

papers.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
papers.abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.
papers.summary: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action such as a payment, several monitors often check it, but monitors that share a base model or read the same poisoned input can fail together. The authors borrow fail-prone system models from distributed computing to define when a rule for combining monitor verdicts is safe (never executes a bad action) and live (never blocks a good one). They test twelve small open-weights monitors, plus `Claude Opus 5.5`, `GPT-6 Astra`, `Gemini 4 Argon` and `DeepSeek-V3.2`, on payment approval. Every reliable fraud approval came through one evidence source and fooled only the monitors that read it, and a rule that counts independent sources instead of votes blocked **0.9% of correct payments versus 7.4%** for the best vote-counting rule at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test still failed, and only adding a rule engine that cannot be persuaded restored a rule that was both safe and live on the measured attacks.

papers.title: Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions
papers.abstract:
Executing vision-language models (VLMs) aboard low-Earth orbit satellites enables flexible processing of observation data without first downlinking it to the ground. On commercial off-the-shelf payloads, however, a request may span multiple execution windows: power and thermal constraints, fault-triggered reboots, and competing payload demands can interrupt inference before it completes. Each shutdown discards volatile activations and KV caches, forcing an unprotected request to repeat work after restart.
  We present OrbitWeaver, a framework that preserves VLM inference progress across onboard interruptions through coordinated checkpointing and recovery. Its phase-aware checkpointing selects recovery boundaries according to the state lifetimes and computational characteristics of vision encoding, language-model prefill, and decoding, balancing storage traffic against recomputation. Its dependency-aware dynamic recovery schedules restoration from partially completed states across the layer and token-chunk dimensions. By overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation, it reduces restart latency; the recovery planner computes an optimal execution order under its scheduling model within 100 ms.
  Experiments on satellite payload hardware using on-orbit telemetry traces show up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD write volume over the evaluated baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth orbit satellites demonstrates that OrbitWeaver retains inference progress and resumes execution across repeated bus-enforced shutdowns.
papers.summary: Running vision-language models (VLMs) on commercial satellite payloads is hard because power limits, thermal limits and reboots can cut off inference mid-request, which wipes activations and KV caches. `OrbitWeaver` checkpoints progress at boundaries chosen per phase (vision encoding, prefill, decoding) and schedules recovery from partially completed states, overlapping checkpoint and weight reads with recomputation. On satellite payload hardware replaying on-orbit telemetry traces, it achieves **up to a 4.07-fold end-to-end speedup** and a 3.56-fold reduction in SSD writes over the baselines. A 72-hour deployment on two low-Earth-orbit satellites showed it resuming inference across repeated shutdowns forced by the satellite bus.

papers.title: A Decade of Learning-Based Control: From Theoretic Foundations to Practical Deployment
papers.abstract: Motivated by ten years of Learning-Based Control Invited Sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), this tutorial paper reviews key advances at the intersection of machine learning and control. We focus on methods that combine the flexibility of machine learning techniques with the structure and theoretical foundations of control to design autonomous systems that are capable, reliable, and safe. We first introduce core notions for establishing stability and safety guarantees, then review approaches that learn dynamics models to improve control under uncertainty, and finally discuss data-driven methods that directly synthesize or learn policies, including reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and Bayesian optimization. We further discuss representative applications and open challenges. The goal is to provide an accessible entry point to the field and to support continued progress toward reliable learning-based control in real-world systems. To support learning and practical exploration, we share implementations and illustrative examples along with our discussion, together with additional resources on our website: https://learning-based-control.github.io/tutorial/.
papers.summary: This tutorial marks ten years of Learning-Based Control sessions at the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC) and reviews methods that combine machine learning with the theoretical structure of control. It starts with the core ideas behind stability and safety guarantees, then covers learning dynamics models for control under uncertainty and learning policies directly with `reinforcement learning`, `imitation learning` and `Bayesian optimization`. It closes with representative applications and open challenges, and **ships code implementations and worked examples** as an entry point to the field.

papers.title: LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation
papers.abstract: Tables in real-world documents, including scientific papers, financial reports, and statistical summaries, frequently use merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Yet the lightweight formats LLMs handle best (Markdown, CSV) cannot express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) impose excessive token cost and parsing complexity. To enable systematic analysis of this trade-off, we introduce a taxonomy decomposing table structure into six atomic features (F1-F6) and corresponding complexity levels (L1-L6), and construct STB (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels. Using this framework, we propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a formally specified, minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and hierarchical headers. Experiments across five state-of-the-art LLMs show that LTEM achieves accuracy comparable to HTML, offers a favorable accuracy-token trade-off relative to HTML and LaTeX, and produces substantially fewer invalid responses than LaTeX; for table generation, LTEM is comparable to MultiMarkdown though HTML is best. We release our taxonomy, benchmark, and format specification to support future research on LLM-table interaction.
papers.summary: The lightweight table formats LLMs handle best, such as Markdown and CSV, cannot express merged cells or multi-level headers, while HTML and LaTeX can but cost many tokens and are harder to parse. The authors break table structure into six atomic features with matching complexity levels and build `STB` (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled set of 1,089 tables. They then propose `LTEM`, a formally specified minimal extension of Markdown that encodes cell spans and hierarchical headers. Across five LLMs, `LTEM` **matches HTML's understanding accuracy with fewer tokens** and produces far fewer invalid responses than LaTeX. For table generation it is comparable to `MultiMarkdown`, though HTML remains best.

papers.title: Reasoning-Search-Augmented LLMs: An Operational Taxonomy, Benchmark Analysis and Controlled Evidence Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive emergent reasoning capabilities, yet they remain constrained by fixed model parameters and finite context windows. Even when augmented with static retrieval, they can produce statements that are unsupported by, or even contradictory to, retrieved evidence. This leads to hallucinations, difficulty incorporating up-to-date information, and failures to correctly interpret or reconcile sources. Recent work addresses these limitations by tightly coupling step-by-step reasoning with interactive search, treating retrieval as an action within an iterative agentic loop rather than a one-shot preprocessing step. This study reviews frameworks that implement such reasoning-search loops by interleaving planning, querying, retrieval, integration, verification, and stopping. We analyze these systems through four architectural axes: retrieval coupling, controller design, knowledge source, and grounding strictness. We separately treat the learning signal as a cross-cutting dimension because prompting, supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning can instantiate the same architecture while producing materially different search, stopping, and grounding behavior. We further distinguish benchmark difficulty from RSA-loop demand and synthesize controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost deltas, avoiding invalid pooling across heterogeneous model backbones, retrievers, corpora, and evaluation protocols. Our goal is to clarify the landscape of reasoning-search-augmented LLMs and outline a unified perspective on the design choices shaping future research.
papers.summary: This survey covers reasoning-search-augmented LLMs, systems that treat retrieval as an action inside an iterative agentic loop of planning, querying, integrating evidence, verifying and deciding when to stop, rather than as a one-shot preprocessing step. It classifies frameworks along four architectural axes: how retrieval is coupled, controller design, knowledge source and how strictly answers must be grounded in evidence. The learning signal (prompting, supervision, preference optimization or reinforcement learning) is treated as a separate dimension, because it can change search and stopping behavior even within the same architecture. The authors **synthesize only controlled within-study ablations and quality-cost comparisons**, avoiding invalid pooling of results across different backbones, retrievers and evaluation protocols.

papers.title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
papers.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.
papers.summary: Existing convergence guarantees for Sharpness-Aware Minimization (`SAM`) assume standard smoothness, which is restrictive. Under the more general (L0,L1)-smoothness condition, the authors show that `SAM` can cycle and its unnormalized variant `USAM` can diverge, because the sharpness-aware step can drift arbitrarily far from the true gradient. They propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (`CS-SAM`), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by curvature upper bounds, and prove **O(1/T) rates on nonconvex objectives** plus linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. In minibatch vision experiments, the (H0,H1) variant achieved the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned `SAM` and `USAM`.

papers.title: Truncated Out-of-Bag Probability Gain: A Noise-Robust Criterion for Random-Forest Wrapper Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Random-Forest wrapper feature selection can use out-of-bag (OOB) predictions as a built-in validation signal, but the criteria that decide each forward step accumulate OOB estimation noise. We propose TOP-Gain (Truncated Out-of-bag Probability Gain), which scores a candidate feature by the mean sample-level increase in the OOB probability of the true class, with decreases truncated at zero. Under a simple noise model, truncation removes about two-thirds of the noise variance contributed by unaffected samples while preserving the signal, and it makes the ranking of candidate features markedly more reproducible. In a pre-registered benchmark on 26 OpenML-CC18 datasets, TOP-Gain achieved the best mean rank in area under the ROC curve (ROC-AUC), accuracy and Macro-F1 among 15 methods; it was significantly better than 13 of 14 baselines and matched the accuracy of VSURF with 21 times less single-core computation. Within an identical wrapper, it selected significantly more stable feature sets than net-gain, Brier, log-loss and accuracy criteria without loss of accuracy. A confirmatory study on 24 further datasets replicated the advantage over all baselines. The accuracy gains were broad rather than tied to specific dataset characteristics, and, as pre-registered, the stability gain grew as relevant features became sparser
papers.summary: Random-forest wrapper feature selection can use out-of-bag (OOB) predictions for validation, but the criteria that decide each forward step pick up OOB estimation noise. `TOP-Gain` scores a candidate feature by the average per-sample increase in the OOB probability of the true class, with decreases truncated at zero, which removes about two-thirds of the noise variance under a simple noise model. In a pre-registered benchmark on 26 `OpenML-CC18` datasets, it achieved **the best mean rank among 15 methods** in ROC-AUC, accuracy and Macro-F1, and matched `VSURF`'s accuracy with 21 times less compute. It also selected more stable feature sets than other criteria, and a confirmatory study on 24 further datasets replicated the results.

papers.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.
papers.summary: Compact vision-language models (VLMs) that locate objects from language prompts are increasingly deployed at the edge in safety-critical systems, but their robustness to physical adversarial attacks has not been compared fairly with that of conventional object detectors. The authors measure whether a patch worn on a person evades detection, using a conditional attack success rate (`cASR`) and splitting failures into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch) and displacement (a box elsewhere). **Grounding VLMs can be as vulnerable as detectors**, and the failure mode tracks a model's output format more than its architecture family. Under distribution shift, VLMs move from omission toward substitution and displacement, which return confident, well-formed boxes that a downstream system cannot easily detect as failures.

papers.title: Reconstruction differences rival individual differences in the fly compass connectome and break trained circuit models
papers.abstract: Neural network models are increasingly constructed from synapse-resolution connectomes, and the same circuit is now available in reconstructions from other animals and pipelines. We do not know whether such models are dependent on the reconstruction they are built from, and whether connectome differences are biological or measurement errors. We studied the Drosophila head-direction circuit in nine versions: four flies (male CNS, hemibrain, Fly Wire, BANC) and five variants of the same fly varying only by thresholds, proofreading or synapse detection. Using wiring-based correspondences validated by anatomical labels, we place all differences on one scale. A change of synapse detection within one fly changed the circuit more than halfway to the smallest inter-fly difference on four distances; proofreading differences were smaller but depended on the metric, and left and right halves of one fly differed no more than a random half. Networks trained on each wiring to hold a cued heading developed near-perfect ring attractors, but their error increased from below 1 degree to 10-28 degrees when all weights changed by 1%. Training on each wiring did not transfer to any other connectome, including other versions of the same fly; refitting thirty cell-type gains, we repaired filtering-level differences but remaining error depended on wiring distance. Training with noise lowered precision and enhanced transfer. Imaging data indicate compasses drift smoothly and do not break; they function despite differences comparable to those of this study.Therefore, connectome-constrained models need to reflect the reconstruction they stem from and the robustness normal circuits exhibit and models lack.
papers.summary: Neural network models are increasingly built from synapse-level connectomes, but it is unclear how much they depend on the specific reconstruction. The authors compare nine versions of the Drosophila head-direction circuit, from four flies and five reconstruction variants of one fly, and find that **changing synapse detection within one fly moved the circuit more than halfway to the smallest difference between flies**. Networks trained on each wiring formed near-perfect ring attractors, but error jumped from under 1 degree to 10-28 degrees when all weights changed by 1%. Training did not transfer to any other connectome, including other versions of the same fly. Training with noise lowered precision but improved transfer, which suggests models lack the robustness that real circuits show.

papers.title: norregel: a preregistered benchmark of dated numeric values in Norwegian law
papers.abstract: norregel asks language models for numeric values in Norwegian statutes, regulations and parliamentary decisions (NOK amounts, percentages, multiples of the National Insurance basic amount (G) and age limits), each at a stated date. The 916 items were extracted mechanically from Lovdata's open data, and each carries the dated history of its provision, so an answer can be classed as correct, outdated, wrong or uninterpretable. We report a first and a second preregistered run on the same items. In the first run (five models, listed publicly only after local analysis), H1, that outdated answers are more frequent for values that took effect after a model's cutoff, could not be tested in substance, and H2 and H3 were inconclusive; Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 4.6 answered 46.7% and 40.2% of the 880 primary items correctly. The second run was preregistered and published before any of its calls, and eight models were analysed. Its pooled primary test supported H1 under the preregistered decision rule (d = 17.8 percentage points, 95% interval [7.7, 28.9], p = 0.0001). In the preregistered sensitivity analysis S8, which counts as outdated only the most recent value that differs from the key, d was 3.9 [-3.6, 12.7] (p = 0.1754), an interval that contains 0. H1 was supported in every other preregistered sensitivity analysis, but S8 is the only one that gives both groups one target value, so we do not regard the support for H1 as robust. The share of outdated answers equal to that most recent value (H2) was 56.1% [46.6, 65.0], an interval that contains 0.5, and the pooled test of a lower share correct in Nynorsk than in Bokm{\aa}l (H3) was inconclusive. Several models, among them Haiku 4.5, gave mostly uninterpretable answers. Items and keys are withheld; item IDs, per-answer classes, code and results are on Zenodo.
papers.summary: `norregel` tests language models on 916 numeric values from Norwegian statutes, regulations and parliamentary decisions, each asked at a stated date, with each provision's dated history attached so answers can be classed as correct, outdated, wrong or uninterpretable. In the first preregistered run, `Opus 5.5` and `Sonnet 4.6` answered 46.7% and 40.2% of primary items correctly. A second, fully preregistered run on eight models supported the hypothesis that outdated answers are more frequent for values that took effect after a model's training cutoff (17.8 percentage points). That support **disappeared in the one sensitivity analysis that gives both groups a single target value**, so the authors do not treat it as robust. Several models, including `Haiku 4.5`, gave mostly uninterpretable answers.

papers.title: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding uses a target model to verify a tree of draft tokens in parallel. We study whether the resulting next-token distributions can help select the next tree. For unrestricted target models, we show that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's complete context. We characterize when retaining this distribution requires sacrificing accepted tokens and establish conditions under which this loss persists across decoding rounds. Across six targets, we find that reranking first-token branches with a separately computed distribution at the current context improves expected acceptance over draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets. Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance over pruning a preselected tree, even at equal mean tree size. In our experiments, both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting. Our findings show that making target probabilities available before tree allocation can improve the efficiency of speculative decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/TargetRows.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a large target model verifies a tree of tokens proposed by a smaller draft model in parallel. The authors ask whether the target's next-token distributions can also guide selection of the next tree. They prove that guaranteed exact reuse requires a distribution computed at the next round's full context, and characterize when keeping it costs accepted tokens. Across six target models, reranking first-token branches with a separately computed target distribution **improves expected acceptance over draft-based ranking, especially at small tree budgets**. Both selection rules also decode faster than draft ranking when the extra target pass overlaps with drafting.

papers.title: On the gradient conjecture at infinity: Finite spherical length for gradient trajectories of definable potentials
papers.abstract:
We prove that for every open $ U \subseteq \mathbb R^n $ the spherical projection of every gradient trajectory $\theta(t)$, $t \geq 0$, of a definable $C^1$-potential $F \colon U \to \mathbb R$ has finite length and, in particular, converges (directional convergence). In other words, every gradient trajectory of a definable $C^1$-potential has finite total angular motion. Here, definable means definable in an arbitrary o-minimal structure expanding the real field.
  Notably, the gradient trajectory in this result is an arbitrary solution of the gradient flow differential equation (whose solutions may not be unique) with no further assumptions: The gradient trajectory may be unbounded and diverge to infinity or it may be convergent. The established theorem therefore provides affirmative answers to both the gradient conjecture at infinity for definable potentials and the definable Thom gradient conjecture.
  We apply our theorem to the training of deep neural networks (DNNs) to conclude that, in the case of definable and continuously differentiable activation and loss functions, the spherical projection of the DNN training flow must always converge (directional convergence).
papers.summary: The authors prove that for any definable continuously differentiable potential (definable in an o-minimal structure over the reals), the spherical projection of every gradient-flow trajectory has finite length. As a result, the direction of the trajectory converges, even when the trajectory itself is unbounded or diverges to infinity. This **affirmatively settles both the gradient conjecture at infinity and the Thom gradient conjecture for definable potentials**. Applied to deep neural networks with definable, continuously differentiable activations and losses, it implies that the direction of the training flow always converges.

papers.title: Huayu-Global: Skillful real-time quasi-global precipitation retrieval
papers.abstract: Satellite precipitation products face a persistent trade-off: real-time estimates are timely but less accurate, whereas the most reliable products are often released months after observation. This delay keeps high-quality precipitation information outside the decision window for flood warning and disaster response. Here we report Huayu-Global, a cross-constellation deep-learning system that combines three geostationary sensor streams from five satellites through a common retrieval framework and generates coherent quasi-global precipitation fields every thirty minutes. Across more than a million independent station records from two periods outside the training years, Huayu-Global improves event detection and precipitation-amount estimation relative to the real-time products evaluated and reaches delayed-product-level skill in key metrics. Huayu-Global therefore turns operational geostationary observations into a timely, high-skill precipitation layer for flood forecasting, water management and disaster response. Its cross-constellation design also provides a scalable foundation for incorporating future geostationary missions into hydrological and weather-prediction systems.
papers.summary: Real-time satellite precipitation estimates are timely but less accurate, while the most reliable products arrive months later, too late for flood warning. `Huayu-Global` is a deep-learning system that combines three geostationary sensor streams from five satellites into one retrieval framework, producing quasi-global precipitation fields every thirty minutes. Validated against over a million station records from periods outside its training years, it outperforms the real-time products evaluated and **reaches the skill of delayed products on key metrics**.

papers.title: Preference Is Not Permission: Personalizing the Auto-Purchase Line in Agentic Commerce
papers.abstract: Personalized shopping benchmarks ask which item fits the user; we ask how far an agent may commit on that item, and pose learning the individual's auto-purchase line as a task. The boundary is evidence-conditioned and three-valued: whether committing is appropriate depends on the sufficiency of product information (warrant), reversibility, price against the user's norm, and urgency, not only on fit; and the natural output is don't buy, confirm first, or buy automatically. Across sixteen instruction-tuned models, autonomous commitment is misaligned with a human authorization reference in which fifteen annotators, role-playing the delegating principal from a given profile, choose the furthest action they would allow without confirmation: models commit even when fit is low and when their own evidence flag reports the warrant missing. This is overreach. The line is individual: these raters disagree, yet the disagreement is structured and partly predictable from a person's own other labels. A shallow learner on a few dozen of a person's own labels predicts their held-out auto-purchase line at a median of 0.79 by 30-40 labels, outperforming every evaluated prompt$\times$model configuration, including a per-annotator oracle over 80 configurations; the learned boundary does not transfer across domains. We release the counterfactual benchmark, human authorization reference, and annotation protocol after acceptance.
papers.summary: Personalized shopping benchmarks ask which item suits a user. The authors instead ask how far a shopping agent may commit on that item: don't buy, confirm first, or buy automatically. Whether committing is appropriate depends on how complete the product information is, how reversible the purchase is, its price relative to the user's norm and its urgency. Across sixteen instruction-tuned models, **agents overreach, committing even when fit is low and when their own evidence flag says product information is missing**, compared with choices from fifteen human annotators role-playing the user. Annotators disagree in structured ways, and a shallow learner trained on 30-40 of one person's labels predicts that person's auto-purchase line better than every prompt-and-model configuration evaluated, though the learned boundary does not transfer across domains.

papers.title: When Multiple Choices Are Correct: Asymmetric Probability Allocation in Jev and Other Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models return normalized probability distributions over candidate choices, which downstream applications can use to select among choices. Although their providers emphasize the reliability of these probabilities, calibration on tasks with a single correct choice does not establish their reliability when multiple choices are correct. We evaluate three decision models (Jev, Liquid d1, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions) on three diverse datasets (MetaTool, HotpotQA, and ECtHR) to study probability allocation and thresholding. Even when models rank every correct choice above every distractor, in 28% to 50% of those lists, at least one correct choice receives a probability below the uniform probability of 1/n, where n is the number of choices. We also present each model with five identical copies of a correct choice and observe probability disparities, with mean gaps ranging from 17 to 79 percentage points. We further show how these allocation disparities affect the recovery of multiple correct choices under probability thresholding. Decision-model probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not identify the set of correct choices.
papers.summary: Decision models return normalized probabilities over candidate choices, but calibration on single-answer tasks says little about how they behave when several choices are correct. Testing `Jev`, `Liquid d1` and `GPT-6 Luna Decisions` on `MetaTool`, `HotpotQA` and `ECtHR`, the authors find that even when every correct choice is ranked above every distractor, **28% to 50% of such lists give at least one correct choice less than uniform probability**. Given five identical copies of a correct choice, the models assigned them probabilities that differed by 17 to 79 percentage points on average. The probabilities can rank correct choices, but a probability threshold does not recover the set of correct ones.

papers.title: PerSPL: Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning
papers.abstract: Personalized reward models require user-specific preference comparisons, but collecting such feedback is costly and provides only limited supervision for each user. At the same time, large pools of responses can be generated without user identities or preference labels, yet existing personalized reward models leave this data unused. Directly learning from these responses is difficult because pairwise objectives constrain relative scores within a prompt, whereas pseudo-labeling individual responses requires scores that are comparable across prompts for the same user. We propose \textbf{PerSPL} (Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning), a backbone-agnostic framework that uses pair-mean score centering to stabilize this cross-prompt score coordinate and iteratively turns unlabeled responses into user-specific training signals. Against seven representative baselines across four benchmarks---PersonalLLM, HelpSteer2, Reddit TLDR, and Chatbot Arena---PerSPL achieves the highest reported mean accuracy among the evaluated methods for both seen and unseen users. The two latter benchmarks provide real-user preference comparisons in summarization and open-domain chatbot interaction, respectively. These results indicate that unlabeled responses can provide additional supervision for personalized reward modeling when per-user preference labels are scarce.
papers.summary: Personalized reward models need preference comparisons from each user, which are costly and scarce, while large pools of unlabeled responses go unused. `PerSPL` (Personalized Semi-supervised Preference Learning) centers each pair's scores on their mean so that scores become comparable across prompts for the same user. It then iteratively turns unlabeled responses into user-specific pseudo-labels for training. Against seven baselines on `PersonalLLM`, `HelpSteer2`, `Reddit TLDR` and `Chatbot Arena`, it reaches **the highest mean accuracy for both seen and unseen users**.

papers.title: Delay-Guided Attention for Quality Prediction in Multistage Manufacturing
papers.abstract: Quality prediction in multistage manufacturing is challenging when inter-stage lags vary over time, as measurements taken at the same timestamp may reflect different process states. Existing approaches often preserve production order but fuse timestamp-aligned features or model delayed dependencies implicitly, without identifying the upstream history relevant to each downstream observation. We propose Delay-Guided Attention for Multi-stage Forecasting (DAMF), which explicitly estimates inter-stage lag distributions and uses them to guide cross-stage information transfer for final quality prediction. For each adjacent stage pair, a lag predictor compares the current downstream representation with candidate lagged upstream representations. An occurrence-magnitude factorization separately estimates the probability of a positive lag and its conditional magnitude, yielding a sample- and stage-pair-specific distribution over discrete lag states without requiring plant-specified delays at inference. DelayAlignment incorporates this soft distribution as a temporal prior into differentiable cross-stage attention, while gated residual fusion regulates information propagation across production stages. For interpretation, segment-wise Viterbi decoding converts pointwise lag distributions into temporally coherent lag paths, whereas forecasting retains the soft distributions for alignment. On the real-world LiquidSugar dataset, DAMF improves final quality prediction over the compared baselines. Evaluations on two controlled-delay benchmarks show more accurate and stable lag recovery, and ablation studies support the contributions of lag prediction, delay-guided attention, and structured temporal decoding.
papers.summary: In multistage manufacturing, the lag between stages varies over time, so measurements taken at the same timestamp can reflect different process states. `DAMF` (Delay-Guided Attention for Multi-stage Forecasting) estimates a lag distribution for each pair of adjacent stages, separating the probability of a positive lag from its size. It uses that distribution as a prior in cross-stage attention, with Viterbi decoding producing interpretable lag paths. On the real-world `LiquidSugar` dataset, **it improves final quality prediction over the compared baselines**, and on two controlled-delay benchmarks it recovers lags more accurately and stably.

papers.title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface unwanted concepts through retrieved documents even when the generator itself is moderated. Compositional Concept Unlearning (`C2U`) suppresses a target concept on the query side, keeping the encoder and document index fixed, by adding a bounded edit to the query embedding derived from a bank of concept directions. Across five datasets, four encoders and three seeds, it **reduces target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points** without degrading retrieval for unrelated control queries. On `ArXiv`, composing four concepts outperformed an averaged-direction baseline.

papers.title: Beyond Binary Labels: Diagnostic Evaluation of LLM Safety with Prompt-Level Rubrics
papers.abstract: Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.
papers.summary: Most LLM safety benchmarks use binary safe or unsafe labels, which explain little and produce inconsistent verdicts across automated judges. `DiagSafe` instead attaches a rubric to each prompt with separate criteria for safety (concrete harms, with exemptions to suppress false positives) and usefulness. It comes with a bilingual English-Chinese benchmark built on an 84-label safety taxonomy, split into `DiagBase` (direct and jailbreak prompts) and `DiagAttack` (harmful intents embedded in complex instruction-following tasks). LLM judges using the rubrics reach **95.34% agreement with human annotations**, versus 69% to 87% for baselines, with Cohen's kappa of 0.864 between judges. The evaluation also shows that leading models differ markedly in unsafe rates and are especially vulnerable in Chinese and multi-turn conversations.

papers.title: Schr\"odinger-Bass Bridge Barycenter Models for Measure-Valued Data
papers.abstract: Barycenter models, based on stochastic and deterministic optimal transport bridges between probability measures, have proven to be useful for supervised and unsupervised learning for (probability) measure-valued data. In this paper, we utilize the directional asymmetry and dual drift-diffusion control arising in the recently proposed Schr\"odinger-Bass Bridge (SBB) between two measures, and propose \textit{SBB-encoder}, \textit{SBB-decoder}, \textit{SBB-symmetric}, and \textit{SBB-Markovian} barycenter models. For each of these novel models, our first theoretical result establishes the existence of the SBB-barycenter under mild assumptions. Our second theoretical result characterizes the decoder SBB-barycenter of Gaussians where we show that for Gaussian input measures, the decoder formulation admits a Gaussian minimizer, reducing barycenter computation to a finite-dimensional optimization and yielding a compact algorithm. For general input measures, we derive a hybrid Wasserstein gradient particle descent scheme for all four formulations using the SBB dual representation. Finally, we utilize these algorithms for solving distributional-inverse/interpolation problems arising in the context of spatial images and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where we show that the SBB-decoder and Markovian barycenter allow us to interpolate between successive time points. Results show that our method outperforms existing barycenter models for measure interpolation and inference.
papers.summary: Barycenter models are averages of probability distributions built from optimal transport bridges, and they are used to learn from data where each sample is itself a distribution. The authors use the directional asymmetry and the paired drift and diffusion controls of the recently proposed `Schrödinger-Bass Bridge` (`SBB`) to define four barycenter models: `SBB-encoder`, `SBB-decoder`, `SBB-symmetric`, and `SBB-Markovian`. They prove that each barycenter exists under mild assumptions. They also show that **for Gaussian inputs the decoder barycenter is itself Gaussian**, so computing it reduces to a finite-dimensional optimization, and for general inputs they derive a hybrid Wasserstein gradient particle descent scheme. On spatial images and single-cell RNA sequencing data, the decoder and Markovian variants interpolate between successive time points and are reported to beat existing barycenter models at measure interpolation and inference.

papers.title: From Scores to Safe Sets: Exact Safety--Constrained Decoding for Medication Recommendation
papers.abstract: Recent generative medication recommendation systems ultimately produce sets of drugs, but drug--drug interaction (DDI) constraints depend on the set as a whole. A natural post-hoc approach is to first predict medications and then locally repair interacting pairs by removing one drug at a time. We ask whether this local repair step itself introduces avoidable error. Using fixed medication scores from FLAME's frozen classifier on MIMIC-III, we compare increasingly strong local repair strategies with an exact global decoder while holding the scores, output size, and DDI constraint fixed. The global decoder jointly selects the highest-scoring feasible medication set using mixed-integer linear programming. Across validation and test splits, global decoding consistently achieves higher Jaccard similarity than greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and degree-aware repair strengthened with exhaustive 1-swap local search. Its advantage is small under loose DDI constraints and becomes larger as the constraint tightens; on the test split it reaches +0.0064 Jaccard over the strongest local baseline at the strict DDI operating point. The finding also holds across a fine accuracy--DDI sweep at matched realized DDI exposure and under three score representations. At the strict setting, global decoding retains more true-positive medications while removing more false positives. These results show that medication recommendation is not only a representation-learning problem: even with a frozen clinical model, how its scores are converted into a constrained medication set can materially affect the final prediction.
papers.summary: Medication recommendation systems output a set of drugs, but drug–drug interaction (DDI) constraints apply to the set as a whole, and the usual fix is to repair interacting pairs after prediction by removing one drug at a time. The authors keep the scores from `FLAME`'s frozen classifier on `MIMIC-III` fixed and compare increasingly strong local repair strategies against an exact global decoder, which uses mixed-integer linear programming to pick the highest-scoring set that satisfies the constraint. Global decoding gets consistently higher Jaccard similarity than greedy repair, degree-aware repair, and repair combined with exhaustive 1-swap local search. The gap grows as the DDI constraint tightens, reaching **+0.0064 Jaccard over the strongest local baseline at the strict operating point** on the test split.

papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
papers.summary: Streaming video understanding (SVU) systems cut answer latency by encoding incoming frames into key-value (KV) caches while idle, but they limit the context available during this prefill, so the cached tokens can miss context the eventual query needs. `FrameBlend` is a training-free, plug-and-play method that, at query time, re-encodes selected video tokens with query-relevant context and swaps their recomputed KVs into the cache. Because of this recomputation, idle-time prefill can use shorter attention windows, which lowers cost and also improves accuracy. Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy rises by up to **3.9 percentage points**, and on `RVS-Ego` per-frame prefill FLOPs fall by over 20% and total processing time by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks, with query-time recomputation included.

papers.title: MA-UITD: Offline Multi-Agent Reward Inference for Characterizing Continuous Social Behavior
papers.abstract: Multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework not only for imitation learning but also for understanding the neural computations supporting social interactions and decision-making. Inferring rewards from interacting agents is challenging because observed choices reflect both personal preferences and expectations about others.
