To address scaling, we extend the framework to a conditional formulation using supersamples, analogous in spirit to conditional mutual information (CMI), and discuss evaluations in the output space as a practical surrogate for estimating dependence. Simulations on Bayesian linear regression illustrate how tuning $\alpha$ can change the tightness of the resulting bounds across regimes. Additional supersample experiments on noisy MNIST and on a pretrained ResNet-50 for CIFAR-10 show similar behavior of the projected loss-space bounds beyond the original clean-MNIST setting.
papers.summary: Derives generalization bounds for randomized learning algorithms using `V_α`, a family of vector-valued L_p correlation measures of how much the learned hypothesis depends on the training data. The family interpolates between total variation at α=1 and variance-like behavior at α=2, and for α>2 the bounds can stay finite even when the loss variance is infinite. The authors show the family is **invariant under smooth reparameterizations of the hypothesis space**, introduce an adaptive density stability condition that holds for Gibbs-type posteriors, and extend the framework to a conditional supersample formulation. Experiments on Bayesian linear regression, noisy `MNIST`, and `ResNet-50` on `CIFAR-10` show how tuning α changes the tightness of the bounds.

papers.title: BIRD-RL: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning over Stateful Data-Centric Environments
papers.abstract: While agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training small language models (SLMs), existing frameworks are predominantly tool-centric and struggle with data-centric environments. Specifically, applying tool-centric frameworks to stateful tasks like SQL debugging introduces severe spatial inefficiencies since proper environment isolation typically requires a separate database container per rollout. Naively reusing databases without tracking evolving states across multi-turn interactions causes trajectory contamination and cross-trajectory interference, which severely destabilizes policy updates. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce BIRD-RL, a novel four-stage agentic RL curriculum that alternately enhances foundational agent reasoning and trajectory-adaptive on-policy exploration to circumvent the instability inherently associated with direct end-to-end learning. Crucially, to support this curriculum, BIRD-RL is driven by a Trajectory-scoped Persistent Execution Infrastructure, which enables safe database replica reuse while preserving trajectory isolation. This design improves spatial RL efficiency by 12.8x, successfully enabling scalable agentic RL for complex data-centric tasks without needs of Kubernettes. Empirical evaluations on the BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite benchmark demonstrate that our 7B and 14B models achieve Success Rates of 44.40% and 48.00%, respectively, showing competitive performance against strong proprietary model-based agents such as Claude-Opus-4.6 Agent (48.20%). Furthermore, BIRD-RL successfully trains unified SLMs capable of both advanced SQL debugging and generation, highlighting its broader potential for multi-objective optimization across heterogeneous, real-world data-centric tasks.
papers.summary: Targets agentic reinforcement learning (RL) for small language models on stateful, data-centric tasks such as SQL debugging. In these tasks, isolating each rollout needs its own database container, while naively reusing databases contaminates trajectories. `BIRD-RL` combines a four-stage RL curriculum with a trajectory-scoped persistent execution infrastructure that safely reuses database replicas, **improving spatial efficiency by 12.8x** without Kubernetes. On `BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite`, its 7B and 14B models reach success rates of 44.40% and 48.00%, close to a `Claude-Opus-4.6` agent at 48.20%, and the same models can both debug and generate SQL.

papers.title: One Act, Many Masks: Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the performance of LLM agents on complex, long-horizon interactive tasks. However, despite progress in fine-grained credit assignment, policy optimization still applies these learning signals through response-specific probability ratios. Different textual responses can induce the same executable effect, yet credit differences arising from subsequent outcomes remain tied to their individual textual realizations. We identify this mismatch as credit-update misalignment. Our analysis reveals that credit-text pairing directly shapes policy-update directions, even when the policy context and executable effect are held fixed. Motivated by this finding, we propose Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization (EMPO), which aligns policy optimization with execution-level equivalence through an effect-level surrogate that couples updates across alternative textual realizations. EMPO preserves the original credit signals, integrates with both trajectory-level and step-level credit estimators, and requires no additional critics or rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban show that EMPO outperforms strong baselines in both task performance and learning efficiency.
papers.summary: Identifies credit-update misalignment in multi-turn reinforcement learning for LLM agents. Different textual responses can produce the same executable action, yet policy updates assign credit to each wording separately, and the authors show this pairing of credit and text shapes update directions. Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization (`EMPO`) instead optimizes an effect-level surrogate that couples updates across responses with the same effect. It works with both trajectory-level and step-level credit estimators and needs no extra critics or rollouts. On `ALFWorld`, `WebShop`, and `Sokoban`, `EMPO` **outperforms strong baselines in both task performance and learning efficiency**.

papers.title: MERP: A Latent-Bottleneck Framework for Robust Multi-Modal Multi-Label Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal multi-label emotion recognition is important for affect-aware systems, but models trained with complete text, visual, and acoustic streams often degrade sharply when some streams are unavailable at deployment. We address this train-test gap by learning a compact representation that preserves emotion-specific evidence from any available subset of modalities. We propose the Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (MERP), which maps the joint sequence into a fixed-size latent bank, thereby keeping repeated reasoning independent of raw input length; it extracts label-specific evidence before and after latent reasoning and aligns the two levels through reconstruction. MERP further uses positive and negative class prototypes, a noise-gated feature enhancer with frequency-shaped perturbations during training, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion to strengthen separability, reduce sensitivity to missing inputs, and combine complementary predictors. Under 20 percent test-time random modality drop, MERP achieves micro-F1 scores of 0.563 on CMU-MOSEI and 0.780 on M3ED, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 0.004 and 0.005, respectively; in the severe CMU-MOSEI audio-only setting, it retains 0.473 micro-F1 versus 0.022 for LDDU. These results show that fixed latent reasoning provides a practical, testable route to robust multimodal emotion recognition without requiring missing-modality examples during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Creative-zcx/MERP.
papers.summary: Addresses multimodal multi-label emotion recognition models that degrade sharply when text, visual, or audio streams are missing at deployment. The Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (`MERP`) maps inputs into a fixed-size latent bank, extracts label-specific evidence before and after latent reasoning, and adds class prototypes, a noise-gated feature enhancer, and confidence-aware fusion. Under 20% random modality drop at test time, it reaches micro-F1 of 0.563 on `CMU-MOSEI` and 0.780 on `M3ED`, narrowly ahead of the best baselines. In the audio-only `CMU-MOSEI` setting, it **retains 0.473 micro-F1 versus 0.022 for `LDDU`**, without using missing-modality examples in training.

papers.title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.
papers.summary: Examines why world models used for planning can render frames faithfully yet still predict the wrong return. A transition-level diagnostic swaps imagined transitions for real ones and measures how much return error disappears compared with a budget-matched random swap. Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, look as good visually as other steps, but **restoring them removes a median 70% of return error**. Restoring the transitions with the largest pixel or perceptual error helps less than a random choice. Event patches beat random patches in 39 of 44 `Atari-100k` model-collection pairs, improve plan ranking, and show the same concentration on control tasks with rare rewards.

papers.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
papers.abstract: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.
papers.summary: Studies how far knowledge distillation can shrink jet-tagging models for Large Hadron Collider experiments, which impose strict inference-cost limits. Six teachers, including two foundation models, are distilled into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, with gains driven mainly by teacher strength. A distilled `L-GATr-slim` with 20 thousand parameters beats every published jet tagger trained from scratch, and **with only two thousand parameters it matches `ParT`**, a model a thousand times larger. Students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed, and all code and weights are released.

papers.title: DynaWeave: Learning to Adapt through Dynamic Scenario Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools to complete tasks in stateful environments. However, many training environments remain largely static apart from changes caused by the agent's own actions, whereas external events introduced by other users, services, or sudden contingencies in real environments can invalidate ongoing plans. To address this gap, we introduce DynaWeave, an automated synthesis framework that transforms existing static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios. The framework generates exogenous events relevant to each task, covering changes in task requirements, environment state, and external information. It uses directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to represent dependencies between events and an execution engine to activate them during agent interaction. A dynamic verifier revises only the evaluation checks affected by events that actually occur and retains all other checks. Using DynaWeave, we collect 2,095 verified interaction trajectories across 36 environments and use them for supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5 models. Experiments on Gaia2, CostBench, and ToolMaze show that DynaWeave achieves consistent improvements in overall performance across all three evaluated model sizes, increasing the task completion rate on CostBench by 67.34 percentage points and even exceeding the performance of Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview on ToolMaze. These results support dynamic scenario synthesis as a practical approach to training agents to adapt to changing environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Miaow-Lab/DynaWeave.
papers.summary: Tackles the mismatch between static training environments for tool-using LLM agents and real environments, where outside events can invalidate an agent's plan mid-task. `DynaWeave` converts static tasks into verifiable dynamic scenarios by generating relevant exogenous events, ordering them with directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), triggering them during interaction, and revising only the evaluation checks the events affect. Supervised fine-tuning of `Qwen3.5` models on 2,095 verified trajectories from 36 environments improves results on `Gaia2`, `CostBench`, and `ToolMaze` at every model size. It raises `CostBench` task completion by **67.34 percentage points** and surpasses `Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview` on `ToolMaze`.

papers.title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.
papers.summary: Introduces `Omnilingual-MsASR`, a benchmark for long-form multi-speaker automatic speech recognition (MsASR) aimed at omni-modal large language models. It covers six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and up to 20 speakers, and supplies parallel audio and video so that cross-modal consistency can be measured. Evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs show that **their tcpWER error rates frequently exceed 100%**. The results point to fine-grained timing, telling speakers apart, and combining audio with video as the main open problems.

papers.title: RegoMender: A Multi-agent Framework for Automated Rego Policy Repair
papers.abstract: Policy-as-Code (PaC) has emerged as a foundational paradigm in cloud-native systems. However, repairing Rego policies remains challenging due to their strict syntax, declarative semantics, and specific verification requirements. Existing automated program repair (APR) methods are mainly designed for mainstream languages and struggle to accommodate the unique policy logic and repair workflows of Rego. Thus, Rego policy repair remains a manual process driven by trial and error. To address this, we introduce RegoBench, the first automated Rego policy benchmark comprising 1,159 real-world defects, and propose RegoMender, a feedback-guided multi-agent framework. Collaborating via a shared blackboard and an atomic toolkit, RegoMender dynamically executes patching, rewriting, or rolling back, to resolve complex repair scenarios. Evaluated on RegoBench, RegoMender achieves syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9\% and 77.9\%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.4\%. Unlike other approaches whose performance drops in complex scenarios, RegoMender maintains effectiveness across single-step and chained repair tasks. Furthermore, it generalizes strongly across HCL and SQL and achieves an 86.4\% repair rate on 132 real-world CVE vulnerabilities, proving its robustness and practical utility for security.
papers.summary: Targets automated repair of Rego policies in Policy-as-Code systems, which general-purpose program repair methods handle poorly because of Rego's strict syntax and declarative semantics. The authors release `RegoBench`, a benchmark of 1,159 real-world defects, and propose `RegoMender`, a feedback-guided multi-agent framework. Its agents coordinate through a shared blackboard and an atomic toolkit to patch, rewrite, or roll back policies. `RegoMender` reaches syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9% and 77.9%, 13.4% above the strongest baseline, generalizes to `HCL` and `SQL`, and **repairs 86.4% of 132 real-world CVE vulnerabilities**.

papers.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.
papers.summary: Argues that agentic reinforcement learning (RL) through a single fixed agent harness, the scaffolding that governs tool use and context management, leads to models that specialize and transfer poorly to other harness configurations. Harness Scaling builds a factorized space of harness configurations, selects a compact training subset with balanced coverage, and trains across harnesses with controlled variation on the same tasks. Across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, this improves generalization to unseen configurations. Models trained on structured white-box variation **transfer to unseen external black-box harnesses better than models trained on a single complex black-box harness**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agentic RL usually trains a policy through one fixed harness, meaning the scaffolding of prompts, tools, observations, context handling and workflow around the model, and the resulting policy can overfit to that setup. `Harness Scaling` treats harness diversity as a new scaling axis: it splits the harness into five components, picks a compact training set of configurations that is balanced across those components and their pairs, and trains each task on several closely related harnesses.

- **Method:** Each component (system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, workflow) has three model-generated variants, giving 3^5 = **243** configurations. A strength-2 orthogonal design picks just **18** of them so that every pair of variants appears exactly twice, and each task is paired with a random anchor harness plus its nearest neighbor by Hamming distance (`K=2`).
- **Unseen in-space configurations:** Trained on `ClawGym-Task` with `Qwen3-4B-Instruct` and `Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct`, the method beats single-harness RL with both `GRPO` and `PPO`. The 4B `GRPO` model's overall average across `ClawGym-Bench`, `JobBench-Easy` and `PinchBench` rises from **29.81 to 39.04**, and its in-space gain is **+9.80**.
- **Transfer to unseen black-box harnesses:** On `Claude Code`, models trained on the white-box harness variants average **37.22 (4B) and 41.20 (30B)**. That beats both supervised fine-tuning (35.08 / 38.08) and RL (33.38 / 36.28) run through the more complex `OpenClaw` harness, and the same trend holds when `OpenClaw` itself is the unseen evaluation harness for the white-box-trained models.
- **Ablations:** How the training set is chosen matters more than how many harnesses it has. Under the same budget, the structured 18-harness set beats both a random set of 18 and the full 243-configuration space, and switching from nearest-neighbor to random assignment costs **2–3 points**. Raising `K` from 2 to 4 brings no further gain.
- **Limitations:** Gains on the base training harness are essentially flat (**−0.19**) while in-space performance rises **+10.48**. Absolute scores on `JobBench-Easy` stay low (roughly 13–19), the harness variants were generated by `Opus-4.7` and may not reflect real-world harness diversity, and only Qwen3 backbones were tested.

papers.title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.
papers.summary: Addresses how long-term dialogue agents can keep user memories stable while still updating them when the user genuinely changes, rather than appending everything or overwriting by heuristic. `PreCoMem`, inspired by predictive coding, stores memories as confidence-weighted beliefs and computes an Effective Surprisal signal from semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, discounted when retrieval is unreliable. A two-threshold gate then chooses among three updates: reinforce a supported belief, hold an ambiguous cue as a low-confidence hypothesis, or decay a reliably contradicted fact. It reports **state-of-the-art accuracy on `LoCoMo`, `LongMemEval-S`, and `PersonaMem-v2`**, and the new `DiMoBench` shows it adapts to belief drift without overreacting to noise.

papers.title: OmniSimulator: Aligning Small Language Models for Authentic Heterogeneous Behavior Modeling
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose user simulators for interactive systems. Prior studies have demonstrated that training on high-quality data can substantially improve model reasoning and downstream task performance. However, the upper bound of user simulation is still constrained by the model's reasoning paradigm: native chain-of-thought often degenerates into shallow pattern matching and fails to adequately model the behavioral factors underlying real user decisions. In this paper, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve the predictive ability of small LLMs for realistic user simulation on short-video platform environments. Specifically, OmniSimulator organizes behavior-oriented reasoning through a structured schema with five dimensions, carefully selects data from real user-behavior scenarios, and introduces a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces under the proposed schema, helping small models learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns rather than relying on superficial behavioral correlations. Based on this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality training instances from three months of historical interaction trajectories of 200 real users, averaging about 50 distilled examples per user. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the average score of Qwen3-8B by 34.33%, achieves performance competitive with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These results suggest that learning structured behavior-oriented reasoning patterns is a promising direction towards scalable and high-fidelity LLM-based user simulation.
papers.summary: Large language models used as user simulators often fall back on shallow pattern matching instead of capturing why real users make the choices they do. `OmniSimulator` trains small models for user simulation on short-video platforms using a five-dimension reasoning schema for user behavior. A teacher model writes reasoning traces that follow this schema for interactions selected from real user data, yielding 9,881 training instances drawn from three months of activity by 200 users. The approach raises the average score of `Qwen3-8B` by **34.33%**, bringing it close to `Claude-Sonnet-4.5` while remaining small enough to self-host.

papers.title: Asymmetry Tunneling Beyond Adaptive Equivariance Relaxation
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks encode prescribed symmetries as powerful inductive biases, yet real-world data may exhibit symmetry-breaking structure that these priors cannot fully capture. Prior work has largely addressed this challenge through model-side equivariance relaxation, seeking an appropriate level of equivariance for the data. This raises a complementary question: must equivariance relaxation be adaptively controlled? To investigate this question, we introduce a residual path alongside a strictly equivariant model and deliberately restrict their interface to examine the transmission of task-relevant structure. Across five benchmarks, we observe both residual collapse and survival despite these restrictions; we call the latter phenomenon asymmetry tunneling. We further characterize this phenomenon through four complementary diagnostics. Our results suggest that adaptive control of equivariance relaxation is not a prerequisite for capturing potential symmetry-breaking structure.
papers.summary: Equivariant neural networks build known symmetries into the model, but real data often breaks those symmetries in part. Earlier work handles this by adaptively tuning how much equivariance the model enforces. The authors instead place a residual path alongside a strictly equivariant model and deliberately narrow the interface between the two. Across five benchmarks the residual sometimes collapses and sometimes survives, carrying symmetry-breaking information despite the restriction. The authors call this survival asymmetry tunneling, study it with four diagnostics, and conclude that **adaptive control of equivariance relaxation is not required** to capture symmetry-breaking structure.

papers.title: Density-Level Backward Error for Low-NFE Generative Flows
papers.abstract: Low-NFE generative ODE sampling is constrained not only by solver order, but also by how a fixed budget of network evaluations is distributed along the flow. We develop a density-level backward-error framework that identifies the component of a solver's modified-equation defect that changes the evolving marginal, while excluding solenoidal trajectory distortion that is invisible in Wasserstein tangent geometry. The resulting residual induces a solver-order-aware compute-allocation rule and, through gauge freedom, an objective for selecting numerically favorable velocity representatives of the same density path. This separates our approach from schedule search driven by trajectory or endpoint surrogates and from higher-order solver design. Exact Gaussian and mixture models establish the mechanism, including cases where curvature-based allocation fails and continuum-optimal transport is not discretization-optimal. On a pretrained CIFAR-10 EDM probability-flow ODE, density-aware allocation consistently improves fixed-update Euler sampling in the low-NFE regime. Matched-seed convergence to a dense Euler reference confirms that the method accelerates approximation of the same high-NFE flow rather than changing the asymptotic sampler.
papers.summary: When a generative ODE sampler gets only a few network function evaluations (NFE), quality depends on where along the flow those evaluations are spent, not only on the solver's order. The authors develop a density-level backward-error framework that isolates the part of a solver's error that changes the evolving probability distribution and ignores trajectory distortions that leave the distribution unchanged. This residual gives an order-aware rule for allocating steps and an objective for choosing numerically favorable velocity fields that produce the same density path. On a pretrained `CIFAR-10` `EDM` probability-flow ODE, density-aware allocation **consistently improves low-NFE Euler sampling** while converging to the same high-NFE flow.

papers.title: Generative Modeling via Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Bridges and Branching Diffusions
papers.abstract: We propose a new generative modeling framework grounded in forward-backward partial differential equations (PDEs). These equations arise naturally in mean-field game (MFG) theory, and are closely related to nonlinear Schr\"odinger systems. Our main contribution is to reinterpret this connection within the setting of generative modeling and to develop an efficient numerical methodology for its practical implementation. Specifically, we derive and characterize a nonlinear extension of the classical Schr\"odinger bridge problem through a coupled system of PDEs, yielding a model we call SBNL (Schr\"odinger Bridge NonLinear). To compute its solution, we design a simulation algorithm based on branching diffusions and the probabilistic representation of semilinear PDEs. The resulting method is embarrassingly parallel, scalable to high dimensions, and applicable to a broad class of nonlinear interaction functionals. We validate the approach through numerical experiments, including recovery of the classical Schr\"odinger bridge, nonlinear extensions with convex penalties (Gross-Pitaevskii) as well as potential interaction terms, and high-dimensional generative tasks such as image synthesis on the MNIST and FFHQ human face dataset. Furthermore, the same framework embeds score-based generative modeling, diffusion models, and tractable gaussian Schr\"odinger bridges.
papers.summary: The authors build a generative modeling framework on coupled forward-backward partial differential equations (PDEs) taken from mean-field game theory and related to nonlinear Schrödinger systems. The result, `SBNL` (Schrödinger Bridge NonLinear), extends the classical Schrödinger bridge problem to nonlinear interaction terms. It is solved with a simulation algorithm based on branching diffusions that is embarrassingly parallel and scales to high dimensions. Experiments recover the classical bridge, handle Gross-Pitaevskii and potential-interaction terms, and generate images on `MNIST` and `FFHQ`. The framework also **contains score-based diffusion models as special cases**.

papers.title: TenetBench: A Clause-Anchored Russian Corpus for Evaluating Language Models against Professional Codes of Ethics
papers.abstract: Codes of professional ethics guide and restrict specialists, who increasingly work with assistants built on large language models. Such an assistant can breach the user's code, or help the user breach it, without the user noticing. Evaluations reporting broad categories of harm cannot show how often this happens or which provision is breached. TenetBench pairs 3,433 requests conflicting with clauses of fifteen Russian-language professional codes with benign twins that differ only in the legitimacy of what is asked. An automated pipeline generates the tasks from the text of a code, so the corpus grows with every code added and a provision yields new tasks on every run. It also produced tasks and human-validated verdicts from two English codes of other jurisdictions. In human validation of the frozen pipeline, specialists rated 0.995 of the conflicting tasks plausible, and the model judge agreed with the adjudicated label at Gwet's AC1 of at least 0.894 on 1,860 elements. We evaluated fourteen model and reasoning-mode combinations on whether they produce the conflicting text, decline or warn. Eleven of the fourteen produce conflicting content on most such requests, mostly without a warning, and nearly three warnings in four accompany conflicting content. The models that conform more do so by declining while still serving the legitimate twin, and enabling reasoning halved the refusals of two models. We hope the dataset and pipeline will help evaluate how language models observe professional norms and let diagnostic datasets be built for particular professions and organisations.
papers.summary: `TenetBench` tests whether language-model assistants breach, or help users breach, specific clauses of professional codes of ethics. It contains 3,433 requests that conflict with clauses of fifteen Russian-language professional codes, each paired with a benign twin request, and is produced by an automated pipeline that can generate tasks from any code's text. Specialists rated 0.995 of the conflicting tasks plausible. **Eleven of fourteen model and reasoning-mode configurations produced conflicting content for most such requests**, usually without any warning. Turning on reasoning halved the refusals of two models.

papers.title: RubricOpt: Self-Revision of Semantic Rubrics for Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: A model's failures can reveal gaps in the behavioral criteria guiding its training. We introduce RubricOpt, a framework that lets a policy revise these criteria within preference optimization. The policy diagnoses its own rubric-free outputs, retains requirements already covered by the rubric, and edits clauses that leave recurring failures unaddressed. A shared semantic representation connects task demands, preference-data contrasts, and rubric clauses, while a deterministic gate checks evidence references and fixed semantic anchors. The rubric then guides Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) during training, with preference pairs, labels, and the objective held fixed, and is removed at evaluation. Our analysis relates the local effect on rubric-free success to semantic alignment and a residual beyond the measured factors. Experiments on capability and open-ended generation benchmarks show that rubric conditioning can improve outcomes over ordinary DPO, with gains and regressions varying across models and datasets. A matched continuation isolates the contribution of revision from additional training and finds mixed incremental effects for the tested edit, whose feedback overlaps the evaluation set. RubricOpt thus brings the behavioral specification itself into the policy's feedback loop.
papers.summary: `RubricOpt` allows a policy model to revise the behavioral rubric that guides its own preference training. The policy diagnoses its own outputs produced without the rubric, keeps requirements the rubric already covers, and edits clauses that leave recurring failures unaddressed. A deterministic gate checks each edit against evidence references and fixed semantic anchors. The revised rubric conditions Direct Preference Optimization (`DPO`) during training and is removed at evaluation. On capability and open-ended generation benchmarks, rubric conditioning **can beat ordinary DPO, but gains and regressions vary across models and datasets**, and the revision step itself produced mixed incremental effects.

papers.title: An Exact 93-Move Solution to a Nonlocal Crystal-Exchange Puzzle
papers.abstract: We determine the minimum number of directional commands needed to solve alevel of Order of the Sinking Star, modeled as a crystal-exchangepuzzle on an 11*11 board. A command swapsthe player with the nearest crystal in the selected row or column, regardlessof distance; only an empty ray permits an ordinary unit walk. Two gates admitthe player to the exit exactly while all sixteen crystals occupy their targetcells. We give an explicit 93-command solution and exclude every shortersolution by an exact, cost-bounded breadth-first search. The search representsa position by its seventeen occupied cells and one active cell. Its admissibleheuristic partitions command costs between a compressed core abstraction andresidual motion, strengthened by a necessary activation detour and a cornervisit condition. The completed computation retained 605,349,215 occupied setsand 1,863,925,136 states. We prove the reductions and pruning conditions,describe the exact storage scheme, and provide source code, execution logs,and a reproduction driver. The result is a computer-assisted proof for thespecified instance, with an explicit implementation trust boundary.
papers.summary: The authors find the minimum number of moves needed to solve one level of the game `Order of the Sinking Star`, modeled as an 11×11 puzzle in which each directional command swaps the player with the nearest crystal in that row or column. They give an explicit 93-command solution and rule out every shorter one with an exact, cost-bounded breadth-first search guided by an admissible heuristic and proven pruning rules. The search kept about 1.86 billion states, and source code and logs are released so the result can be reproduced. The result is a computer-assisted proof that **93 moves is optimal** for this instance.

papers.title: A Strong MoE Is All You Need for Process Supervision
papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for multi-step reasoning, yet obtaining reliable process labels remains a central bottleneck. Existing approaches typically rely on human annotation, rollout-based estimation, or auxiliary verification. In this work, we explore a different source of process supervision natively exposed by Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models: expert routing. We show that simple routing statistics provide an intrinsic process-confidence signal that is competitive with conventional output-logit confidence. Building on this observation, we construct routing confidence by combining overall routing mass, head routing mass, and within-step routing variation, and introduce RoCo-Rethink, which identifies the least confident reasoning step and selectively regenerates the subsequent trajectory. We further introduce RoCo-PRM, which uses a strong MoE to automatically annotate reasoning trajectories with routing-derived step scores and distills them into a standalone PRM. Across multiple MoE architectures and diverse reasoning tasks, both RoCo-Rethink and RoCo-PRM consistently outperform strong baselines, while RoCo-PRM transfers effectively across both model architectures and tasks. Our findings suggest that expert routing is more than a computational dispatch mechanism: it provides an architecture-native source of process supervision for reasoning.
papers.summary: Process reward models (PRMs) score each step of a model's reasoning, but reliable step-level labels are expensive to obtain. The authors show that expert-routing statistics in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models give a built-in step-confidence signal that is competitive with confidence derived from output logits. They use it in two methods. `RoCo-Rethink` regenerates the reasoning from the least confident step onward, and `RoCo-PRM` uses routing-derived scores from a strong MoE to label reasoning traces and distills them into a standalone PRM. Both **outperform strong baselines across MoE architectures and reasoning tasks**, and `RoCo-PRM` transfers across architectures and tasks.

papers.title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
papers.abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.
papers.summary: Parallel thinking has a language model explore several reasoning paths at once. The authors find that when this is trained with reinforcement learning (RL), the paths tend to collapse into near-copies of one another. `Diverse Parallel Thinking` (`DPT`) adds an RL reward that penalizes paths for sharing similar prefixes, pushing the model to try distinct strategies. Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, `DPT` **outperforms previous parallel-thinking methods**, supporting the claim that path diversity is a key ingredient. Code is released.

papers.title: Rethinking Agentic Model Orchestration for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) perform unevenly across forecasting tasks. Recent work uses agentic model orchestration (AMO) to select or combine TSFMs, often outperforming individual forecasters. Yet these gains may reflect stronger or more complementary candidates rather than better orchestration. To disentangle these effects, we introduce FairAMO, a controlled evaluation protocol with frozen candidate forecasts. Experiments on GIFT-Eval show that AMO improves accuracy, but its gains are bounded by the candidate TSFMs. The best orchestrators reduce MASE by less than 6% relative to the best single TSFM across all tasks. These gains depend on complementarity (different candidates excel on different tasks) rather than the number of candidates. Adding members yields diminishing returns, and a redundant member can erase these gains. The value of historical evidence also saturates quickly. A few recent windows capture all gains, and further history adds none. These findings separate system-level forecasting gains from the contribution of orchestration itself.
papers.summary: Agentic model orchestration (AMO) systems select or combine time series foundation models (TSFMs) for forecasting. The authors test whether reported gains come from better orchestration or simply from stronger candidate models. Their protocol, `FairAMO`, fixes the candidate forecasts in advance so that orchestrators can be compared fairly. On `GIFT-Eval`, the best orchestrators cut mean absolute scaled error (MASE) by **less than 6%** relative to the best single TSFM. These gains depend on candidates that excel on different tasks rather than on the number of candidates, a redundant candidate can erase them, and a few recent windows of history capture all the benefit.

papers.title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC
papers.abstract: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) enables Bayesian inference for models with intractable likelihoods by estimating parameter posterior distributions from simulated data. Sequential ABC methods improve sampling efficiency by iteratively adapting the proposal distribution toward regions of high posterior probability. However, these methods typically operate in generations, where each generation must wait for its slowest simulation before the next can begin. On a parallel machine, this synchronization barrier leaves workers idle and reduces throughput, particularly when simulation runtimes vary substantially. We introduce a generation-free ABC sampler that updates its proposal when simulation results arrive and sends a new candidate to each available worker. The proposal is based on the best particles evaluated so far. To estimate the posterior, we reuse the full history and reweight particles against a reconstructed mixture of sampling proposals. We show how errors in approximating the mixture of sampling proposals affect the estimated posterior and establish consistency for the smooth-ABC posterior when the approximation becomes asymptotically exact. In our experiments, the method achieves well-calibrated posterior estimates where a pyABC baseline with the same kernel and bandwidth schedule under-covers. From the asynchronous run's timing alone, we predict how much a synchronization barrier would slow the sampler. These predictions agree with measured synchronization penalties ranging from 1.2x to 400x. On a Cellular Potts tissue simulator, the asynchronous sampler completes 2.1-2.4x as many evaluations as pyABC in the same hour, and the discrepancy threshold for its best 100 evaluations is 4.1x smaller. With the starting bandwidth set from prior-predictive discrepancies, it also produces a more concentrated two-parameter posterior with a larger effective sample size than pyABC.
papers.summary: Sequential approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) runs simulations in generations, so on parallel hardware every worker waits for the slowest simulation before the next generation can start. The authors propose a generation-free sampler that updates its proposal distribution as each result arrives and sends new candidates to idle workers. It estimates the posterior by reweighting the full history of particles against a reconstructed mixture of the proposals used, and the authors prove consistency under stated conditions. On a Cellular Potts tissue simulator, it completes **2.1–2.4× as many evaluations as `pyABC` in the same hour** and gives better-calibrated posteriors.

papers.title: Keeping Time vs. Understanding Time: Neither Alone Explains Temporal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.abstract: Temporal reasoning is widely assumed to decompose into two modes: temporal arithmetic (date and time calculations), and temporal semantics (understanding temporal and causal relations). This dichotomy shapes how benchmarks are designed, how models are trained, and how progress is measured, yet its empirical validity has never been directly tested. We provide two lines of evidence that challenge it. First, we test whether tasks labelled as arithmetic or semantic by the benchmarks support transferable gains within their purported mode. Finetuning on these subsets yields predominantly dataset-specific gains ($+6.8$ to $+23.1$ percentage points), while transfer to a different dataset in the same mode ranges from $-3.2$ to $+1.1$ percentage points. Across the two benchmark families used in the transfer analysis, this pattern provides little evidence of coherent, transferable temporal abilities. Second, using cognitive-demand-based model evaluation, we examine which capabilities actually drive performance on these benchmarks. We find that quantitative and logical reasoning, the assumed proxies for temporal arithmetic and temporal semantics, are not the primary drivers; knowledge is. Together, these findings show that current temporal reasoning benchmarks do not cleanly realise the arithmetic-semantics distinction and instead largely reward models for remembering how time typically works.
papers.summary: Temporal reasoning benchmarks usually divide tasks into temporal arithmetic (date and time calculations) and temporal semantics (temporal and causal relations), but this split had never been tested directly. Fine-tuning on one benchmark's subset for either mode improves that dataset by 6.8 to 23.1 percentage points, yet transfer to another dataset of the same mode ranges only from −3.2 to +1.1 points. An analysis of which cognitive demands drive model performance finds that **knowledge, not quantitative or logical reasoning, is the main driver**. Current benchmarks therefore largely reward models for remembering how time typically works.

papers.title: Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation for Long-Tailed Recognition
papers.abstract: Real-world datasets often follow a long-tailed distribution, making generalization to tail classes difficult. We revisit this problem through the lens of shortcut learning, where models prefer the easiest predictive cues (e.g., background or textures) over object-centric semantics, especially under scarce and biased supervision. We find that this tendency is amplified for tail classes: limited examples often share similar contexts, making non-semantic signals highly correlated and thus tempting shortcuts, whereas head classes with diverse appearances and environments encourage more stable object-focused representations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation (SRCD), a plug-and-play framework that transfers object-focused explanations from head to tail classes. SRCD operates in the Class Activation Map (CAM) space, where a CAM provides a class-specific spatial evidence map for a prediction. SRCD aggregates CAMs from a small set of head-class candidates into a shortcut-resistant teacher using an energy-model weighting based on coherence and concentration, and distills it to the tail-class CAM. We provide a theoretical analysis that quantifies shortcut reliance as shortcut-region evidence mass in CAM space and shows that SRCD suppresses tail shortcuts. Extensive experiments on long-tailed benchmarks consistently improve strong baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Haifeng3/SRCD.
papers.summary: In long-tailed datasets, rare classes have few examples that often share similar contexts, so models learn shortcuts such as backgrounds or textures instead of the object itself. `Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation` (`SRCD`) works in Class Activation Map (CAM) space, where each map shows the spatial evidence behind a prediction. It combines CAMs from a few head-class candidates into an object-focused teacher, weighted by an energy model based on coherence and concentration, and distills that teacher into the tail-class CAMs. A theoretical analysis shows that this suppresses shortcut reliance. The method **consistently improves strong baselines** on long-tailed benchmarks.

papers.title: A unified approach for estimation of unnormalized models via Stein operators
papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop a unified framework connecting proper scoring rules and Stein's method for the estimation of unnormalized models. We construct a class of proper scoring rules that encompasses score matching, ratio matching, pseudolikelihood, and noise contrastive estimation. We show that these proper scoring rules naturally induce Stein operators. This connection yields a new construction principle for Stein operators, and enables us to study estimators based on these scoring rules through the geometry associated with the induced Stein operators. Using this geometric perspective, we provide a unified characterization of the asymptotic efficiency of the resulting estimators.
papers.summary: The authors build a unified framework that links proper scoring rules with Stein's method for fitting unnormalized statistical models. Their class of scoring rules includes score matching, ratio matching, pseudolikelihood, and noise contrastive estimation, and **each such rule naturally induces a Stein operator**. This connection gives a new way to construct Stein operators and a common geometric framework for characterizing the asymptotic efficiency of the resulting estimators.

papers.title: BRIDGE: An Acceptance Gate to Block False Improvements in Model Updates, with a Retrospective Clinical Evaluation
papers.abstract: Models are updated repeatedly, and an update that looks better on validation data but not on new data is a false improvement that can misguide clinical decisions. The naive rule accepts every positive validation gain and is optimistic when the same data choose and judge the update. BRIDGE is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that decides each update from predictions and the available labels, with fixed settings. Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The four settings are (A) 11 new datasets, (B) synthetic tasks, (C) 12 retrospective clinical tasks, and (D) 39 supporting datasets. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. The 95% upper bound on the false-improvement rate is below 5.5%: formal in (B) for independent tasks (3.56%), and conditional on the real data tested (0.33% to 5.40%).
papers.summary: A model update can look better on validation data and still fail to improve on new data, which is risky in clinical settings. `BRIDGE` is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that judges each update on data folds not used to choose it (cross-fitting) and accepts it only when the lower bootstrap bound of the gain exceeds a margin. Across synthetic tasks, public dataset collections, and 12 retrospective clinical tasks, it lowers the false-improvement rate from roughly 12–26% under naive acceptance to about 0–1.7%, **removing 97–100% of false improvements**. Its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times that of the naive rule.

papers.title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding
papers.abstract: While Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), recent studies have shown that final answers do not always depend on the generated rationales. In particular, LLMs may rely on query-specific shortcuts rather than the information provided by their reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate whether context-aware decoding (CAD), an existing contrastive decoding method, can mitigate such shortcut behavior when applied to CoT reasoning. We study this application as Rationale Contrastive Decoding (RCD), which contrasts the next-token distributions conditioned on the query with and without its rationale, amplifying tokens whose likelihood increases due to the rationale. We provide a theoretical interpretation of this decoding rule via a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Experiments across five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RCD improves answer accuracy over standard CoT. Furthermore, intervention analyses using ground-truth and random rationales reveal that RCD increases the behavioral dependence of final answers on the rationale content. Our findings suggest that contrastive decoding offers a simple, training-free approach to mitigating query shortcuts.
papers.summary: With chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, a language model's final answer may rely on shortcuts in the question rather than on its own reasoning steps. The authors apply context-aware decoding, an existing contrastive decoding method, as `Rationale Contrastive Decoding` (`RCD`). `RCD` compares next-token predictions made with and without the rationale and boosts tokens that the rationale makes more likely. They interpret the rule as a KL-regularized reward-maximization objective. Across five reasoning benchmarks, `RCD` **improves accuracy over standard CoT without any training**, and swapping in correct or random rationales shows that answers depend more on the rationale content.

papers.title: Supervision-Adaptive Curriculum and Guarded Anti-Curriculum Learning for Dense Prediction
papers.abstract: Curriculum learning orders samples by difficulty, but difficulty alone does not establish supervision reliability for dense prediction. Easy samples can expose shortcuts, hard samples can be informative, and noisy or ambiguous samples can mislead training. Building on our conference method CurriSeg, we present PaceShift, a stabilize-then-challenge paradigm combining supervision-adaptive curriculum selection with guarded spectral post-training. A learning-dynamics view motivates separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and applying spectral challenges after stabilization. The first phase estimates reliability from available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction certainty. Temporal statistics guide sample weighting, while pixel-uncertainty weights reduce the early influence of uncertain regions. The second phase ranks predictions from multiple spectral views using supervision agreement, robustness, reference consistency, and penalties. A pairwise preference objective measured against the frozen Phase-I reference, together with an anchor, refines the prediction. The framework supports full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Experiments across context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), broader dense-prediction tasks, and foundation-model and cross-modal adaptations show accuracy gains. Targeted diagnostics indicate improved pooled calibration and corruption robustness in the evaluated settings. PaceShift preserves the deployed architecture and adds no inference computation. Code will be publicly released.
papers.summary: Curriculum learning orders training samples from easy to hard, but for dense prediction tasks such as segmentation, difficulty does not tell you whether a sample's labels are reliable. `PaceShift`, which extends the authors' earlier `CurriSeg`, trains in two phases. The first weights samples by estimated label reliability and down-weights uncertain pixels early on, and the second refines predictions with a guarded preference objective across multiple spectral views, measured against the frozen first-phase model. The framework works with full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-generated labels. It **improves accuracy, calibration, and corruption robustness without changing the architecture or adding inference cost**.

papers.title: Beyond the Vote: When Do LLMs Add Value to Retrieval-Based Tabular Classification?
papers.abstract: Retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict tabular labels from similar examples, but it remains unclear whether LLM inference improves on direct voting over those same examples. We address this question by comparing four general-purpose LLMs with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (Distance-KNN) using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets. With the number of demonstrations fixed, enlarging the retrieval candidate pool improves accuracy for all predictors, yet Distance-KNN achieves the highest mean accuracy at every pool size. More detailed analyses reveal that LLM gains are concentrated where retrieved neighbors exhibit low label consensus and vary across models. These gains further depend on the average feature-space distance to the test query: under low label consensus, some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN in close and intermediate neighborhoods, but all fall behind on average in the most distant group. Complementary experiments on the number of demonstrations, prompt formulation, retrieval representation, and label-balanced demonstration selection largely preserve the overall findings. These results characterize when LLM inference adds predictive value beyond distance-weighted voting in retrieval-based tabular ICL.
papers.summary: Retrieval-based in-context learning lets a language model classify a table row from similar labeled examples, but it is unclear whether the model does better than simply voting over those same examples. The authors compare four general-purpose language models with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (`Distance-KNN`) on identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular datasets. **`Distance-KNN` achieves the highest mean accuracy at every retrieval pool size.** Language-model gains appear mainly when the retrieved neighbors disagree on the label and lie close to the query, and they vanish for the most distant neighborhoods.

papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-late, a pair of 0.6B and 9B multilingual and multimodal late-interaction models. Both models achieve state-of-the-art results within their respective size classes across a range of text, image, and visual document retrieval benchmarks. On visual document retrieval tasks, pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b is competitive with models several times larger than itself. The models are trained via representation distillation from an 18B teacher. Consequently, they share an embedding space that supports asymmetric deployment: documents can be indexed with the 9B model and queried with the low-latency 0.6B model. Both models are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/perplexity-ai/pplx-embed-v2.
papers.summary: `pplx-embed-v2-late` is a pair of multilingual, multimodal late-interaction retrieval models with 0.6B and 9B parameters, both distilled from an 18B teacher. Both achieve **state-of-the-art results for their size** on text, image, and visual document retrieval benchmarks, and the 0.6B model is competitive with much larger models on visual documents. Because the two models share an embedding space, documents can be indexed with the 9B model and queried with the faster 0.6B model. The models are publicly released.

papers.title: Geometric knowledge spaces, Attention pairing and Architectures
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a geometric approach to deriving attention mechanisms and exploring potential new transformer architectures. We begin by formalizing the notions of knowledge worlds and attention pairings, then demonstrate how this framework naturally leads to the architectures of standard attention, causal attention, linear attention, tensor attention, and recurrent neural networks. Finally, we introduce several new geometric spaces that may inspire novel neural network architectures.
papers.summary: The authors propose a geometric framework for deriving attention mechanisms, based on formal notions of knowledge worlds and attention pairings. They show that **standard, causal, linear, and tensor attention, as well as recurrent neural networks, all fall out of this framework**. They also introduce several new geometric spaces that could inspire new neural network architectures.

papers.title: RCSD: Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Domain-Specific Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by employing a compact draft model to propose candidate tokens that are verified in parallel by a target model. Conventional training relies on soft-label distillation, which forces the draft model to mimic the target's full output distribution, including high-entropy regions that degrade acceptance rates and increase early rejection risk. We propose RCSD (Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Speculative Decoding), a training framework that aligns draft model optimization with the system-level objective of maximizing acceptance length. RCSD leverages naturally occurring accepted and rejected sequences during speculative inference to construct implicit preference pairs, with masked loss to avoid penalizing target-aligned tokens. Evaluated across multiple benchmarks, RCSD improves average acceptance length by 35% over HASS and achieves 1.35x faster end-to-end inference than HASS on practical workloads, without compromising generation quality.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a small draft model propose tokens that a larger target model verifies in parallel. Draft models are usually trained by soft-label distillation, which forces them to copy the target's full output distribution, including high-entropy regions that lower acceptance rates. `RCSD` (Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Speculative Decoding) instead trains the draft model to maximize acceptance length directly. It builds implicit preference pairs from the sequences that are accepted and rejected during normal speculative inference, and masks the loss so tokens already aligned with the target are not penalized. Across several benchmarks it improves average acceptance length by **35% over `HASS`** and runs end-to-end inference 1.35x faster on practical workloads without hurting generation quality.

papers.title: Are Joint-Embedding Predictive Objectives Effective for Longitudinal EHRs?
papers.abstract: Masked language modelling (MLM) is the dominant pretraining objective for transformer encoders applied to longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). However, reconstructing individual events may overemphasise noisy or weakly informative observations and does not explicitly encourage learning higher-level patient states. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) instead learn by predicting representations in latent space and have shown strong performance in a variety of domains. In this paper, we investigate to what extent JEPA can be adapted to EHR sequence representation. Our empirical investigation using MIMIC-IV shows that although all three of our JEPA formulations train stably without representational collapse, they consistently underperform standard MLM. We find that target size, not target heterogeneity, increases prediction error, yet reducing the target size does not recover downstream performance. This suggests that stable latent prediction alone is insufficient for competitive EHR representation learning and highlights the challenge of defining clinically meaningful latent targets for EHR.
papers.summary: Transformer encoders for longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) are usually pretrained with masked language modelling (`MLM`). Reconstructing individual events this way can overweight noisy observations instead of learning higher-level patient states. The authors adapt Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (`JEPA`), which predict representations in latent space, to EHR sequences and test three formulations on `MIMIC-IV`. All three train stably without representational collapse but **consistently underperform standard `MLM`**. Larger prediction targets raise prediction error, yet shrinking the targets does not recover downstream performance, which suggests that defining clinically meaningful latent targets is the main obstacle.

papers.title: Residual-Based Causal Discovery via Pretrained In-Context Quantile Regression
papers.abstract: Residual-based causal discovery assumes that each variable is generated from its parents and an independent noise source. It estimates this noise and tests its independence from candidate causes. For identifiable functions such as additive-noise models (ANMs) and the broader class of location-scale noise models (LSNMs), this principle identifies the causal direction, as only the causal model admits this independence. Existing LSNM methods rely on parametric assumptions to obtain standardized residuals, risking model misspecification. In contrast, the RESIT-framework allows for nonparametric estimation of residuals to iteratively identify sink nodes, but was proposed for ANMs. To close this gap, we propose Loscar, an extension of RESIT to LSNMs that estimates the conditional mean and scale via quantile regression, enabling pretrained tabular foundation models as plug-in estimators. We compare it with a feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) variant, which is consistent given suitable basis functions. Across bivariate and multivariate causal-discovery benchmarks, in-context quantile regression substantially outperforms FGLS with flexible function classes, particularly for multivariate causes.
papers.summary: Residual-based causal discovery infers causal direction by estimating each variable's noise term and testing whether it is independent of the candidate causes. The nonparametric `RESIT` framework was designed for additive-noise models, while existing methods for the broader location-scale noise models (LSNMs) rely on parametric assumptions that risk misspecification. `Loscar` extends `RESIT` to LSNMs by estimating the conditional mean and scale through quantile regression, so pretrained tabular foundation models can be plugged in as in-context estimators. On bivariate and multivariate benchmarks, **in-context quantile regression substantially outperforms a feasible generalized least squares baseline**, especially when there are multiple causes.

papers.title: Phase Transitions in Learning Driven by Extremal Data
papers.abstract: We study an extremal regression problem, an example of multiple instance learning (MIL), where the predictors are given as multisets, called bags. The bag elements (called instances) possess hidden labels which are pooled to produce an observed bag-level label. Max pooling is common in MIL applications, but gives rise to vanishing gradients. To handle this, modern MIL pipelines approximate the max with a softmax, treating the sharpness as a learnable parameter, denoted $\lambda$. When the max pooling model is the true data generating process, learning will be successful when $\lambda$ is increased during gradient descent, thereby driving the dynamics into regions of parameter space with vanishing gradients. To understand the conditions under which gradient descent breaks down, we study a minimal model and derive a low dimensional projection of the gradient flow in the joint limit of large bags $n$ and high dimension $d$ with $\alpha=\ln n/d$ fixed. The flow has two distinct phase transitions: an intrinsic freezing transition related to the random energy model of disordered systems, and a retrieval transition occurring in modern Hopfield networks. Numerical simulation confirms both the phase diagram and the convergence of the finite-size training gradient to its predicted asymptotic form.
papers.summary: In extremal regression, a form of multiple instance learning (MIL), each input is a bag of instances whose hidden labels are max-pooled into one observed label. Max pooling causes vanishing gradients, so practical pipelines replace it with a softmax whose sharpness is learned during training. The authors analyze a minimal model in the joint limit of large bags and high dimension and derive a low-dimensional description of the gradient flow. That flow shows **two distinct phase transitions**: a freezing transition related to the random energy model of disordered systems, and a retrieval transition like the one seen in modern Hopfield networks. Numerical simulations confirm both the phase diagram and the predicted asymptotic gradient.

papers.title: Block Diffusion for Longitudinal EHR: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Representation Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models have proved effective for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but impose strictly sequential generation on trajectories containing temporally clustered and interdependent clinical events. We investigate block-based masked diffusion (BD) as an alternative on MIMIC-IV under matched tokenisation, context length, model capacity, and evaluation conditions. Across block sizes, BD exhibits a clear quality--efficiency trade-off, with small-block configurations retaining much of the predictive performance of AR while enabling substantially faster inference. A representative $B{=}8$ configuration achieves approximately $1.43\times$ faster evaluation. Although generative rollout remains below AR in most settings, frozen linear probes on BD and AR representations achieve near-identical performance across clinical prediction tasks, indicating that BD learns comparably informative clinical representations. Increasing the denoising budget yields diminishing returns, while alternative decoding strategies provide limited gains. Overall, our results show that block diffusion is a viable and computationally attractive approach to longitudinal EHR modelling, with further improvements in iterative decoding offering a promising route toward closing the remaining generative performance gap.
papers.summary: Autoregressive models work well for zero-shot prediction from longitudinal electronic health records, but they generate clinical events strictly one at a time even though those events often arrive in clusters. The authors compare block-based masked diffusion against autoregressive models on `MIMIC-IV`, holding tokenisation, context length, model size, and evaluation conditions fixed. Small block sizes keep much of the autoregressive model's predictive performance, and a block size of 8 evaluates about **1.43x faster**. Generative rollout still trails the autoregressive model in most settings, but linear probes on frozen representations from the two models perform almost identically across clinical prediction tasks. More denoising steps and alternative decoding strategies yield only small gains.

papers.title: Stochastic Pruning of the DPO Computation Graph: 1.4x Faster Training and Lower Peak Memory
papers.abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
papers.summary: Direct preference optimization (`DPO`) spends compute on output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so supervising fewer tokens does not by itself make training cheaper. The proposed framework randomly selects response positions to score, response prefixes to execute, and preference branches to backpropagate through, and it makes each selection before the corresponding operation so that the skipped work is never computed. Inverse-probability weighting gives a conditionally unbiased gradient estimator for the single-branch case. Position and sequence pruning mainly reduce peak memory, while branch pruning gives a **1.426x step-time speedup** and cuts training time by about 30% compared with stock `DPO` across two model families, at the cost of slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores.

papers.title: PACE: Periodic and Channel-Aligned Encoding of Four-Bit Recurrent States
