papers.summary: Coding agents often explore and test extensively and still produce failing patches, and existing steering methods rely on costly periodic reviews or on monitors that only react to anomalous behavior. `PAUSE` intercepts the agent's first source-code edit, which happens at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, and has a separate Planner read the task and pre-edit transcript to write one repair plan, after which the original agent resumes with its context intact. With `Qwen3-coder` as the agent and `GPT-5.6 Sol` as Planner, online steering **improves resolution by 16.8% on `SWE-bench Verified`** in `OpenHands` and by 14.7% on `SWE-bench Multilingual` in `SWE-agent`. It also beats a rule-triggered advisor at similar cost, matches `SICA`'s periodic overseer at about 11-15% of its Planner cost, and offline recovers 35.4% of eligible failed tasks.

papers.title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.
papers.summary: This review traces methods for extracting materials data and knowledge from the scientific literature, from rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer encoders to large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems that handle text, tables, and figures. It covers downstream uses such as queryable databases, knowledge graphs, materials question answering, AI co-scientists, and closed-loop discovery with autonomous laboratories. The authors assess the resulting datasets' extraction accuracy and computational cost, and **offer practical guidelines for building more reliable extraction pipelines**. Open challenges they identify include sample-level extraction of structure-property-processing-performance relationships, the lack of benchmark datasets, and inconsistent terminology.

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of Learner Errors on Social Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing social bias benchmarks evaluate large language models mostly on fluent, well-formed English, reflecting native speaker usage and leaving non-native writers unrepresented. To address this gap, we investigate how grammatical errors by non-native writers affect social bias. We develop a controlled framework that injects common learner errors into prompts and apply it to three bias benchmarks covering stereotype alignment and demographic preference across gender, race, and religion. We find that grammatical errors increase bias, and the effect grows with the error rate. Among the four common error types we consider, preposition errors produce the largest and most consistent increase in stereotype alignment. Our analysis suggests that errors increase bias when they are more likely to interfere with comprehension. Finally, fine-tuning on erroneous texts reduces the bias increase caused by grammatical errors. Our findings show that bias evaluations based exclusively on well-formed prompts may underestimate the bias experienced by users whose English contains grammatical errors.
papers.summary: Social bias benchmarks for large language models almost always use fluent English, which leaves out non-native writers. The authors inject common learner grammatical errors into prompts from three bias benchmarks covering gender, race, and religion, and find that **errors increase bias, with the effect growing as the error rate rises**. Preposition errors produce the largest and most consistent increase in stereotype alignment, which suggests errors matter most when they interfere with comprehension. Fine-tuning on error-containing text reduces the effect, and the authors conclude that evaluations using only well-formed prompts may underestimate the bias these users experience.

papers.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
papers.abstract:
Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$.
  For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.
papers.summary: Haussler's covering lemma gives the sharp metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes, and the authors prove a sharp global dynamic (sequential) analogue for bounded real-valued classes under normalized l_p distance, for every p from 1 to infinity. A single fixed family of deterministic causal experts of size at most (C/ε^p)^d, where d is the sequential fat-shattering dimension, covers every target on every sequence for every horizon, and a matching lower bound holds. For p=2 this **resolves the horizon-independent sequential l_2 covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari**, and for p=1 it settles open questions about binary classes in terms of the Littlestone dimension. The proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules with shared-parent routing to remove the logarithmic overhead.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Detecting Satirical Code-Mixed Sentences
papers.abstract: Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.
papers.summary: The authors study how code-switching affects satire detection in Romanian, an under-resourced language. They generate over 600k synthetic code-mixed sentences mixing Romanian with English, German, French, and Italian, using four methods, to build `CS-SeLeRoSa` and a human-adjudicated gold set, `CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold`. Older open models degrade to 37-55% macro-F1, while `Gemma 4 31B` reaches 68.1% zero-shot, close to `GPT-5 mini` at 69.5%. Fine-tuning raises `Gemma 4 31B` to **77.5% on the synthetic set and 72.6% on the gold set**, ahead of frontier zero-shot baselines.

papers.title: Tractable Inference with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates in computational science often require not only accurate predictions but also expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants. Conventional neural networks, including Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), generally evaluate these quantities through Monte Carlo sampling or multidimensional quadrature, making repeated inference costly, particularly in high dimensions. We introduce KANs with Tractable Operators for Uncertainty and Constraints (TOUCKANs), whose finite-degree polynomial outer functions yield a decomposable sum--product representation. Under factorizing input measures, expectations and higher moments then reduce algebraically to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional leaf integrals. Independent and shared inner-block variants form a parameter-efficiency hierarchy, and a universal-approximation proof for its most restricted member extends to the complete class. The same deterministic operators allow conserved integrals and normalization to be imposed throughout training. Across uniform and Gaussian benchmarks through 50 dimensions, deterministic mean and variance errors remained below the median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case. TOUCKANs also conserved Cahn--Hilliard mass to machine precision and imposed normalization and orthogonality through deterministic moments, enabling joint computation of the lowest four Schr\"odinger eigenpairs in two, three, and five dimensions. TOUCKANs therefore connect KAN approximation with tractable probabilistic circuits, making statistical operators and integral constraints directly available within an expressive neural surrogate.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates in computational science often need expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants, which usually require costly Monte Carlo sampling or quadrature. `TOUCKANs` are Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) with finite-degree polynomial outer functions, which gives them a decomposable sum-product form. Under factorizing input measures, moments reduce to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional integrals, and the same operators can enforce constraints during training. On benchmarks up to 50 dimensions, **deterministic mean and variance errors stayed below median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case**; the models also conserved Cahn-Hilliard mass to machine precision and jointly computed the four lowest Schrödinger eigenpairs.

papers.title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
papers.summary: The authors test whether a production multimodal LLM, `Gemini 3.8 Flash` at temperature 0, can serve as the decision stage of a privacy-preserving fall screener for older people living alone. It receives one request per short, low-resolution thermal clip, with sound when available, and its predecessor `Gemini 3.7 Flash` answers the same requests. On a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the model caught 69% of held-out subjects' falls and raised no alarm on any of 499 non-fall windows. Over 76 hours of ordinary life in an occupied home it made no false calls but caught only 4 of 9 visible staged falls. **Removing one cautionary sentence from the prompt raised held-out sensitivity from 69% to 83% and home detection to 9 of 9**, at the cost of flagging deliberate lie-downs, while two conventionally trained detectors produced 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home.

papers.title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
papers.abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.
papers.summary: In a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system, a prediction model estimates cost vectors that feed a linear program, and only the resulting decisions are returned to users; the paper studies how an attacker who submits context queries could extract that hidden prediction model. For linear models, the authors give sufficient conditions under which the model can be recovered up to positive scaling from decisions alone, and they build an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with sampling near decision boundaries. As a defense, they perturb decisions only when the predicted cost vector lies near a decision boundary. They prove a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius and **a lower bound on the extraction error of attackers who fit the defended responses**, and experiments on synthetic and real data quantify the resulting security-performance trade-off.

papers.title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
papers.abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning LLMs to hold specific human values is becoming a common post-training step, but evaluations usually check only the targeted value. The authors fine-tune four instruction-tuned LLMs along individual `Hofstede` cultural value dimensions and then measure effects on untrained values and broader behaviours. They find that **value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits**. They argue that value alignment should be paired with broader behavioural evaluation and that more work is needed on where value training belongs in the training pipeline.

papers.title: Privacy in Context Is Being Overlooked in the Age of General-Purpose LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.
papers.summary: In this position paper, the authors argue that research on prompt privacy for general-purpose LLMs is drifting toward a single, unified privacy framework. Drawing on decades of privacy research, they contend that **privacy is inherently contextual, so a one-size-fits-all framework is misleading and can create a false sense of security**. They also argue that any such framework faces fundamental tensions between desirable privacy properties. They recommend application-specific LLM deployment, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy among users.

papers.title: Task-Preserving Multilingual Instruction Tuning for Open-Ended QA in WMT 2026 MIST
papers.abstract: This paper describes our submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. We adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA using organiser-provided data, EuroAlpaca, a multilingual instruction dataset created through task-preserving localisation, and CrossEuroAlpaca, a cross-lingual augmentation that assigns different source and target languages to instructions, contexts and responses. Our system targets open-ended question answering (QA-OEG) in ten shared-task languages represented in the auxiliary data. Under matched decoding, adaptation improves the mean Gemma-4 judge score on target-language QA-OEG by 7.8% relative to the base model. On an additional evaluation using the Aya Evaluation Suite across all shared-task languages, it yields relative gains of 41.5% in macro-averaged ROUGE-L and 2.9% in BERTScore-F1, with larger improvements in target languages. However, these gains are task- and language-specific. Gemma-4 scores improve for QA-OEG and summarisation in the target languages but decline for context-grounded QA there and across all three tasks in the non-target languages.
papers.summary: This shared-task submission adapts `Qwen3-8B` with `LoRA` for open-ended question answering in ten European languages for the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. Training combines organiser data with `EuroAlpaca`, a localised multilingual instruction set, and `CrossEuroAlpaca`, which mixes different languages across the instruction, context, and response. The adapted model improves the mean `Gemma-4` judge score on target-language open-ended QA by 7.8% and macro-averaged `ROUGE-L` on the `Aya Evaluation Suite` by 41.5% over the base model. However, **the gains are task- and language-specific**: judge scores drop for context-grounded QA in the target languages and for all three tasks in non-target languages.

papers.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
papers.abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.
papers.summary: The authors treat a benchmark as an empirical distribution over item difficulty and use that view to formalize two failure modes. In measure mismatch, a benchmark's difficulty distribution differs from the one its users intend to measure; in coverage gaps, missing stretches of the difficulty axis hide real but localized training progress. They propose two diagnostic metrics with theoretical guarantees and apply them to 25 popular benchmarks across 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. They find that **many benchmarks overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions warrant caution, while others leave large parts of the difficulty axis uncovered**, and they introduce `BenchFill`, a difficulty-targeted item-rewriting algorithm that reduces these gaps.

papers.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
papers.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.
papers.summary: `FrontierCS 2` tests whether LLM agents can contribute to frontier computer science research. Each of its 48 tasks takes a published paper's released code, deletes the paper's contribution, and uses the deleted code as the human reference to beat. Agents work inside the inherited repository and may submit patches at any time; each patch gets a development-suite score, while the final grade comes from a private held-out suite compared against the reference. Across 13 domains and 12 agents, **the best agent, `Claude Opus 5.5`, passes 58% of its runs**, no run passes on 16 tasks, and most runs that beat the reference on the combined score still fall short on some individual metric or workload.

papers.title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that build knowledge graphs for multi-hop question answering lose context when text is distilled into discrete symbols, and they create a mismatch between fragmented graph structures and the continuous text LLMs are trained on. `ThreadRAG` instead groups retrieved documents into context-intact semantic nodes and links them with narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. Its `Energy-Driven Pathfinding` step uses energy diffusion to find a query-relevant subgraph and linearizes it into coherent textual evidence paths. On three multi-hop QA benchmarks it gains 14.4% exact match (EM) over text-centric methods on `HotpotQA` and 5.8% EM over the best baseline on `2WikiMultihop`, **while using only 23.3% of the strongest baseline's token cost**.

papers.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
papers.abstract: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
papers.summary: LLM agents struggle to represent uncertainty about a partner's state in text, which hampers theory-of-mind (ToM) reasoning in multi-agent settings. `ToM2Vec` gives each agent a fixed budget of continuous latent reasoning tokens, trained to match a compressed form of the partner's actual thoughts, and at test time those tokens condition the agent's own thoughts and actions. Across collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments, including `Overcooked-AI`, `Hanabi`, `Decrypto`, and multiparty negotiation, it consistently beats the base model and a range of trained and prompted baselines. **Performance drops when the same reasoning is expressed in text**, the training generalizes to partner model families not seen during training, including `GPT-5.4`, and probing indicates the tokens encode partner beliefs, desires, and next actions rather than task-specific information.

papers.title: Towards English - Mizo Legal Machine Translation: Corpus Creation, Analysis, and Benchmarks
papers.abstract: Indian court proceedings are held in English, so speakers of languages with limited translation technology have limited access to them. We present the first English Mizo parallel dataset of Indian court judgments. It contains 13,168 sentence pairs from the Gauhati High Court and the Supreme Court of India. Professional native Mizo translators translated complete documents; sentence pairs were manually aligned, and two independent reviewers checked the results. Our study finds that English words are borrowed in a very selective way: official and legal terms are almost always kept in English, but words for everyday things like actions, situations, and results are usually expressed in native Mizo. Mizo diacritics are also used inconsistently across the corpus. When we fine tune the NLLB 200 1.3B model on our training data, it scores 27.47 BLEU on a balanced legal test set of 1,000 sentence pairs, an improvement of 7.16 BLEU over the base model. However, it still uses English words about three times more often than a human translator does.
papers.summary: The authors release the first English-Mizo parallel corpus of Indian court judgments: 13,168 sentence pairs from the Gauhati High Court and the Supreme Court of India, translated by professional native Mizo translators and manually aligned and reviewed. Their analysis finds that official and legal terms are almost always kept in English, while everyday actions and situations are expressed in native Mizo, and that Mizo diacritics are used inconsistently. Fine-tuning `NLLB-200 1.3B` on the corpus reaches **27.47 BLEU on a 1,000-pair legal test set, 7.16 BLEU above the base model**. The fine-tuned model still uses English words about three times as often as human translators.

papers.title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.
papers.summary: Accuracy alone says little about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, so the authors bring the `InterModel Vigorish (IMV)` into machine learning; it expresses a difference in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. They build three tools on it: `SHAP-IMV` attributes fit gains to features through Shapley-weighted comparisons, `Multi-IMV` evaluates class discrimination, and `Ablate-IMV` assesses components through ablation. Experiments on tabular, image, sensor, and graph data show that feature rankings vary across estimators and that **high one-vs-rest accuracy can coincide with negligible improvement over a null model**. The open-source `imvpy` library accompanies the work.

papers.title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
papers.abstract: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.
papers.summary: The authors test whether legal AI abstains when the correct legal authority is missing, comparing System One decision models, which return a calibrated probability for each option instead of generating text, with six generative LLMs. They extend `CaseHOLD` so that the correct holding is removed in 1,670 of 5,314 items. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items, against 30% for the most cautious decision model. On standard `CaseHOLD` a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) **at 1/55 of the cost**; accepting the LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling decision-model probabilities into `Qwen3-8B` without labels yields a well-calibrated local model.

papers.title: CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents
papers.abstract: Joint reinforcement learning and self-distillation combines task rewards with dense teacher guidance for agent training, but their gradients can partly cancel. A mixing coefficient controls relative scale without selectively removing opposing components. We present CORD, a general framework for conflict-aware optimization of two objectives. CORD separates the choice of protected objective from the condition that triggers projection, and combines the gradients once per optimizer mini-batch. A nearest-point formulation yields a closed-form update and characterizes its first-order effect on the protected objective before optimizer transformations. Gradient diagnostics connect conflict in agent training to lost local optimization progress and motivate selective correction. As a gradient-combination mechanism, CORD can be added to different joint training recipes while retaining their objectives. Across three such recipes, it improves ALFWorld success by 1.5-15.9 percentage points. On WebShop, it improves two of the three pairs, with SDAR rising from 60.7% to 64.6% success. Our analyses explain why protection direction and projection gate must be chosen together, and why the distillation objective and its mixing weight remain consequential after projection.
papers.summary: When LLM agents are trained with both reinforcement learning rewards and self-distillation from a teacher, the gradients of the two objectives can partly cancel, and a simple mixing weight cannot remove only the conflicting components. `CORD` is a conflict-aware optimization framework that chooses one objective to protect, decides when to project away the conflicting gradient, and gives a closed-form nearest-point update once per mini-batch. Added to three existing joint training recipes, it **improves `ALFWorld` success by 1.5-15.9 percentage points** and improves two of three recipes on `WebShop`, with `SDAR` rising from 60.7% to 64.6%. The analysis shows that the protection direction and the projection trigger must be chosen together, and that the distillation weight still matters after projection.

papers.title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
papers.abstract: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.
papers.summary: Most LLM cultural benchmarks are English-centric and test factual recall rather than applied cultural understanding. `CulturalRiddles` collects original, human-written riddles through a participatory community effort, covering 62 cultures, 45 countries, and 51 languages; solving them requires abductive and compositional reasoning, social knowledge, language skill, and culture-specific associations. The authors evaluate 28 LLM configurations with both automatic and large-scale human evaluation and find that **even frontier models reach at most 22% accuracy for some communities**. All artifacts are released with an open process for contributing new languages and cultures.

papers.title: FaultGene: LLM-Assisted Fault-Augmented Test Generation for Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation of Autonomous Driving Systems
papers.abstract:
Reliable validation of autonomous driving cyber-physical systems requires testing not only nominal driving behavior but also failures arising from faults in sensing and embedded computation. Physical road testing provides realistic system behavior but is costly and difficult to reproduce, while simulation enables scalable evaluation but cannot fully capture hardware-dependent behavior and fault propagation. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation bridges this gap by executing the driving stack on real embedded hardware within a simulated environment. However, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains largely a manual process, limiting test coverage, scalability, and efficiency.
  We present FaultGene, an LLM-assisted framework for automated generation of executable fault-augmented tests for HIL fault-resilience validation. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test case that captures the effects of HIL-level fault injection. During offline refinement, semantic-consistency checks and execution-level feedback are used to correct candidates that fail to preserve the intended scenario context or produce the desired fault-induced degradation, and to construct high-quality supervision for fine-tuning. The resulting generator then produces fault-augmented tests directly at deployment time without requiring manually engineered reference executions or repeated refinement loops.
papers.summary: Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing of autonomous driving systems runs the driving stack on real embedded hardware inside a simulator, but preparing fault-injection scenarios for it is still largely manual. `FaultGene` uses an LLM to turn a baseline `Scenic`/`CARLA` scenario and a structured fault specification into an executable, fault-augmented test case. During offline refinement, semantic-consistency checks and execution feedback correct candidates that lose the scenario context or fail to produce the intended degradation, and the corrected outputs become fine-tuning data. The authors claim that **the fine-tuned generator then produces fault-augmented tests directly at deployment time, with no manually engineered reference executions or repeated refinement loops**.

papers.title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.abstract: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. However, decision-makers also require reliable inference on current treatment effects: differences between intervention and reference-arm mean rewards at the present time, rather than historical averages. These objectives conflict: reward maximization favors better interventions, whereas current-effect inference requires continued exploration of potentially suboptimal interventions as outcomes change over time. We characterize this tradeoff for $K$-arm bandits with H\"older-smooth mean rewards of exponent $\beta\in(0,1]$ and constant $L$. Requiring high-probability simultaneous coverage of all current effects by confidence intervals of width at most $w$, we establish matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on expected dynamic regret. Over horizon $T$, our algorithm TRACE (Tracking Rewards and Current Effects) achieves regret of order $\widetilde{O}_{\beta}\left(\sqrt{KT}+K^{\beta/(2\beta+1)}L^{1/(2\beta+1)}T^{(\beta+1)/(2\beta+1)}+Kw^{-2}(1+L^{1/\beta}w^{-1/\beta})\right)$, where the notation hides logarithms and constants depending only on $\beta$. This regret--precision tradeoff separates reward-learning regret from the cost of refreshing current-effect estimates, which remains unavoidable even when one arm is uniformly optimal. An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to realized prediction errors while preserving worst-case guarantees. When within-block drift is negligible relative to sampling error, all observations, including reward-learning observations, can be reused for asymptotically normal pointwise inference and stronger local stationarity yields local asymptotic efficiency. Finally, we show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness and support our theory with extensive numerical experiments.
papers.summary: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor better interventions, yet decision-makers also need valid confidence intervals on current treatment effects, which requires continued exploration of suboptimal arms as rewards drift. For K-arm bandits whose mean rewards drift smoothly over time (Hölder-smooth), the authors prove matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on dynamic regret when every current effect must be covered by a confidence interval of a given width. Their algorithm `TRACE` attains these bounds, and **the analysis separates reward-learning regret from an unavoidable cost of refreshing current-effect estimates that remains even when one arm is uniformly optimal**. Extensions cover adaptive exploration through an empirical-Bernstein e-process and reuse of all observations for asymptotically normal inference, and the authors show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness.

papers.title: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
papers.abstract: Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model's underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.
papers.summary: Aggregate benchmark scores hide what a model can and cannot do. `Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE)` recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and assigns samples to groups, and a behavior-based information gain picks the split. Applied to five models on four benchmarks, it surfaces fine-grained contrasts invisible in aggregate scores; for example, **`Claude Opus 4.6` scores 100% on microeconomic market reasoning versus 83.3% for `GPT-5.4`, but trails it on contract-law reasoning, 77.8% versus 88.9%**.

papers.title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
papers.abstract: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.
papers.summary: Discovering causal structure in high-dimensional nonlinear time series is costly because the number of candidate directed edges grows quadratically with the number of variables. `SCDM` treats each target variable as a meta-learning task and learns a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix, updating only a subset of targets per episode so evidence accumulates without fitting a separate model per target. A post-training readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores. The authors prove that, under stated assumptions, thresholding these scores recovers the true graph when the statistical, optimization, and readout errors are small enough, and experiments on synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, and real benchmarks show **competitive causal recovery with better scalability on large systems**.

papers.title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Long-term memory for multimodal agents must keep fine-grained visual evidence while tracking how entities change across sessions; compressing images into text loses detail, while storing raw images makes identity tracking hard. `MHG-Mem` is a multimodal hypergraph memory whose typed hyperedges group mentions of the same entity, synthesize how its state evolves, and link back to the source visual evidence. A hypergraph-based agentic search chooses an entry layer, traverses the typed hyperedges, and inspects the original observations when fine-grained verification is needed. Across three benchmarks it **improves performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
papers.abstract: Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. If undiscovered until implementation, resolving them is far more costly than addressing them early. Although ambiguity and vagueness are widely studied, less attention has been given to assumptions embedded in requirements that appear clear and reasonable. We propose HiddenLens, a novel six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline and, to our knowledge, the first framework engineered to detect, classify, question, and resolve hidden assumptions rather than merely flag ambiguity. Layer 1 uses BERT attention entropy to localise unresolved spans; Layer 2 uses CoT-prompted LLM reasoning to articulate each assumption and its failure risk; Layer 3 uses fine-tuned BERT to classify assumptions into six non-functional requirement categories: performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain; Layer 4 generates ranked clarification options using FS LLM prompting; Layer 5 enables human validation through confirmation, editing, or rephrasing; and Layer 6 rewrites the requirement using the confirmed resolution, producing an explicit, testable, and traceable requirement. We also introduce the HiddenLens Corpus (HLC), comprising 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions across six NFR categories. Inspired by PROMISE and PURE, HLC addresses the lack of annotated data for this task and is, to our knowledge, the first dataset developed specifically for it. HiddenLens outperforms keyword-based and QuARS-Adapted baselines by 71% and 61%, respectively, achieving an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79; its BERT-based NFR classifier achieves an F1-score of 0.847. These results indicate that HiddenLens can help analysts resolve hidden assumptions before they propagate through software development.
papers.summary: Natural-language software requirements often contain unstated assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints that look reasonable but become costly when they surface late in development. `HiddenLens` is a six-layer pipeline that combines `BERT` and LLMs: it locates unresolved spans via attention entropy, uses chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting to articulate each assumption and its risk, classifies it into one of six non-functional requirement (NFR) categories, proposes ranked clarifications, collects human validation, and rewrites the requirement into a testable form. The authors also release the `HiddenLens Corpus`, 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions. The system **achieves an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79, outperforming keyword-based and `QuARS`-adapted baselines by 71% and 61%**, and its `BERT` NFR classifier reaches 0.847 F1.

papers.title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.
papers.summary: PPO-style clipping in reinforcement learning (RL) for LLM reasoning looks only at the probability ratio of the current token, even though the prefix the token is conditioned on was also generated by the policy. This mismatch matters most for long responses and off-policy training. The authors model autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and show that the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix is the exact importance weight for each policy-improvement term. They then build a prefix-level trust region on the exact reverse-KL quantity r−1−log r, which gives `EPIC`, a sequence-clipping method. In off-policy RL on a sparse mixture-of-experts model, `EPIC` **consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks** and stays competitive with routing-replay methods, without needing expert-routing replay.

papers.title: Every Alarm Has a Cause: An Open Generator of Telecom Alarm Storms with Exact Root Causes, Bound to NORIA-O, RFC 8632 and TMF642
papers.abstract:
Alarm root-cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence.
  We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm -- a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines.
  A one-line rule -- rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm -- takes top-1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.
papers.summary: Research on root-cause analysis of telecom alarms is held back because operator logs are confidential and public benchmarks lack per-incident labels or clear licences. The authors release an open generator instead of a fixed dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the `Internet Topology Zoo`, records the exact root cause and propagation path of every alarm, and binds every field to the `NORIA-O`, RFC 8632, RFC 8345, and TMF642 standards. Across nine baselines, **a one-line rule that ranks the device raising the earliest critical alarm wins top-1 accuracy at 0.650**, beating the authors' own temporal method and an LLM with or without graph queries, and the same rule also wins on real operator alarms. Power-loss faults, where a site goes silent, defeat every method that ranks alarmed devices; only methods that walk the topology to a silent candidate solve them.

papers.title: Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: AI-generated text detectors are increasingly deployed in consequential settings---peer review, education, admissions, journalism, and content moderation---where their outputs directly affect individuals. Yet the strongest detectors are fine-tuned neural classifiers whose decisions are opaque, while transparent alternatives (stylometric and linguistic-feature classifiers) underperform them by wide margins. We present a pipeline that converts a fine-tuned neural detector into a classifier that operates on human-readable concepts. We accomplish this by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) directly on a detector's residual stream, assigning auto-interpretation labels to each SAE feature, and retaining only features whose generated descriptions pass a global fidelity threshold. We then train a lightweight classifier on just the interpretable features. We find that our SAEs recover latent concepts that correspond to highly specific and predictive linguistic "tells" of AI-generated text. Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.
papers.summary: The strongest detectors of AI-generated text are opaque fine-tuned classifiers, while transparent stylometric alternatives trail them badly, which is a problem in high-stakes uses such as peer review and admissions. The authors train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on a fine-tuned detector's residual stream, label each feature with auto-interpretation, keep only features whose descriptions pass a fidelity threshold, and train a lightweight classifier on those interpretable features. The recovered features correspond to specific, predictive linguistic "tells" of AI text. The resulting classifiers are interpretable and **generalize better to out-of-distribution text than both the neural and stylometric baselines**.

papers.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
papers.abstract: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.
papers.summary: Model collapse, the loss of diversity when generative models are trained on their own synthetic data, is studied here through the eigenvalue spectrum of a learned Markov transition operator. Sampling at temperature below 1 acts like repeated sharpening: subdominant eigenvalues move toward the unit circle, the spectral gap narrows, and accumulating data does not appear to stop the drift. The authors analyze `Dreaming Learning`, a regularizer that adds a loss on the model's own samples drawn at temperature above 1, which **keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle**. Spectra measured over 5000 generations match this picture, and the mitigation carries over to `LSTM` language models and a 124M-parameter `GPT-2`.

papers.title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them
papers.abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.
papers.summary: LLM agents with similar success rates can still act very differently, and comparing them usually means running new rollouts. An `Agent Behavior Map` places each LLM-plus-harness combination in a coordinate space using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, so the target agent never has to be run in the environment. The authors derive error bounds linking squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL divergence, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, `ALFWorld`-based coordinates support performance prediction and reveal **behavioral similarities that persist after controlling for success rate and model size, even across model families**; harness-component changes also roughly compose as displacements in the map.

papers.title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
papers.abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.
papers.summary: Large, fast-changing codebases are hard for engineers to understand and hard to feed to an LLM, which needs a method's surrounding repository context as well as the method itself. `Code Comprehensor` combines a code dependency call graph, `CodeScribe` (code-aware LLMs that write hierarchical documentation across the call graph), and `CodeContrast`, a CLIP-style dual encoder trained on that documentation to align text and code embeddings. Retrieved code neighborhoods then ground an MCP-based (Model Context Protocol) LLM orchestrator that answers domain-specific questions. On `OpenCV` and a proprietary 5M-line repository, richer documentation-derived supervision improves text-to-code retrieval, and `RAGAS` LLM-as-a-judge evaluation gives **above 90% faithfulness**.

papers.title: GuideEvolve: Self-Evolving Agent Framework with Expert Guidance and 3Ts Mechanisms
papers.abstract: This study introduces GuideEvolve, a self-evolving agent framework incorporating expert guidance and three autonomous regulatory mechanisms, collectively termed the 3Ts: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback, and Termination by choice. The framework addresses critical limitations in extant self-evolving agent paradigms through dual innovations: (1) a task-specific expert-evaluation-driven evolutionary pipeline, and (2) the integration of 3Ts mechanisms to facilitate cognitive optimization, performance recovery via temporal rollback, and adaptive termination protocols. Empirical validation across the MGSM and MMLU benchmarks demonstrates that GuideEvolve attains performance metrics comparable to current state-of-the-art models (89.8% accuracy versus G\"odel Agent's 90.6% on MGSM; 89.1% versus 87.9% on MMLU), while exhibiting notably reduced variance (25-59%) and enhanced robustness. Furthermore, the framework achieves a 100% evolution success rate, superior to the baseline's 82%, diminishes required optimization iterations by approximately 50% (from 30 iterations in baseline to 15.1 and 13.4 across tasks), and provides improved stability for production deployment.
papers.summary: `GuideEvolve` is a self-evolving agent framework that drives its evolution with task-specific expert evaluation and adds three regulatory mechanisms: Think Fast and Slow, Throwback (rollback to recover from performance drops), and Termination by choice. On `MGSM` and `MMLU` it roughly matches the `Gödel Agent` (89.8% versus 90.6% on `MGSM`; 89.1% versus 87.9% on `MMLU`) while reducing variance by 25–59%. The authors also report a **100% evolution success rate against the baseline's 82%** and about half as many optimization iterations.

papers.title: ExGrad: Beyond Suppression - Explicit Clean-Gradient Subtraction in Adversarial Training
papers.abstract: Adversarial training derives updates from surrogate losses, but source-loss descent does not directly characterize an update's effect on adversarial margins. We introduce ExGrad (extrapolative gradient recomposition), which constructs clean-input, adversarial-input, and adversarial-weight-perturbed (AWP) gradients. Virtual steps measure their margin responses, and a globally solvable three-variable problem selects coefficients over a bounded affine domain without nonnegativity constraints. Across affine radii on CIFAR-10, negative clean coefficients rapidly predominate and increase in magnitude with the radius. Cross-zero interventions show that setting the clean coefficient to zero is insufficient: mild subtraction improves PGD-20, while stronger subtraction trades clean accuracy for further PGD-20 gains. In CIFAR-10 WRN-28-4 controls, none of the three candidate-removal variants matches full ExGrad. Projection diagnostics show that negative clean coefficients usually coexist with positive net clean-axis projections, although both decrease as the radius grows. Norm-matched controls indicate that update magnitude alone does not explain the moderate-radius gains. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 show radius-dependent improvements over AWP. On CIFAR-100, ExGrad at $R=0.8$ improves all five reported metrics, including clean and AutoAttack accuracy by 3.84 and 1.75 percentage points. On ImageNet-100, the same radius improves all four robust metrics over both AWP and PGD-AT. These results identify clean-gradient subtraction as a response-revealed update preference whose strength and clean-robust operating point are controlled by the affine radius.
papers.summary: Adversarial training updates come from surrogate losses, which do not directly describe how an update changes adversarial margins. `ExGrad` (extrapolative gradient recomposition) builds clean-input, adversarial-input, and adversarial-weight-perturbation (`AWP`) gradients, measures each one's effect on margins with virtual steps, and solves a bounded three-variable problem for mixing coefficients that are allowed to go negative. The solution consistently favors **subtracting the clean gradient**, with the subtraction growing as the allowed radius grows; mild subtraction improves `PGD-20` robustness, and stronger subtraction trades clean accuracy for more robustness. On `CIFAR-100`, `ExGrad` improves clean and `AutoAttack` accuracy by 3.84 and 1.75 points over `AWP`, with gains also on `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-100`.

papers.title: Stationarity Constraints Improve Both Energies and Densities of Machine-Learned Exchange-Correlation Functionals
papers.abstract: Empirical exchange-correlation functionals are fitted on fixed orbitals but used self-consistently, so better energies often come with worse densities. We show that the Brillouin residual of a trained functional on the Kohn-Sham orbitals of an accurate density controls, to first order, both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing it requires no self-consistent-field solution during training. Trained on 6 energies and 11 CCSD densities, a neural meta-GGA surpasses SCAN in both atomization energies and densities of unseen molecules.
papers.summary: Machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals for density functional theory are fitted on fixed orbitals but used self-consistently, so better energies often come with worse electron densities. The authors show that the Brillouin residual of a trained functional, evaluated on the Kohn-Sham orbitals of an accurate density, controls to first order both the self-consistent density shift and the gap between fitted and self-consistent energies. Penalizing this residual needs no self-consistent-field solve during training. Trained on only 6 energies and 11 `CCSD` densities, **a neural meta-GGA beats `SCAN` on both atomization energies and densities** of unseen molecules.

papers.title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents act on documents. Before an agent can follow a policy, answer a compliance question or file a ticket, some ingestion layer must turn a Word file or PDF into tokens - and that layer is where an agent deployed in the wild silently loses information. We show that one layer is lost by every mainstream converter - the meaning an author encodes in how text looks - and that the loss makes agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. We build a task from 76 real policy documents: recover the requirements the author singled out, scored against the file's own OOXML properties by a deterministic matcher with no LLM judge. Formatting-blind ingestion collapses from micro F1 0.690 to 0.150 (docling) and 0.075 (plain text), a gap that replicates across six answering models from two vendors - five Claude models spanning the Opus, Sonnet and Haiku tiers, and OpenAI's GPT-5.6. An agent that cannot see the cue guesses, and docling's false-positive rate on requirements the author did not flag is four times ours. A span-level leave-one-out localises the loss to two cues - highlight (+0.302) and colour (+0.262), both Holm-adjusted p < 1e-4 - while bold, italic, monospace and strikethrough each sit within +/-0.003 of zero. The same asymmetry appears in PDF. Colour is also the cue no mainstream converter preserves and no parsing benchmark scores, and it is common: 32.8% of 6,460 documents carry a deliberate colour or highlight, 10.3% on an obligation. A pre-registered test shows that typing a cue for the agent adds +0.085 beyond merely preserving it (Holm-adjusted p = 0.049). We validate the labels against rendered page images through an independent modality (kappa = 0.72) and bound what wording alone can achieve (AUC 0.664). For agent builders the practical finding is that ingestion, not reasoning, is where this reliability is won or lost, and that the fix is cheap and measurable.
papers.summary: Enterprise agents read Word and PDF files through an ingestion layer, and every mainstream converter drops the meaning authors encode in visual formatting, which leaves agents confidently wrong rather than visibly incomplete. On a task built from 76 real policy documents, scored deterministically against the files' own OOXML properties, **formatting-blind ingestion drops micro F1 from 0.690 to 0.150 with `docling` and 0.075 with plain text**; the gap holds across six answering models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Leave-one-out analysis traces the loss almost entirely to highlight and colour, while bold, italic, monospace, and strikethrough contribute almost nothing, and 32.8% of 6,460 surveyed documents use deliberate colour or highlight. A pre-registered test shows that explicitly typing the cue for the agent helps beyond merely preserving it, which places this reliability problem in ingestion rather than in reasoning.

papers.title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
